LADIES AND GENILEMEN, In fulfilment of a promise made several months ago that I would, if called upon by the working people of St. John's Ward, again figut your cause, and in response to the request of your deputation that I should fulfil that promise. I now have great pleasure in placing myself and services at your disposal lint I only consent to do so as a free and inde- pendent capdidate- I will not agree to become the nominee or tool of any party, politic tl, religious or otherwise, and if elected I will not laoin myself responsible to anybody except the electors who reposed their trust in me. Nevertheless I am prepared to give my honest and faithful sapport to any member or section of the Council whom I believe are doing good work for the general welfare Of the town and who will endeavour to procure for ritrelasses a fair and equal share of the municipal services in proportion to the rates they pay. I am pleased to see Vast by my exposing the scandalous condition of your Ward and the wretched state of your streets, I forced the Corporation to begin to make some improvement, that is to say, the paving of 'Winifred-street and better lighting of the neighbourhood, and by the same means I hope to force the esessment Committee to levy the rates equally on all property, thereby relieving the over- burdened working people, and making the wealthy monopolies bier their equal burdens of the town's expenses. I strongly object to the expenditure of public money at the present time on alterations to Warring- ton Bridge or any other such undertaking until the more urgent necessities of your district have had attention, such as better paving. cleansin.r, and lighting of the streets where working people ccave to live,a healthy recreation ground for your children to play in. a branch library and reading room in St, John's Ward for the instruction and enlightenmen4 of the young people, and an efficient circular tram- way service through your district, which would be a really profitahle enterprise as well as a much-needed Improvement to the neighbourhood ; all these things are much more necessary than the widening of those roads which lead out of the town to the handsome Suburbs, where so many of Our present Councillors and Alderman have their mansions and rasidenees. I shall continue to insist upon a full and searching enquiry into the alleged illegal trading with the Corporation by the members or their friends. I demand this in the interest of the town as well as in the interest of the accused and their accusers, but I don't ask for enquiry merely as an election cry. I mean a real enquiry held immediately ; for I am fully convinced that no real reforms can be effected until the I-resent campaign of abuse and scurrility has been brought to an end. I again declare that I object to all outside interfer- ence in our town's affairs. by MEN WHO HAVE NO DIRECT OR INDIRECT INTEREST IN US EX- CEPT TO SECURE THEIR OWN FAME OR NOTORIETY, AT THE EXPENSE OF OUR GOOD NAME. I am also opposed to all "cliques " and parties who domineer over our Council and our townspeople • no matter what title they assume for themselves either to-day or in the future and whose only aim seems to be the accomplishment of their own selfish ends, or the tyrannical display of their power. If von do me the honour of electing me as your Ward's representivive, I hops to be able to do some- thing for you in a more useful and prattical direction than &laming my fellow citizens. I shall strive to promote the growth and increase of established industries,and to encourage new enterprises to begin the erection of new factories in our town,bringingthe working:classes more opportunitiesof earning honest wages by honest labour. The increase of employment would, by causing the increase of buildings, raise the total ratr.ble value of the town and would do more permanent good to the community than all the cheese paring " economies which are now being paraded as the cure for our present high rates. I would insist that all Corporation Contracts should be given, so far as is possible to Warrington Manu- facturers and Tradesmen, when their tenders are towel or as low as those coming Iron. outsiders, I mh oepne rteoe es ievei ni in tah faire n lairy gt uwr gael nCrOtrhpeoirra twi onnr kw. oarnkd- I wluhi make it a condition that all Corporation Con- trze-ors must pay the recognised rate of wages. In conclusion, ladies and gentlemen if you honour me by election to the Town Council I will faithfully edgonaalll treatment my power tohtaot sgei cvue to oo r .31Sotr.e John l 'tsh yWaanrdd aristocratic parts of the town and this I am sure you are not getting at present. I aek you therefore to suppert me, YOUR I NDE- PKNOENT CANDIDATE with yi ur votes on the Polling day, and thus place in my banns the power to uphold your cause against all comers. I am Ladies and Gentlemen, Yours ever faithfully, JOHN MAGINN. 85, Bridge street, Warrington. ,

If you agree to this course there is no reason ! why the case should not be removed forthwith." The CLERK said there was also a long letter written by pr. Braide to the Medical Officer of Health protest- ing against the course taken in the matter, but he did not think it necessary to read it. It transpired that the ease was one which could not be removed now as it would be dangerous to remove the patient. There was great difficulty attending the whole matter as related in the report of the Master. He (the Clerk) did not know what the Town Clerk might have read or seen, or what new idea had presented itself to• him, to lead-him to break away from the course which had been followed for so many years. Personally he (the Clerk) adhered to the view that what had been done in the past was correct and that the Borough hospital authority was bound to admit the cases that arose within the Borough. The Board paid rates to the Borough on an assessment of £1,204 and were entitled to the same privileges as any other ratepayer. With regard to the suggestion of the Town Clerk's that the opinion of the Local Government Board should be taken, he (the Clerk) would not advise the Board to take that step. He would suggest that Messrs. Jeans and Son, solicitors, be engaged on behalf of the Board. Messrs. Jeans represented the Board in athe important case brought by the Newton Commis- sioners against the Board in an objection of this kind, when the Judge decided in favour of the Board on all points. Personally, he had not the least doubt that the Judgment of the superior courts would be in favour of the Board. Meanwhile he would try to ascertain from the Town Clerk under what circumstances he deviated from the old arrangement. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said it occurred to him that the suggestion of the Town Clerk's was an eminently reasonable and equitable one. There was a special Act of Parliament in which it was laid clown that the Local Government Board could act as arbitrator in a matter of this kind. Surely in a dispute of this kind a between an urban authority and a rural authority, the legal advisers of the Local Government Board were competent to give a sound opinion. He confessed it ' seemed to him that the suggestion of the Town Clerk that the matter should be referred to the Local Govern- : ment Board was an equitable one. No reason had been put forward to suggest that it was not an equitable one. The CLERK pointed out that the officers of the Local Government Board were not law officers of the Crown. The point he would raise—and it was probably one that had not been laid before the Local Government Board— was that inasmuch as the maintenance charges for all inhabitants of the Borough who were removed to the idtkintions diseases hospital came out of the public rate, 1.. ici'livhich the Board contributed on a large assessment, lvdrilaould they be excluded from the advantages given tizajutz inhabitants? After this simple act of piety and affection her thoughts turned once more to the living. She ordered the carriage, and told the man half groom, half gardener, to drive her dowr to the station. She intended to take the next train to Llanfihangel, and tell Tredegai the result of her interview with the sergeant of police. It was now three o'clock in the afternoon, and if she did not catch the 3.3! train, she would not be able to get back thai night. Before the carriage came round to the doot however, there was the sound of wheels on the drive, and a loud ring at the bell. She slipped into the hall and caught the old butler as he was on his way to answer the door.

"I cannot see anyone, James," she said hurriedly. "Say I am not at home," and she slipped back into the drawing room. Through the half open •door she heard the butler arguing politely with someone whe insisted in coming in. At that moment there was the sound of the carriage coming round to take her to the station,and she saw that her lie would be patent to the visitor. "Very well," she heard a feminine voice say decidedly; " I will wait here till Miss Morgan comes out. I must -see her. Per- haps you will kindly take in my card." _ _ _ _ _
A few moments -later the old man hobbled into the room and handed a card to Mavanwy. She glanced at it, and told the butler to show the lady in. It was Cynthia Cantrip.
BY HARRIS BURLAND, AUTHOR OF 'DACOBRX,E7C.

had made him a wealthy man. When Mavanwy had finished, Cynthia put her fingers to her throat, and drew out the half of the gold disc which she wore suspended from a thin. gold chain. "Take she said, passing the chain over her nead. . " It is the only thing Emrys has ever given me. I have no right to it. I can only nope that when the two halves are once more in the por,session of the same person, all the sorrow and death connected with the treasure will come to an end."

Mayanwy took it in silence, but there were tears in her eyes, and her 'hand stole gently to Cynthia's fingers. The latter looked away from the girl's face, and seemed to be entirely absorbed by the scenery through which they were passing.

The latter entered with a faint flush on her cheek, and a dangerous sparkle in her eyes. "You have a faithful servant," she said drily. Then she saw Mavanwy's face, white and drawn with all the suffering she had been through, and she noted the black dress, and remembered that this was no time for bitter words. She advanced with out- stretched hands, and taking hold of Mavanwy's cold white fingers, leant forward and kissed her on the cheek.

"Forgive me, dear," she said almost tenderly; "I have no wish to intrude on your sorrow. I only heard an hour ago that you had returned. It is natural that I should wish to see you." "Would you have been very sorry if I had never returned," said Xavanwy in a low voice.

" I should have been very sorry," Cynthia replied. " During the last few days the thought of your death has been very horrible to me. lam no,t a good woman, Mavanwy, but now that Emrys is safe and has passed out of both our lives, a voice has whispered to me that I have done both you and him a great wrong. Every night I have seen your face, white and still, every night I have looked on your body, bruised, torn, and broken. And all the time he has stood by your side, and there was that in his eyes that will haunt me to the day of my death. Ido not like you, Mavanwy. I could never be much troubled about your happiness. But I cannot bear that he should go through life in misery. I did my best to tempt him from you. I have failed. He will never, love me. I had almost made up my mind, although I thought you to be dead, that I would never see him again. Men like Emrys do not love more than once, and he would love you, even if you were in your grave. The news of your return to life has only confirmed the resplui- tion. I did not know I was so weak. But somehow the pity of it all has touched my heart. I seem to have come into your lives both to help and to destroy you. lam only a woman after all. I might have been all good or all evil. As it is I have been both. I wish now to blot out the evil. Perhaps this is only a passing qualm of consciousness. To-morrow I may desire to blot out the good. But to-day I have come to give you back your lover. You must trace him at any aost. I have money here with me," and pulling out a thick packet of bank notes, she leld them out to Mavanwy. "What do you mean ? " gasped Mavanwy. There was a knock at the door and the butler mtered.
"There is onl3i just time to catch the train, Nliss," he said.

' Et does not matter," she answered. Tell Williams, I will drive all the way to Llanfihangel." The man left the room. "What do you mean, Cynthia ? " she repeated eagerly. "I mean," Cynthia replied slowly, "that I release you from your oath, and that you :an marry Emrys Tredegar as soon as you :an find him."

Mavanwy looked at the speaker in astonish- ment, then she moved, towards her, and throwing her arms about her neck, buried her face on her shoulder and burst into tears. Cynthia frowned, and gently disengaged the arms from her neck. Then she took the white face in her two hands and gazed into the tearful eyes.

"You silly child," she said. "Why should you cry. Look at me. There is no tear in my eyes. And yet—l think my heart is broken." And turning away from rviavanwy, the walked over to the door, and laid her hand on the knob. Then she came batk and hdld out the notes. Mavanwy shoqk her head.

"I don't want them," she said in a trem- bling voice. " Emrys is in England still. He came back to look for me when he saw the news. He it was who killed that horrible monster and saved me from death. He is within a few miles of here. lam told by the police that his acquittal is assured." " Emrys here ! " said .Cynthia. "Then you have fooled me—you have—No, no, I don't mean what I say. lam glad that he is here. I shall leave Garth to-night. Now that Walroyd is dead there is no need for my father to stay. We can go up by the night mail. But Emrys here! Tell me all that has happened. You owe me that at least."

"I owe you everything," she said, taking Cynthia's hand and pressing it to her lips. ".May I drive you back to Garth. I must be at Llanfihangel before it is dark." Cynthia glanced at the clock. "You will not do it if you go round through Garth." she said. "I will come with you to Llanfi- hangel. I should like to see Emrys once more. I know it is toolish of me -to cip so, but we women ate fools sometimes. You have much happiness before you, Mavanwy. I have much sorrow. I .should like to come with you—just for the last time." "You shall certainly come," said Mavanwy. "He would like you to come. You have been a good friend to him. Oh, Cynthia, if it was not for—if only things had been other- wise, we should all three be happy to-day— three be friends."

"Let us go," Cynthia said hoarsely, moving towards the door. "We have only just tithe $.9 get to Llanfihangel—before it is dark." Mavanwy followed her from the room and they both stepped into the victoria which was waiting at the door. Cynthia sent her own try, hired from the Tredegar Arms, back to Garth, and instructed the man to tell her fafrher that she should n9t be back till late, and might possibly spend ,the night with Miss Morgan.

As they trotted briskly along the road to Idanfihangel, Mavanwy told Cynthia all that hi happened to her during the last few days. She spoke in a low voice so that the man on the box could not hear, but her story lost nothing of its strangeness and horror by her quiet method of telling it. She remembered Tredegar's warning, and ran over Walroyd's narrative in a few hurried word,

Cynthia was particularly fascinated by the account of the hidden treasure, and she told gavanwy how her father had been employed to dispose of it in London, and that the mere tomniission he received on the transaction

Wlien they reached Llanfihangel they drove to the north end of the parade and told the man to take the horse to the Red Lion and return in an hour's time. Then they des- cended a flight of steps from the parade and made their way along the shingle. It was now long after five o'clock, and the tide was rising. The sun had set almost to the level of the sea, and a great bank of clouds above it glowed with crimson and gold. The cliffs at this part of the coast towered up almost perpendicularly from a narrow belt of sand dotted with great bouldei-S. The walking was easy in comparison with some parts of that rock strewn shore, but Mavanwy was so tired that she could hardly drag her weary limbs across the sand, and more than once Cynthia had to stop and hold her arm to prevent her from falling. At last they passed round a projecting point of the cliff and came in view of the place where Tredegar was hiding. No one looking at it from where they 'stood would have supposed that behind the heap of rock lay the entrance to mile after mile of sub- terranean passages. Even those who crept between the rocks would find themselves faced with a great bank of shingle, and would merely suppose that the small cavern over their heads was a hollow scraped out in the base of the cliff by the ceaseless action of the sea. It was small wonder that no one had even discovered the steps leading to the long passages that lay beyond the barrier of pebbles.

- The two women made their way towards the place, and when they were twenty yards away from it Mavanwy called Emrys' name loudly, three times. She did not care who aeard it now. There was no reply, and the wily sound was the splash of the waves against some large boulders that lay half covered by the sea, and the plaintive cries of some sea- gulls that hovered about the cliffs a hundred feet above her head.

"He is asleep," she said softly. "He must be worn out. I will go and wake him." Mavanwy went close up to the rocks and peered through an opening. She could see the bank of shingle beyond, but the place was empty. She called out to Cynthia, who came forward and stood by her side. "He is not here," Mavanwy said. "Where can he have gone. Ah, perhaps he is beyond the shingle. It would be darker there, a better place to sleep in, and it Would not be so damp—see, the stones are still wet with the last tide."

She slipped through the opening between the rocks, and Cynthia followed her. The latter shivered as she entered the little cavern. It seemed very dark and cold. She thought it very unlikely that anyone would go to sleep in such a place, especially, a man who had had rheumatic fever.
"He is probably, as you say, asleep on the other side of these stones," she said. "You had better call out to him."

Mavanwy went across to the shingle, and climbed up the bank till she reached the opening Tredegar had made. She leant over into the dimly lighted cave beyond, and called his name. Her voice echoed down the long passage, but no one replied. She began to be alarmed though she re-assured herself by remembering that it would take more than the sound of a girl's voice to wake a man who had been for three days without sleep. _ _ _ _ .

Then both the worhen heard the -faint sound of footsteps in the distance, and a look of eager expectation crossed' their faces. The sounds were faint and muffled. Then sud- denly they heard a long rasping cough, and the sound seemed quite close to them, though the footsteps appeared to be a long way off. They had entirely misjudged the distance. The person who had approached so close to them must have worn felt slippers or else walked on his bare feet. They both started. Then they leant over the bank of shingle and peered into the' twilight beyond. Emrys," Mavanwy- 'cried. "It is all right, Ernrys ! I have scch news for you— such splendid news." She stopped. No one answered, but she could hear the sound of breathing. " Why don't you answer, Emrys ? " she continued nervously, and with a tclie vexation in her voice.

Then suddenly something moved on the other side of the shingle, a loud yell of rage broke the silence, two great hairy arms shot out from the gap above the stones, two great hands grasped the two women, and a horrible mass of hair was thrust out into the light. The light of reason had once more vanished from the eyes. James Heatherbutt had relapsed again into insanity.- He drew the two shrieking women towards him, and glared into their white faces. And it was' thus, after an interval of ten . years, that husband and wife were fated to meet again.
CHAPTER XXX,

div.head: "ONE OF THE THREE MUST DIE; BUT
div.p: "ONE OF THE THREE MUST DIE; BUT
WHICH ?"

NEITHZ Et. of the two recognised each other. Cynthia could discern nothing of her hus- band's features in the bruised and horrible face before her, while Heatherbutt's madness clouded his brain and blotted out all recol- lections of the past. The light, moreover, was dim, and Cynthia's back was towards it. The madman drew the shrieking women over the top of the bank of shingle, and flung them down on the floor of the cave beyond. Their voices echoed through the long 'pasage, but could scarcely be heard from tUe shore owing to the intervening rocks and pebbles. They were no mere idle cries of terror, but uttered as loudly as possible in the hope that they might reach Tredegar's ears. Mavanwy knew that he could not be far Off. "Stop that screeching! " growled Heather- butt; and they stopped from sheer astonish- ment at the sound of the voice.

Cynthia had never seen the monster before, but she had understood from Mavanwy's stoiy that it was dumb. Mavanwy herself was as overcome with horror as Tredegar had been when he first heard a human voice crying from those bestial lips. Then a quick flash of hope illuminated her mind. Tf the thing could speak, it was human, and might be moved to pity. "Where is Mr. Tredegar ?" she said, faintly. "I expected to find him here." Heatherbutt laughed wildly, and pointed into the darkness of the passage. Mavanwy's heart grew cold, for there was the ring of madness in that horrible laugh, and she realised that she could expect no pity from a homicidal maniac. Then a horrible thought struck her. -

"Where is he ?" she cried, piteously. "Oh, Cynthia, he is dead—he has been killed !" She struggled to her feet and laid her hands on a piece of sharp rock, prepared to fight for her life. Heatherbutt laughed, and rubbed his hands together with glee. She hurled the

lump of stone at him, and it glanced harmlessly loff his arm. Mavanwy sank to the ground, her feeble strength was exhausted, ary.„l she lay helpless, with her face buried in her hands. Heatherbutt sprang towards her, and picking UP some pieces of cord. began to bitld her l' hand and foot, He did not notice that Cyn- ; thia had drawn something from her hat, and ! was silently dragging herself over the rocky floor towards him. Then he heard, a faint sound behind him, and, turning quickly round, received five inches of a stout. steel hatpin, driven with all the strength of a desperate woman, in the upper part of his arm. Another second, and he would have been too late, and the long weapon would have pierced him through the back to the heart. He sprang to his feet with a yell of pain, and lifting up the wretched woman with the other hand, hurled her down , to the rock with so much force that she lost consciousness. Then he began to pull out the pin from his arm, yelling .horribly. For the point had turned on a bone, and it made a fearful wound as he . dragged it out through the quivering flesh. Heatherbutt's returning madness was now goaded to a wild frenzy, which saw the whole world through a mist of blood, and which only heard a voice calling out to him to slay and spare not. The blood trickled down from his arm, and he sucked the wound savagely with his lips, till there was a crimson froth on his great toothless jaws. He spranc, forward with crooked fingers as though he was about to tear the two women to pieces. Then he suddenly restrained himself, and, , stooping down, he bound Cynthia's hands and feet. When he had accomplished this, he sat down and regarded his two victims with a grin of satisfaction, licking his lips as he saw their prostrate bodies on the ground. Three days ago he would have battered the life out of them in less than a minute. But he had only partially lost the reason that had been restored to him. - Previously he had been a mere wild beast that killed because its natural instinct was to do so. Now he was more than half human—a man with a monomania, with the lust of killing in his heart, and sufficient method in his madness to kill in a way that would give him the most pleasure. And so, instead of falling upon his two victims and destroying them as quickly as possible, as a lion or a tiger might have done, he sat down and contemplated them thoughtfully, trying to think out how he could make them suffer before death released them from their agony, , "Emrys I Emrys ! " murmured Mavanwy. Heatherbutt laughed. In all respects but one he was now a sane man, and hes under- stood everything that was said to him. "Either he is talking, or he is pursuing, or he is on a journey, or peradventure he sleepeth, and must be awaked," he cried out mockingly, calling to mind a verse of the Bible which was familiar to him in the days of his childhood. Mavanwy shuddered. It was terrible to hear ' such words from those lips. She saw that the man still had his wits about him. "Have pity !" she cried, feebly. "We have never done you any harm. Where is he? Oh, Emrys, come quickly! Emrys 1 Emrys !" and she raised her voice to a scream. Heatherbutt laughed again. Then he rose

to his feet and leant over- the barrier of rocks behind him. " Emrys !" he yelled, mimicking her voice. "Come quickly! Emrys ! Emrys I" Then he crawled up the pile of broken slate, and disappeared in the darkness beyond. Ten minutes afterwards Mavanwy heard the sound of something heavy being dragged over the ground, and then Heatherbutt's face appeared over the heap of rock. He has answered you," he said, with a ghastly grin. Mavanwy grew cold as death, and stared at the evil face with, parted lips and a look of horror in her eyes. "He is dead !" she shrieked. dead !" And she tried to struggle to her feet, but fell backwards, and cried out the name of her lover.
"He is

Again Healherbutt laughed. Then he began to remove the rocks from the barrier Dne by one, till he had made a large opening. Then he crawled through, half-lifting, half- dragging something after him. He laid his burden close to Mavanwy. It was Emrys Tredegar, and his eyes were wide open. He was alive, but his hands and feet were bound, and his mouth was gagged with a handkerchief. " Emyrs ! Emrys ! " cried Mavanwy. "Thank God you are alive ! " In the dim light she could hardly see his face, but she heard the creak of the straining cords that bound his hands, and saw the flashing of his eyes. If only she could free him they would all be saved. He would tear this inhuman monster limb from limb. The meeting appeared to amuse Heatherbutt. He dragged Tredegar to the wall and set him with his back against it. Then he arranged the other two in a similar position at distances of two yards apart. He was like a child playing with three dolls. Then he sat down in front of them and rubbed his hands together. The blood was still running from the wound in his arm. Cynthia gave a sigh, and ()Aped her eyes. At the sight of Tredegar she gave a cry of surprise. She had been placed between him and Mavanwy. She leant over towards him, but could not get near enough to whisper in his ear. Then she faced Heatherbutt with flashing eyes. "What is all this foolery," she said. "Do you know that the police are now on your track, that they are coming here this evening to find Emrys Tredegar? They were only half an hour behind us." "So much the more ne-ed for haste," Heatherbutt answered. "I will not detain you longer than I can help. It will be very pleasant for me to see you all die. But I have decided to spare one of you. Do you think you can decide among yourselves which one it will be ? " The three prisoners looked at each other and then on the ground before them. Trede- gar was unable to speak, but he indicated by a motion of his bound hands that he at anyp rate would not take advantage of Heather- butt's offer. "You can kill me," said Cynthia, casting a loving look at Tredegar. You can kill me ! " Mavanwy was silent. Of a truth the madman's offer had been most devilishly devised. None of the three would care to live when the other two were dead. For life would mean nothing to either Mavanwy or Tredegar if one, of them were killed, and Cynthia, who might have found a savage pleasure in seeing the death of the man who had scorned her love, or of the woman who had been her successful rival, had only one thought uppermost in her mind that her own life was worthless, and ought to be the first to be taken. But Tredegar alone grasped the real terror of the situation, namely, that Cynthia was Heatherbutt's wife, but his lips were sealed.

"Come, hurry up," snarled Heatherbutt, stretching out his muscular arms as though he longed to seize something by the throat. They were still all three silent. He chuckled. This was worth a dozen deaths any day of the week. He was sufficiently sane to appre- ciate the difficulties of the situation. He noted the look of love in both women's eyes as they glanced at Tredegar, and he saw that Tredegar only gazed at one of them. "I will decide for you," he cried. "The man shall die, and you, pointing to Mavanwy, shall be the next." He had some hazy recollection that Tredegar was his enemy, and he longed to choke the life out of him. Be- sides, in his animal cunning he realised that if he let the man go, his own life would not be worth a moment's purchase. "No," cried Cynthia. - "You have offered us our choice. Let fate decide. We will draw lots. Hold three pieces of stick, or cord, or anything in your hand. We, will draw them. The one who draws the longest shall live. The one who draws the shortest shall die first. That is fair." Heatherbutt was silent. His brain was trying to grasp Cynthia's words. Then he broke into a laugh and clapped his hands. :` A great game." he cried, " a great game."

But Heatherbutt suddenly stopped in his' advance, and stared wildly round the cavern. Tredegar watched his face, and saw the madness die from the eyes, like the last spark from a glowing ember. This was the moment of his revenge, and he resolved to spare the madman nothing of the horror of the situation: The dead body of Cynthia called for ven- geance. " Where am I ? " said Heatherbutt faintly, "and why do you stand there with your hands like that?"
"My hands are bound," Tredegar replied slowly. "You were kind enough to bind them while I slept. You have just done the foulest deed of your vile life. Look behind

Heatherbutt looked and saw the limp form sf Cynthia Cantrip. He bent down and stared into the wide open eyes. Then he grasped the body and lifted it up so that the light which came over the top of the shingle fell full on the face. The past came back upon him like a wave of fire, scorching all the blood from his body, and stiffening the muscles till it seemed as though they had been dried into strips of bone. "My wife, he muttered in a trembling voice. "My wife—my wife ! " "Your wife," replied Tredegar glancing at Mavanwy, who was still unconscious. Heatherbutt laid the body tenderly on the ground. "My wife," he cried in a voice of anguish, staggering back from the [silent form. Then he sank upon his knees, and began to crawl towalds it, blubbering like a whipped child, and only muttering the words, My wife! Cynthia, my wife! my dear wife! my dear wife 1 " _ _ _

When he reached the side of the dead woman he touched the hair with his fingers and remained silent for quite five minutes, passing his hand over the face and peering into the eyes. Then he bent his head down. and made as though he would kiss the lips. But it seemed as though a sheet IA glass lay between them and his own horrible mouth. He could draw no nearer to them.. .

Then suddenly he rose to his feet with a terrible cry of anguish, and seizing his own throat with his muscular fingers, he literally tore it apart, holding open the gaping flesh, till the blood streamed down his arms, and he rolled over, and fell with a crash to the ground. There was the sound of voices outside, and the footsteps of men on the sand. Tredegar staggered over to the dead body of the woman who had done so much for him, and stooping down kissed her reverently on the forehead, and thanked God in his heart that she had died without knowing the awf•A history of her hutf.band's li[e.

TIIE QUACK "MOTHER'S FRIEND." "Science Siftings" says :—A remarkable inquest has been held at Earlestown,Warrington,and we feel that the verdict of the jury l needs further qualification. "Death from misadventure" hardly, in our opinion, sums up a fatality resulting from administering to a seven-weeks'- old child a preparation containing 15 grains of morphia to the fluid drachm. The mother administered this drug in good faith for flatulency; and seeing that the preparation was labelled with the innocent and promising title of " The Mother's Friend," there will be none to blame her. But a medical witness, Dr. Salomons, declared that death was due to narcotic poisoning, and that the congestion of the lung from which the child was suffering would have been accelerated by the drug. The question is, should so dangerous a " soother " be placed in the way of often ignorant women? We may add that a quack is never a mother's friend.

Then he groped about among" the shingle and found three thin little pieces of stick, dry and brittle as touchwood. He laid them on his palm, and looked at them. They were all of different lengths. But he did not show them to his three victims. Then he placed his hands behind his back, and held out one great hairy fist, from which three short ends of Qtick Protruded. Tredegar was the first to draw, then Cynthia, Ind then Mavanwy took- the last piece. Pi the twilight none of them could see the length that the other held awkwardly it their fettered hands. Then Mavanwy thought she heard a little snap on her left, so faint that it was scarcely audible. Heatherbutt looked at their faces and grinned. He had purposely not shown them the pieces before they drew. They were still ;n uncertainty as to their fate. "Hold them up," he said, and they held up the twigs between two fingers. He went to each and examined the fatal pieces of wood. Mavanwy's was the longest, Tredegar's the next in length, and Cynthia's the shortest of all. But neither Tredegar, nor Mavanwy, nor Heatherbutt knew that half of Cynthia's piece had been snapped off and lay upon the ground by her side. Heatherbutt took Cynthia up in his arms. She uttered the single word " Good-bye " and looked Tredegar straight in the eyes. Mavanwy fainted. Tredegar placed his bound hands to the gag that had silenced him and tore at it with his fingers till the knot at the back of his neck seemed to be Cutting through his spine. Inarticulate sounds broke from his throat. . Then he tried to struggle to his feet. But it was all over in a second. There was no cry, no moan, not a sound, but a faint snap, such as Cynthia herself had made as she broke the twig in her white fingers. Heatherbutt laid the dead body on the ground, and laughed long and loudly.' Then all of a sudden the laughter died away in his throat and he pressed his hands to his forehead, and staggered blindly towards Tredegar. The latter had succeeded in forcing the bandage from his inouth. The corner of his lip was split, and the blood ran down his face. He managed to get to his feet, and leant against the wall panting, and with his great arms uplifted to strike the shaggy figure that was coming towards him, and ward off the fingers that he knew would be soon at his throat.

div.head: EVENTS OF THE WEEE..
div.p: EVENTS OF THE WEEE..
THE DUKE'S SUCCESSOR,

At last Mr. Balfour has finally completed nis Ministry, and one of the most notable of the latest appointments is that of the Mar- quess of Londonderry to be Lord President of the Council, in succession to the Duke of Devonshire. This post, which, though an important one carrying great prestige, does not entail any very onerous duties, Lord Londonderry will combine with his present Post of Minister for Education. The latter office, which was insti- tuted for the first time by Mr. Balfour,was given to him in consequence of the good work
he did as Presi-
dent of the Lon- THE MARQUESS OF LONDON- don School DERRY, NEW LORD PRESIDENT Board. For OF THE COUNCIL. man y_ years

Lord - London- derry had been prominent in politics, though holding no official position in the Cabinet, but it was not till 1900 that he was asked to join the Administration, when the Duke of Norfolk resigned the. office of Postmaster- General in consequence of going out to the front with the Yeomanry. Since then his promotion has been very rapid—first, Post • master - General in 1900, then Minister for Education in 1902, and now Lord President of the Council. The Marquess of Londonderry is a very wealthy and influential peer, who is a great social force., and' a personal friend of the King. Indeed, this very week his Majesty has been his guest , at his splendid country seat, Wynyard Park. His new office gives him considerable advancement in precedence, and now after the blood royal he ranks fifth.

div.head: PREMIER FOOTBALL GROUND.
div.p: THE PREMIER FOOTBALL GROUND.

This is the day when football grounds are not only criticised in point of the play- ing quality of the turf. Their habitues expect many things of them. They must be large enough to give the spectators the idea that they are facing some vast tract of open country however closely surrounded by smoking factories; they must be enclosed as com- pletely as possible to furthur this idea, ii necessary, and in any case to take off the keen edge of the blasts that are only to be expected when -footer is played; they must provide a shelter from the rain for anyone paying more than the humble "tanner," and even at this price a covered seat is now often

QUEEN'S PARK NEW GROUND AT GLASGOW. to be had; every seat, from the cheapest to the most luxuriously cushioned one in the stand, must command a good view of the field of play; and there must be a very good pavilion, replete with all the comforts of a first-class golf club-house, except the beds, where the , inner man can be warmed and cheered at a tolerably cheap rate. Football enthusiasts are very general critics, and very pronounced and audible is their • comment if hostile.- Clubs have responded to the de- mands for better enclosures in no . marked degree lately, and many first-class grounds may be said to be -near perfection. However, the best is-just being completed at Hampden Park, Mount Florida, Glasgow, for the Queen's Park Football Club. The ground has .been built in a natural basin, and it covers an area of thirteen acres. The pavilion alone, when completed, will have cost upwards of 43,000. The price paid by the club for the site was £Io,OOO, and the enclosure repre- sents a total sum of £30,000. McCreatis and Stevenson were the engineers for the under- taking. The new ground is situated south of the Queen's old field, and is close to the Mount Florida Station of the Cathcart District Railway. The ground will be opened to the public on the occasion (4 the league matck between the Queen's Park and the Celtic.
DOWIE'S PAYING GAME.

Dr. Dowie, whose latest craze of leading a huge missionary army to attack New York is attracting world-wide attention, is a rich man, and were he to retire to-day it would be to the enjoyment of a fortune of anything from E,2,000,000 to 4,000,000. Under sixty years of age, his figure
is Of medium stature,his voice
clear and strong, his eye penetra- ting, and his
countenance,
naturally stern, lights up with
smiles when he hears of some-
to the
credit, especially financially, _of
the cause. He
is a Scotsman,
and his early
efforts were
made behind a
desk in Edin- burgh in a prac- tically penniless DR. JOHN ALEXANDER DOWIE, state. Now he THE "PROPHET OF PROFITS." claims dominion over a congre- - - -

gation numbering something like 60,000, drawn from every civilised country in the world. His fortune may largely have resulted from his face, but another strong factor in his success is that he does not believe in the paying of salaries to pi-teachers of religion. Indeed, he extracts as a gift a small matter of a tithe of their worldly possessions from all who em- brace his _doctrine. Looking at the size of ins congregation, and remembering that his banking account can be put down at a very comfortable figure, one begins to wonder what it is about this man and 'his doctrine which has attracted so many followers. His fellows believe in him to such an extent that they go on paying the tithe demanded with a cheerful face, obey the stringent rules he lays down, and cheerfully depend- for good health -upon the prayers of their pastor. When any one of his followers is taken ill, and desires to be made well, he . has merely to write a letter asking to be fprayed for. When next the prophet is at liberty, he takes a sheaf of these letters, and holding each aloft in turn for the space of- a second, during which the healing prayer is offered up, he dramatically places the letter beneath the indiarnbber stamp of the machine, which is something like a small printing-press, and, with a sudden thump of the hand upon the handle, impresses upon the sheet the words "Prayed for at three o'clock" (or whatever the time is, as registered .by the clock attached to the machine). The sufferers must then be quickly healed. Dowie began his work of " restoring " New York on Sunday, holding meetings morning, afternoon, and evening. The attendances were limited only I by the capacity of Madison Square Garden 4 Dowie sat in the centre of the platform, with his wife, son, and three " elders ' to his right and no one to the left. At the back of him was a string orchestra of women, and behind

Dowie said no one was hurt, but refused to permit the police to investigate. The studies from natural history were also very interesting and instructive, al- though perhaps it was a little disconcerting,to view the microscopic life which inhabits such necessary commodi- ties as water and cheese on such a highly-magnified scales as was shown on the screen. The humour of the evening was supplied by Mr. Hallard with his usual success. His rendering of "The Village Blacksmith,"in "four spasms."had an originality and versatility about it, truly Hallardian, and was quite equal to anything he has done in Warrington. Mention must also be made of the gramophone selections by Mr. E. They produce remarkably loud and clear sounds, and do away altogether with the" tinny" or metallic sounds ;that are so disagreeably manifest in most other phonographs. Messrs Geo. H. div.head: TRAFALGAR DAY.
div.p: TRAFALGAR DAY.

Wednesday, October 21st, is one of the most famous, if not actuq,lly the most famous, anniversary. in the history of Great Britain. It is second not even to Waterloo in import- ance, as, had it not been for Lord Nelson's brilliant victory at Trafalgar, very likely the final fight of the king Napoleonic wars would not have been so glorious and successful as it was ten years later. Nelson's great victory in 1805 "saved England from Napoleon's pro- jected invasion and 'confined the war to Europe; and, though it cost him his own life, it brought him undying fame. His famous signal from his flagship, the old Victory, "England expects every man to do his duty," has grown into the language of the country, and is one of its proudest and most brilliant traditions. On the morning of October 21st, 1805, Lord Nelson met the com- bined fleets of France and Spain under Admiral Villeneuve and routed them utterly,
THE MONUMENT AS DEC, WEDNESDAY.

though mortally wounded for a • large part of the time during which he was conducting operations. Each year since London has celebrated the great anniversary by deco- rating the statue of the famous admiral in Trafalgar Square, which, by its very name, bears testimony to his victory. Though close upon a century ago, memory is still green in the grateful hearts of his fellow-countrymen, and on Trafalgar Day his statue is a splendid sight. The day is this year further to be celebrated at the Earl's Court Fxhibition, which will be the centre of a combined attack of the naval and military forces of the country, together with all firemen and policemen. Anyone holding these qualifications will be admitted free througliyut the day by present- ing himself in unifdrm at the turnstiles in Warwick Road, and a special programme has been arranged for the occasion.

div.head: COURT FAVOURITE,
div.p: A COURT FAVOURITE,

Colonel the Hon. Sir William James Col- ville, his Majesty's Ma.ster of the Ceremonies, who has been laid tr. his last rest this week, was 76, and had sliffefed from congestion of the lungs. He passed away peacefully in the presence of the members of his family. Dur- ing his illness inquiries were made as to the progress of the patient by the King and Queen and the Prince and Princess of Wales. Colonel Colville w'as a brother of the late Viscount Colville of Cul- ross, who pre- deceased him about three months ago. The deceased officer was ap- pointed Master of the Ceremon- ies in 1893, the appointment being continued
E LATE SIR W COLVILLE.

at the accession of King Edward. Like his brother Sir William was a general favourite in Court and Dfficial circles, and will be keenly regretted and missed. His knowledge of Court cere- monial was probably unrivalled, and his charm of manner and his unostentatious abili- ties were proverbial. Few men were entitled to wear more orders and decorations—British and foreign—than he, and his full dress figure was as imposing as it was well known at Court functions and State ceremonials. His duties had brought him into contact with prPctically every foreign potentate who had v.sited these shores in a long course of years. He was a great favourite with Queen Vic- toria. He was educated at Sandhurst, and entered the army in 1843, served with the znd Battalion Rifle Brigade in Canada and the Crimea, and was on the staff rof General Sir James Simpson, commanding the army at the fall of Sevastopol. He afterwards served as Assistant Inspector of Volunteers, and was, in 1872, appointed Comptroller of the House hold of the Duke ot Edinburgh.

div.head: NEW GAIETY.
div.p: THE NEW GAIETY.

The outside of the new Gaiety in the Strand is already becoming a familiar land- mark to Londoners. It is a splendid house, tar more commodious and convenient than its predecessor, and it promises to carry on the old traditions attached to the name. It stands next door to the old Gaiety, which is in the hands of the housebreakers, at the corner of Aldwych, the new avenue of London. It is a handsome building of greystone, and the inside is beautifully decorated on a scheme of rose pink and apple green-, with plenty of gilt. It has great seating capacity, and the seats are far more comfortable than in the old house. The piece with which Mr. George Edwardes opens is "The Orchid Hunt," a musical comedy on the old lines, which pro- -410,fr
THE NEW THEATRE, AS IT WILL APPEAR IN FRONT WHEN FINISHED.

mises to be as great a success as he always achieves with this class of production. It is written by his usual syndicate of writers, I\lessis. James Tanner, Harry Greenbank, Adrian Ross, Ivan Caryll, Lionel Brnugh, and Paul Ruebens. The scene is first laid at the Countess of Barwick's Horticultaral College, and the plot turns on the search for a rare and wonderful orchid. The caste, too, is the old Gaiety caste, which is so familiar to the public, and all the old names appear in the list. Miss Ethel Sydney, Miss Gertie Miller, and Miss Connie Ediss play the principal ladies' parts, and Mr. Edmund Payne is the leading comedian. The opening of the new Gaiety is quite an event in the theatrical world, and many cordial wishes for good luct go with Mr, George Edwardes ill his new homei

div.head: RICHMOND GAS STOVE AND METER COMPANY LIMITED.
div.p: THE RICHMOND GAS STOVE AND METER COMPANY LIMITED.
Presentation at the Parr Hall
EMPLOYEES AND FRIENDS ENTERTAINED.

At the invitation of Mr. and Mrs. John A. Ransome theWarrington employes of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company Ltd,and their friends,over 600 in num- ber, sat down to tea in the Drill Hall, Warrington, on Saturday evening. Subsequentl§ a much larger com- pany was entertained by Mr. and Mrs. Ransome at a social gathering in the Parr Hall, and here Mr. H. M. Thornton (Vice-chairman of the Richmond Gas Stove and Meter Company Limited) presented Mr. and Mrs. Ransome, on behalf of the staff, workpeople, and friends, with a pianoforte, and an Angelus piano- player (with organ combination) in commemoration of their marriage on the 15th September last.

Mr. John A.-Ransonae has been general manager of the Warrington works for about four years (the last year as managing director) and during that time has been very popular with the staff and workpeople.A. proof of his popularity was forthcoming when it be- came known that he was about to be married, for within a short time of a subscription list' being opened for the purchase of a suitable present, sufficient was subscribed to purchase a handsome Bechstein piano and Angelus piano player. The proceedings on Saturday evening may be said to have taken the form of an "at home." Tt was impossible for Mr. and Mrs. Ransome to entertain their numerous Warrington friends at their home at Lymm,land consequently two of the largest halls in the town were requisitioned. An excellent knife and fork tea .was provided for the six hundred guests who assembled in the Drill Hall. The guests were hospitably received by the host and hostess. The bride was the cynosure of all eyes and looked exceedingly handsome in a biscuit-coloured dress, with hat to match. She is a daughter of Mr. C. C. Morland. J.P., Croydon. The walls of the hall had been emblazoned with gome of the most attractive 'picture posters, originally designed for the firm, by the late Phil May. There were pictures of Kruger " bringing his goose to be cooked " and the com- panion picture" nicely done," in which Lord Roberts is carrying 'off the honours. In addition, there were coloured sheets advertising the gas fires of the firm, prominence being given to the " Royal Sovereign." It was a gathering such as the late Mr. E. W. T. Richmond would have been delighted to take part in, and there were many who missed his cherry face and pleasing voice. Amongst those present were Mr. Land Mrs. John A. - Ransome and Miss Ransome, Mr. H. M. Thornton Mr. G-. Newton (of the firm of Messrs. G. Newton, Limited, of Oldham), Mr. C. R. Adamson, Mr. W. B. Hudson (George Glover and Co., Limited), Mr.H. P. Hughes (cashier), Mr. J. Pollitt (advertising department), Mr. J. F. Davy (works manager), Mr. W. H. Sherburn (designer), Mr. John King (manager enamelling department), Mr. L. A. Voisey, Mr. Isaac E. Barlow, Mr. F. Taylor and Mr. E. J. Hall, Miss H. H. Tuxford (lecturer), Mr. H. S. Gray,Mr. W. Fowler,Mr. Mclntyre (Stratford works' manager), &c., &c. After tea, the company adjourned to the Parr Hall for a musical evening. There would be nearly 2,000 persons present when the proceedings commenced. The first business was the presentation of the piano and Angelus piano-player. Mr. H. M. THowgroN. who presided,ihad a cordial reception, said his duty that night afforded him the greatest pleasure. A meeting of that kind might almost have been organized for some political gathering when some great scheme was to be expounded; in fact, he might almost say that even Mr. Chamberlain would have been proud to have faced such an audience. (Applause.) One of their great politicians only the other thy—he referred to Lord Rosebery—commenced his speech by words which were novel in a political speech—" What do You think of it all ?" Now he asked those present: What do you think of it all?" (Applause.) That was a most magnificent gathering, and showed the great respect in which Mv. and Mrs. Ransome were held by all of them. He had read somewhere that, "uneasy lies the head that wears a crown," and if another had said instead "Uneasy is the mind of the man who has to make a presentation," it would have been more appropriate in his case. (Laughter.) He was naturally anxious on such an occasion to sound the right note, and to adequately convey to the recipients of the presents the expression of good-will which undoubtedly existed. He understood from the stewards that a lengthy speech was neither desirable nor necessary, and he was glad, that that was so for several reasons. His (Mr. Thorn- ton's) acquaintance With Mr. Ransome had extended over a period of six years. He had had the privilege of knowing him before any of the employes did, or many of them. Then, as now, his uprightness of character, his thoroughness in all he undertook, won him the respect and esteem which they all felt for him that evening: (Applause.) Mr. Ransome had a:record of which any man must be proud, and it must be as gratifying to his frieads as well as to him- self to occupy the position he did that night. Not content with the conquests of business, he laid siege to a lady's heart, and, what was more important, with his usual persistency of character, he had captured it. (Laughter and applause.) He was sure it would be their wish to cordially welcome Mrs Ransome that night. (Applause). In making the presentation,the Chair- man said: On behalf of all the subscribers,who are too numerous to mention by name, but who include all shades of opinion, and who occupy positions humble and exalted, I present you with this beautiful piano and Angelus, expressing the hope that you may live long to enjoy the music which both can produce. (Loud Applause). Mr. RANSOME, who was loudly cheered on rising to acknowledge the presents, said it was exceedingly diffi- cult to find words in which to adequately convey the gratitude of himself and his wife to them. The presents were so beautiful and just what they required and wished for, that words would not convey to those present the gratitude which Mrs. Ransome and himself felt. The piano and Angelus would add very, much to their plea- sure, for music had much to do with their happi- ness in this life. (Hear, hear.) He need not draw a picture of a regiment going down a street with a band. Where would the regiment be without the band? There were brave men, proud hearts, heads erect, all in ' step, marching down the street, but the principal I attraction was the band. • Then, again, if any of them were in great trouble, what was more soothing ; thana well chosen melody played quietly? They had I their likes and dislikes in music ; some preferred the Iclassical, which was very often difficult to follow, and others stirring marches. Why even the small boy had his mouth organ on which to play his favourite tune, Iwhich he had probably heard from a barrel orgain. ; (Laughter). They all had their likes and dislikes in pianos, but he thought the Bechstein was nearly as well known as Richmond's gas stoves. (Laughter and applause) At any rate, it was a tip-top piano and he thought they would agree with him when they heard it played., ' although they would not get the full effect in a lofty building as they would in a drawing-room. The gentle- men who organized the presentation gave his wife and himself an opportunity of choosing the piano in London, and they selected this one on the platform as being thoroughly to,their taste, so that the audience might restassured that both of them were satisfied. The Angelus was a very necessary adjunct. Mr. Ransome proceeded to describe the Angelus, which he said, was a mechanical player worked with air obtained by bellows at the foot of the instrument. They had had many presents, but nothing had come up to the piano and Angelus, and he hoped all present would accept their deepest and most heartfelt thanks. (Applause.) In conclusion, he would like to say how pleased he and his wife were at seeing so many present. They were also indebted to the stewards who had devoted so many , hours in making the arrangements. Once more he I thanked them for that beautiful present and he could ; assure them that he and his wife would appreciate and use it for the whole of their lives. (Applause.) I The audience than sang "For he's ajolly good fellow " ' and raised three cheers for Mr. and Mrs. Ransome. The entertainment was. of a miscellaneous character and proved very enjoyable. The first item was Wagner's , well-known overture to " Tannhauser," and this was pla:ed on the pian,oforte by the Angelus piano-player. Subsequently, Mr. R. H. Pearson , ' contributed another selection by means of the 1 same instruments. The piano, which is a hand- some Bechstein, is, of course, intended for the drawing- room and not the concert hall, but the audience was ; able, notwithstanding the largeness of the hall,- to appreciate the rich tones of the instrument and the 1 advantages of a piano-player with organ-combination. Songs were contributed by Miss Nellie Anderton and Mr. J. M. Greenhalgh, two local artistes. Miss Anderton is a singer of much promise, and possesses a contralto Ivoice of fine range and quality. On Saturday , she acquitted herself admirably in her two songs I "The land across the sea" (Barnard) and "By the iFountain" (Stephen Adams). She was twice encored and further pleased the audience by singing as encores "On the banks of Allan Water," and 'Within your heart," a lyric composed by Mrs. Hubi-Newcombe and set to beautiful music by Trotere.Mr. Greenhalgh's robust voice vvas heard to advantage in the songs "Hybrias the Cretan" (Elliot) and "The Bedouin love-song " (Pinsuti). PQr his very fine rendering of the first named song he was encored, and complied with "Anchored." Professor Weber, who has now been before the public for 30 years,proved a host in himself in his ventriloquial sketch and conjuring entertainment. The exhibition of ani- mated pictures by cinematographic photo-micrography, by Captain Shaw, of "Hamilton's Excursions" was ' also a feature of the evening's proceedings. Some interesting scenes were shown, illustrative of the

div.head: REV. ARTHUR MURSELL AT WARRINGTON. Lscture on Richard Cobden.
div.p: THE REV. ARTHUR MURSELL AT WARRINGTON. Lscture on Richard Cobden.

The REV. ARTHUR MURSELL of London, the dis- tinguished lecturer and preacher, paid a visit to War- rington on Thursday. In the afternoon he preached in Golborne street Baptist chapel and at night lectured on "Richard Cobden. There were fairly large con- gregations, both afternoon and evening, but the wet weather undoubtedly kept many away. Mr. Mursell's afternoon discourse was taken from Ecclesiastes "The sun riseth and the sun setteth." The preacher em- phasized the worth of platitudes. The text was a platitude and the preacher proceeded to explain that the commonplaces of life were after all lithe most real.

From the announcements respecting the evening lec- ture many were led to suppose that Mr. Mursell was to speak on" Free Trade," and touch upon the present fiscal problem, but he confined himself to a review of the life and work of Richard Cobden, which proved deeply interesting and instructive. It was delivered in Mr. Mursell's rapid and florid style, but was instinct with meaning and lessons for the present day in which Cobden's principles are being so fiercely contested. In the unavoidable absence of Councillor William Pierpoint, the chair was taken by the Pastor (Rev. Herbert Dunnico) who briefly introduced the lecturer. At the outset, Mr. MURSELL said he could remember, no doubt in common with the senior portion of the audience, how people used to talk of Cobden and the League eta how that "the Times," before the penny papers entered upon their rivalry used to hold column after :column of those cool arguments with which Cobden converted Sir Robert Peel to the repeal. of the corn laws and discomforted the men who would seek to cheat the workingman of his daily bread. After reviewing the early life of Cobden—the Sussex yeoman as he was called—the lecturer passed in review the foundation and early struggles of the "British United Corn Law League." Among the leaders who laboured hard to teach the people the politics of "cheap bread and no monopoly, none said the lecturer, proved so clear headed or patient and successful as Richard Cobden. The lecturer related an incident at Leicester in which he was taken by his father to a meeting addressed by Richard Cobden, and how in his boyish enthusiasm he endeavoured to touch the coat of Cobden, but touched his head instead, at which Cobden turned round and stroked him on the cheek. From that pnoment,when a boy of six, the lecturer continued, "I was a Free Trader." Cobden, he said, made the people understand his policy and soon the words "cheap bread and no monopoly," became a common hue and cry, resounding in the Market Place, in the Exchange and in the haunts of men. Cobden's oratory captivated while it convinced. Cobden was no demagogue. He was not the sort of man people would hoist on their shoulders. It was a tribute to his power that within seven or eight years, he and his league were able to bring about an entire revolution of the national mind. It was because of the power and persistence of his voice as well as the grandeur and justice :A his cause that his victory was so signal and his renown so illustrious. Passing from Cobden's great victory in the conversion of Sir Robert Peel to the abolition of the corn laws, the lecturer said Cobden somewhat tarnished his popularity but not his honour i by the attitude which he took up n reference to Lord Palmerston's policy relating to the Crimean war. Reference was also made to Cobden's diplomatic triumph in concluding a commercial treaty with France, and to his advocacy of temperance and thrift. The lecturer paid a glowing tribute to Cobden as a peacemaker, in which he referred to him as an apostle of peace and goodwill to men. The CHAIRMAN said he was sura Mr. Mursell had given not only an interesting but an instructive lecture, and those who had the pleasure of hearing him 25 or 30 years ago would agree that he had lost none of his power. Mr. Mursell had steered clear of the fiscal controversy, but nevertheless those who had studied that question would have found much food for thought. Councillor JAMES EVANS, in moving a rote of thanks to the lecturer, said some of them would remember the day that just followed the triumph of Cobden, and they knew something of the sweetness of life that had emanated from the work of that noble man.

Mr. Er.wELL seconded, and said it was fitting that the life of Cobden should be brought before them. He was one of the foremost apostles of cheap food for the poor • people of this country, and it behoved them, especially I the workingmen, not to lose the privileges that were I obtained for them by such men as Cobdes,. Bright and I Villiers. Some of them might be induced to be led as- tray by the politicians of the present day,who advocated preferential tariffs, but he was-afraid they would' find • preferential tariffs a curse instead of a boon. (Hear, ! n ear.) t The vote was carried unanimously. ( In acknowledging the vote of thanks, Mr. Mursell said whoever called him to Lancashire laid him under an obligation. He would not leave Warrington without I expressing the pleasure he had in the opening career of Mr. Dunnico, and invoking, if he might, as an old man, • the rich and abundant blessing of God upon his minis- try, which he trusted would be very fruitful with the best spiritual results. (Hear,hear.) If any disappoint- ment had been felt at his not discussing the fiscal question, he would plead as an excuse that he did not understand it. Those present understood the pro- posals a great deal better than he did. He thought i there was a great deal to be said all round this great question, but that was no reason why they should not • pay their tribute of honour and regard to the memory of a great human benefactor. (Hear, hear.)

An interesting find has been made among some Tndi an- grown corn at a Lancashire flour mill, namely, a heavy, massive, solid silver ring, supposed to have been lost off the finger of an Indian native whilst thrashing the corn. It is one ounce in weight.

div.head: NORTHERN UNION.
div.p: THE NORTHERN UNION.
WARRINGTON v. WIDNES.

The first meeting between these two teams took place at Widnes on Saturday afternoon, and as the result counted in the South West Lancashire Competition as well as the Northern League there was much excite- ment as to the result. Several hundred Warringtonians accompanied the visiting team which was far from being at full strength. Dickenson was the latest absentee, in addition to Harris and Edmunds, and the vacancy was filled by Mahoney at centre and Jordan, an A "teamer, at half back. There was a crowd of about 4,000, well above the average for Widnes. The teams were as follow:

Widnes—Tilley, back; Wailing, Peacock, Taylor, and Hughes, three-quarter backs; Lally and Kennedy, half backs; Aspey, Curtis, Lynch, Leyshon, Power, Rigby, Webster, and MacDonald, forwards. Warrington—Hallam, back; Forster, Mahoney, Isher- wood, and Fish, three-quarter backs; Davies and Jordan, half backs; Morrison, Boardman, Swift. Harmer, Lunt, Edmondson, Naylor, and Thomas, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. Priestley, Broughton; touch judges, Messrs G. Robinson, Runcorn. and T. Little, St. Helens. Warrington won the toss, and chose the wind. Aspey opened, and Thomas made a mark. Tilley was troubled , through Aspey mulling, but the ball was dropped clear. , Widnes were fortunate ih obtaining two penalties, and by these gained ground. Aspey kicked well to touch, but Fish retaliated. A round of passing was spoiled by Peacock knocking on. Widnes pressed, and smart play by Lalley compelled Fish and Isherwood to tackle tieez promptly. Swift drew capitally away, and kick d safely to Tilley. Smart work by Lalley almost gav Wailing a. chance to reach the line. Aspey made a nd mark, but the essay at goal by Tilley, prove a failure. Widnes were directing hostilities ose in, but Davies stepped in and found ch at centre. Tilley mulled a long kick giving Warrington an open- ing. Taylor got in a return smartly from Fish in his own 25. Fish made a mark near the centre, and placed for goal. The ball, however, just missed. A punt by Hallam ended in Tilley being brought down under the posts. Fish 'iras given a fine chance by Isherwood, but he could not get clearto pass to Hughes. After Widnes had- kicked dead, Fish's powers of scoring were again tested, but he found the home defence too keen. A mull by Taylor saw the game transferred to the Widnes line, where Isherwood kicked to Fish, but careful watch- ing of the "flyer" frustrated another opening. Hallam played gallantly, and frequently beat one or two of the home forwards. Hallam was again applauded fora fine display. Davies and Jordan were passing carelessly. From a break-away by Isherwood, Fish accepted, and, after a fine run, was brought to earth by Titley on the line. Half-time : Widnes, nil; Warrington, nil. Davies opened the second moiety. Widnes, with the aid of a penalty, took the leather in Warrington terri- tory. Jordan was given an opening, but was brought down by Curtis. Tilley was promptly collared by Swift, after taking his time. Hughes luckily beat Fish with a kick, and, consequently, Hallam, who had &R opportunity of clearing, was grassed by Leyshon. Warrington, however, transferred to midfield by touch- kicks. Taylor knocked on at a critical moment, in an attempt to beat Fish. The latter, a minute later, had almost an ()Pen field.. Warrington "bucked" up, and as often as Widnes gotpossession they stopped the move- ment. Tilley was given a penalty, but made little use of it. Strong forward play by Warrington resulted in Isherwood tackling the home skipper. Wailing inter- cepted with a vigorous knock-on, and ran right round the posts. The referee after having a conversation with the linesman, disallowed the try, much to the chagrin of the Widnesians. Isherwood afterwards tried to drop a goal, and failed. Final.—Widnes till, Warrington nil. OLDHAM v. RUNCORN.

These teams met at Watersheddings before 6,000 spectators. There was very little wind when Frater kicked off. Runcorn were the first to attack, Houghton taking two free kicks in succession. Then followed a smart passing bout by the home three-quarter backs, Civil being pushed into touch by Houghton as he was nearing the line. S. Lees obtained from the scrummage, dribbled across, and the ball going over the line Wilkin- son dropped on it. .S. Lees kicked a goal. After mid- field play the visitors attacked strongly, end Ruse was collared when within an ace of scoring. Both ends were visited in turn, Runcorn being repeatedly danger- ous. Half-time score—Oldlifan 1 goal, 1 try (5 points), Runcorn nil.

Runcorn resumed, and Oldham faced the first scrunt- mage in Runcorn territory. The latter were soon agaidi troublesome. Two players were cautioned for rough- ness, and even play followed. Phil Thomas put in clever work, and, on one occasion in coming into con- tact with Houghton, he was injured sand had to leave the field. Oldham had a free kick and Ferguson kicked a val. Phil Thomas now re-appeared with his head bandaged. A. Lees made a mark near the centre line, and Ferguson taking the kick sent the leather over the bar, and Oldham won by 3 goals, 1 try (9 points) to Runcorn nil. Teams :

Oldham—R. L. Thomas, back; Spottiswoode, Tyson, Phil Thomas, and Civil, three-quarter backs; A. Lees and S. Lees (jun.), half backs; Fritter, Ferguson, Ellis, J. H. Wilkinson, Topham, Kershaw, Wright, and Kelley, forwards.

Runcorn—Houghton, back; Harriscn, Price, Butter- worth, and Jones, three-quarter backs; Richardson and J. R. Faulkner, half backs; S. Walker' Woods, Moulton, Longley, Tomlinson, Poole, Joseph Walker, and A. Richardson, forTards. Referee—Mr. Smirk, Preston; touch judges, Messrs. W.Lancaster, Rochdale, and J. A. Squires, Broughton.

div.head: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. SALFORD.
div.p: HULL KINGSTON ROVERS v. SALFORD.

The first match between these clubs this season was played at Hull before about 10,090 spectators. The game throughout was stubbornly contested, and the tackling was so vigorous at times that stoppages for injuries to players were of frequent occurrence. The open- ing stages were evenly contested, but eventually Barry got clear away from a scrummage, and from the opening West got the ball and scored a try for the Rovers,which Carmichael failed 1..; improve. After this Salford attacked vigorously, but Baker missed a fine opportunity to score :trough knocking forward. The Rovers were penalised, and Lomas placed a goal for Salford. Madley dropped a goal for the home team, who led at half-time by five points to two. Early in the second half Salford took the lead by Preston scoring a try, which Lomas improved. The lead of two points was kept until close on time, when a sensational ending of the game occurred, Carmichael placing a penalty goal for the Rovers just as the whistle sounded for "no side." The game was drawn, both clubs having scored seven points each.

div.head: SWINTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: SWINTON v. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

Winning the toss, Swinton placed the Rangers to face the sun and wind in the first half. Bufris retired injured in the first five minutes. Swinton had several opportunities to cross the RR agers' line, but through weak combination and erratic passing the clr.tices were lost. A fide effort by Hogg- brought about the only score before the interval He caught the ball from a kick by Harry, dodged through the home backs, and scored a try, which W. James failed to improve. Ends was changoa with the Rang(:rs leading by three points to nothing. A score quickly came to the Rangers from a combined movement by Wilson and Hogg. Together they raced down to Chorley, when Hogg repassed the ball to Wilson, who pla, - d it behipd the Swinton posts and S. James kicked a goal. No ftirther scoring took place until just on time, when Hogg. after kicking the ball over Chorley's head, regaint .Ipossession and scored a try for the Rangers. Result :—Broughton Rangers, one goal and three tries (11 points) ; Swinton nothing. HUNSLET v. BATLEY.

Hunslet attacked for the greater part of the first half of this game on their own ground, and when the interval arrived had the useful advantage of seven points to nothing. The remainder of play favoured Hunslet,who, through the agency of Albert Goldthorpe, scored two goals, while Whiteley with a try put them three more points ahead, the final score reading :—Huuslet, four goals and two tries (14 points) ; Batley, nothing.

div.head: HUDDERSFIELD v. WIGAN.
div.p: HUDDERSFIELD v. WIGAN.

The play during the initial half of the game at Huddersfield was of an interesting character. Each side in turn held the advantage. Deere scored an uncon- verted try for Huddersfield, Holroyd following with a penalty goal. Lowe ran in a try for Wigan, and Sutcliffe added a try and kicked a goal, the interval score being :—Huddersfield, 10 points, Wigan three. Upon recommencing Lowe registered an unconverted try for Wigan. The visitors continued to attack strongly and had the best of matters,the result being :—Hudders- fleld, two goals and three tries (11 points).

div.head: BRADFORD v. HULL.
div.p: BRADFORD v. HULL.
At Bradford, before 6,000 spectators. Result : Bradford, five goals and three tries (19 points) ; Hull nothing.

div.head: HALIFAX v. LEEDS.
div.p: HALIFAX v. LEEDS.

At Halifax. Owing to recent heavy rains the groundat Halifax was on the soft side. Capital work was showrt by both sets of forwards lathe openinghalf, and after the interval Moffatt was stopped when just on the line. Still, neither side were able to score, and a fine for- ward game ended in a pointless draw.

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON " A " V. WIDNES "A."

At Warrington before 1,500 spectators. Harris made his first appearance this season and was given a hearty reception. Fairhurst kicked off for Warrington towards the pavilion goal, but Bradshaw returned to centre field with a good kick. By easy stages the locals worked their way into Widnes quarters, and Harris almost scored. Jackson kicked to half way and Harris and Radcliffe next took up the running, and the first-named ploughed his way through the opposition in fine style and kicked across to Watkins. The left winger had only to beat the full-back, but his opponent proved too quick for him. Warrington again threatened danger and the three-quarter line combined effectively, but the Widnes back division tackled accurately. Knight was applauded for a splendid save, and after this the game slowed down somewhat. The visitors pressedandHazris saved splendidly, after Knight had failed to clear. A free kick availed the "Wirepullers" little for Widnes assisted by the wind still kept on the attack, and at last their efforts were rewarded, a try being scored near the corner by the left wing man. The kick at goal proved futile Jackson was next conspicuous in parting to Watkins, at the opportune moment, but the latter could not get away. Warrington were attacking when half time was called with the score :—Widnes "A,' one try; War- rington "A," nil. On resuming Warrington had the advantage of the wind. Play was of a give-and-take nature for a time, both sides attacking in turn. % Jackson with tricky play took the game to the Widnes 25, where several scrummages ensued. The visitors' full-back in attempting to clear a dangerous rush, was hurt, and the game was stopped in consequence. Faulty fielding by Warrington led up to Widnes taking play to. Warrington half. The home half-backs gave a miser- able exhibition, and Fairhurst eventually came out of the pack and partnered Hardman. At last the Warring- tonians forced the pace, and Harris, after eluding several opponents scored, but through some infringe- ment the point was disallowed. The locals again put On pressure and from a scrummage under the posts the ball was again rushed over and Ratcliffe touched down but the referee also overruled this point. Widnes raa out winners by one try to nil.

div.p: THF YORKSHIRE TEAM.

Little (Halifax) ; Davies (Batley), Llewellyn (Leeds), and Sinton (Bradford); Marsden (Bradford) and Barry (Hull Kingston Rovers), Laidlaw (Bradford), Knight (Huddersfield), Balmer, Swinbank, and MaHinson (all Halifax).
Resorves.—Taylor (Hull); Wimpenny (Huddersfield), Mosby (Bradford), and Deere (Huddersfield); New- bould (Wakefield Trinity),Moffatt (Leeds), and Fletcher ,(Hull Kingston Rovers).
