div.head: IRON MASK.
div.p: THE IRON MASK.

Amongst the instruments of torture which were used in what people are pleased to call "the good old days," one of the most revolting was the iron mask. This was an iron case, with spikes inside. As the mask closed upon the victim, the fine-pointed spikes pierced the flesh until a truly horrible death ensued. With corres- ponding severity the human frame is racked by rheu- matism. Happily the ingenuity of man has devised a means by which the most acute form of rheumatism can be cured. Charles Forde's bile beans cure rheuma- tism, as is proved by thousands of cases. Miss Ellen Elizabeth Mead, a 3, Wickham-street, Tyers-street, Lambeth, S.E., said to a "Weekly Budget" reporter : "Some timer ago I was attacked with severe rheumatism in my feet and legs, which swelled to such an extent. that I was in bed a week, unable to move about. 0" The pains in my limbs were almost unbearable. Fromthe legs the swelling went to my arms and bands, and for fully a week I was unable to feed myself or touch a thing. I was absolutely helpless. The pains were like cutting, twisting, and drawing my limbs. "Every time I moved I had to scream, the agonywas so intense. I could not afford to go to a doctor, and as I saw that Charles Forde's bile beans were advertised to cure rheumatism, and I had had a box of the beans at Christir;as for sickness and pains in the back andthey then did me a lot of good, I decided to try them again. After taking the first few doses I continued with the beans until I had three boxes, when I felt as" right as rain." The swellings and pains ab- solutely disappeared, not only from my hands and legs, but also from my side and back, where at times they used to catch me. Ido not think there is any neces- sity to pay long doctor's bills when such a fine medicine as *Charles Forde's bile beans may be had. lam satis fled that they have cured me permanently," Charles Forde's bile beans, which effected this mar- vellous cure, are sold by all chentlsts at one-and-three , halfpence or two-and-nine-pence per box.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Baptist Church, Colborne-street.

On Sunday afternoon a'united meeting of the Bible Class and Sunday school was held for the purpose of presenting to Mr. and Mrs. Dunnico two wedding gifts, which, as the chairman, Mr. N. Balmford, remarked, came better late than never. Mr. Barnes on behalf of the Bible class presented Mr. and Mrs. Dunnico with a barometer, while an electro cruet from the Sunday school was presented to Mrs. Minnie() by Miss Mabel Freeman and Master Cyril Wilson. In the evening the pastor preached on "Why I am a Christian ," being the first of a series of fouraddresses. He was a Christian becanse every man was constituted for and must have a religion. Religion, the preacher stated, was the recognition of that essential relationship which existed between the human soul and God. He chose Christianity as his religion because he held that nothing else could make one's life so noble and ones' character solbeautiful. as a firm belief in Jesus Christ. Christianity was not a creed or system of beliefs,:but a life lived in conscious communion with a divine person, and that person Jesus Christ.

div.head: Buckley Street Methodist Free Church.
div.p: Buckley Street Methodist Free Church.

IThere were special services at the Methodist Free Church, Buckley street, on Sunday to celebrate the re- opening of the building after re-decoration. Many of the members of the church have worked assiduously to bring about its7present pleasing appearance, and they, with the decorator, Mr. J. Unsworth, Manley ; Street, deserve the highest praise for• their excellent workmanship. The sermons were preached I both morning and evening by Mr. E. H. Smith (the blind evangelist), of Sheffield. In the mornin_g the preacher based his discourse upon the words "I will arise," and in the evening he preached on "Christ's Crucifixion." There was a large congregation in the morning, and in the evening the building was so crowded that many could not obtain admission. Special anthems I were rendered by the choir, under the leadership of Mr. !J. Ryder. Miss M. Plinston, A.L.C.M., was the organist. The collection amounted to £ll. In the afternoon a mus- ical service was held,presided over by Mrs. W. Pierpoint ; and WAS largely attended. Instrumental selections were ' given by Mr. A. Bate's party.—Messrs. J. Scott, sen., G. Clarke, J. Scott, jun., Taylor, and J. Jackson—and. their rdkiderings were highly appreciated. Miss I. Hewitt was heard to advantage in" 0 rest in the Lord" and "The first prayer." Mr. NV. H. Wallington de- lighted the assembly with "Christe Salvator " and j "The first Palm Sunday." The solos, "The last mile- stone" and "Waft her, angels, to the skies," were well ; rendered by Mr. S. Hassan, and Miss L. Fairhurst gave fine expositions of " Abide with me " and " 0, dry those tears.' A public tea was held in the schoolroom on Monday evening, and was followed by a lecture by Mr. • E. H. Smith, on "A trip to London," illustrating stirring incidents of his walk to the Metropolis bare- footed. The chaiiqwas taken by Mr, J. Drury, in the unavoidable absence of Councillor W. trough. Both. tea and lecture were yell attended.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
OCTOBER 2lth 1903.

Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S / SOME NEGLECTED belief that he can TRUTHS. carry conviction by mere repetition is not wholly encouraging to his friends. The "Times," for instance, is by no means satisfied by his reiterated assurance to the workmen that his scheme will cost nothing, but will put money in their pockets straight off. "We could wish that, with his capacity for appealing to the enthusiasm of his hearers, he would deal a little more with the view that some sacrifice may be needed, but that the consolidation of the Empire is worth it, and it will ultimately be repaid tenfold in increased and assured employment." The mis- giving here confessed is natural and pathetic. The "Times" sees through the glamour of Mr. CHAM- BERLAIN'S hypothesis into a rather disquieting void. It is so easy to affirm on platform after platform that our fiscal system can be changed without any sacrifice, and the Empire consolidated by the mere waving of a wand. But the hazard is enormous, and every successive speech of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S makes this plainer. He persists in manipulating the figures as if they concerned only the workman, whose needs are few and simple. Everybody else is ignored. The complicated needs of the whole community do not come into the calculation. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN SUMS it up RS if , it were purely an affair of the household budget of one class, and did not concern the multifarious expenditure of all the rest. He does not consider it worth while to examine the contingency that the moment his policy was translated into action the price of everything that is necessary to the whole body of coosumers would go up with a bound. Every tradesman would find that his livelihood was at stake, and would seek to recoup himself without loss of time. All that saving on tea and sugar which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN now parades as a miracle of statesmanlike benefi- cence would look pitiful enough when reckoned against the dearness of every manufactured article in the market. This is what the " Times" means when it says that "some sacrifice may be needei," and that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN ought to show us how it can be " repaid tenfold in increased and assured employment." That is just what a great many people, not all of them classed as working men would like to know. Tao multitude whose incomes are fixed and small want at least an ink- ling how they are to get the increased and assured employment which will compensate them for the sacrifice which, however Mr. CHAMBERLAIN may disguise it, would be inevitable and universal. But on the cardinal point we seem unlikely to obtain any illumination. MT. CHAMBERLAIN points to the prosperity of Protectionist countries. Is there anything in the condition of the German people, apart from their educational advantages, that excites our envy? Is the standard of living higher in Germany than in Great Britain? Mr. CHAMBERLAIN will scarcely maintain that it is. With singular maladroitness he invited our attention to the growing comfort of the French peasantry. The most striking quality of the French peasant is his thrift, which to the foreign observer is almost uncanny. But does any economist who is familiar with the social conditions in France pretend that the peasant is really well off? The truth is that with all his thrift he is constantly in the clutches of grinding penury. The average

Frenchwomaq of the humbler classes has a geniuS for household economy which is the admiration of the world; but that genius is tasked to the utter- most to keep body and soul together in many a village commune. Mr. CHA.MBERLAIN is fond of repeating that Free Trade is only a contributory cause of our prosperity. He has not yet acquainted himself with the fact that French thrift con- tributes a good deal more to the credit of France than Protection. In Germany the material condition of the working classes is pretty much what it was in England before the factory legislation and the development of the Trades -Unions. German manufacturers are enabled to make their profits by low wages, long hours, child labour—all the abuses which were abolished in this wuntry long ago. When Mr. CHAMBERLADI talks of German prosperity he leaves these things out of the account. He tells us to study compara- tive statistics, but ignores their most vital signific- ance in relation to the welfare of the toilers in other countries. He denies that Free Trade deserves the chief credit of our commercial expan- sion, but does not answer the question whether Protection deserves the discredit of the German workman's lack of all the advantages of organised labour. And yet these considerations are of the highest importance when we are asked to embrace Protection because it stimulates the energies of our commercial rivals.

Councillor Dodds in another column alludes to our criticism of Mr. Norbury Williams' remarks last week,wherein Mr. Williams expressed a desire to" dictate the policy of the Town Council." Mr. Dodds assures us that neither he nor Mr. Norbury Williams has any such object in view, and that the word " dictate " does not convey the meaning Mr. Norbury Williams had in his mind. We accept the assurance, and all the more readily because we believe that these two gentlemen at any rate, have no desire to "dictate the policy of the Town Council " any further than is necessary to secure the elimination of municipal trading and bring the inquiry to a satisfactors issue. Mr. Norbury Williams made some incau- tious utterances at Parr Hall, and it is as much in his own interest, as for any other reason, that we pointed out last week so glaring an inconsist- ency in his remarks. We are very glad to hear, on the authority of Councillor Dodds,that instead of "seeking to,raise up a band of ruthless dictators our aim is precisely the opposite."

Captain Crosfield has succeeded during the past few w ceks in convincing us of one fact, i.e.,that he is in deadly earnest as regards his advocacy of the objects of the National Service League. But be quite failed to convince us that there is any necessity for compulsory military service in this country. His letter this week we are inclined to think—perhaps egotistically—strengthens our case more than his own. He certainly advances some strong arguments for the increase of the Navy, but this, unfortunately, is not what be aims at. We are much more concerned about the Navy than the Army,and taking Captain Crostield's facts seriously, we think he unwittingly makes crut an excellent case for an enlarged navy vote. With regard to Switzerland, which Mr. Crosfield was the first to instance, he admits that this country's great natural barriers make it less neces- sary for the people to undergo prolonged military training, and then argues that the natural barriers "do not abolish the necessity for some training, or why should they train ?" We presume they train in order to make things as awkward for an invader as Vossible. This is animal instinc4 pure and simple, and it is just what impels this country to keep a standing army, with a reserve of volun- teers, yeomanry, militia and the like—added, of course, to the necessity for policing the empire. Our natural barrier is the sea, and we rely to a great extent on the security of that barrier, which we also seek to strengthen by our ships of war. We would ask Ciptam Crosfield a plain questioo, which, we think, pertinently affects the issile„. Presume that this barrier is broken down bY enemy; of what use wceild our compulsor,ll', trained men be, except to make things awgwaru...- We are too inferior numerically to offer s.rnY serious land resistance to a continental army. Mr. Crosfield, we must rely on the natural barrier and direct our policy towards strengthening th.e same. Our army and volunteers will answer thel.re purpose exceedingly well in their present form It they are efficiently maintained.

When the proposals of the Manchester Ship Caual Company with reference to the construction of a river diversion and other works at Lower Walton were made public about a month ago, We ventured to point out what we considered to be most objectionable financial obligations. The company asked the Corporation to pledge Its credit for the whole cost of the works, the interest and sinking fund to be repaid by the Canal Corn" pany in yearly instalments until the loan was liquidated. Furthermore the Corporation was presumably to pay the cost of the diversion of the sewers which the scheme would involve. The Rivers Committee has now drawn its pen, as it were, through both these proposals. With reference the suggestion that the Corporation should pro- vide the Company with the necessary funds, the Committee has decided riot to entertamit,and,they have forther decided that the cst of any diver sion of the sewers must be borne by the companY• The Rivers Committee then goes a step further :rind suggests that the company should pay the Corporation's costs as between solicitor and client in the recent action. In the event of the Canal Company agreeing to tile committee's recommends tions, the proposed scheme,so far as the ratepayers of Warrington are concerned will be shorn of sole of its most objectionable features. The Canal Company are likely to gain the most from the pre - posed works, if they prove a success, and it is oulY just and equitable that they should bear the brunt of the financial obligations which the experiment involves. Unless they are prepared to do so, there seems little likelihood of the ratepayers of War: rington lending support to the scheme, which needs further very serious consideration.

The members of the Warrington Board of Guardians were on Wednesday on the horns of ° dilemma with respect to the isolation of fever cases occurring in the Workhouse. Hitherto th° Warrington Corporation has relieved the Work' house of its infectious diseases cases and isolated them in the Aikin-street hospital free of charge; The Town Clerk now appears to have discovere° that the Corporation is under no obligation to dc: this duty free of charge, and on a requet being sent to the Medical Officer of Health ,to admit a fever-stricken nurse at the Wort; house into the Infectious Diseases .flospit' a prompt request was made for a written under' taking to pay the cost of maintenance. This WI refused and the patient was not remove' to the Isolation Hospital. The Clerk to tile. Guardians contends that no case has been reat: out for this new departure and holds the that as the Guardians pay Borough rates oo large assessment they are entitled to the 8°14: privileges as the inhabitants of the Borough it respect to the isolation of infectious disea.st cases. The Town Clerk suggests that the ooio of the Local Government Board should . taken,but Mr. Sutton seems in favour of obtaiol7o a decision from the Superior Courts. We lON that our local authorities will be able to their differences without squandering the rit, t payers' money on law. It is to be regretted tuit. the point was not raised and settled ere a fe. case occurred. The spectacle of two authoritise disputing about thi, fees, while a fever. c.lO awaits removal, is not an enviable one. This.' pression is deepened on learning that the patleriv succumbed to the disease on Thursday.

These are the days of record-breaking. Ruhne"' swimmers, cyclists, motorists and baioonists srei busylgoing for records with a persistence worthY ° a better cause, and now the weather has be•eri seized with the competitive record-breaking alani"

div.p: much to the discomfort of humanity. It was announced Dn Thursday that all reliable rainfall records for one year had been eclipsed at noon, When the total for the current year amounted to 32 inches, against the previous best of 31.99 inches in 1879. And there are nine • weeks of 1903 -still to run! Jupiter Pluvius evidently intends placing his new figures on an inaccessible pinnacle, and we hope he will succeed,for a thorough soak- ing this year can be better endured by reflecting that the equal of such a rainfall may never again be seen. "A plague upon" the "Daily Mail" and its ten years forecast t It reveals a sad lack of faith and optimism.

The views of Lord Randolph Churchill on the 'Tariff question, like that remarkable statesman's career itself, were exceedingly varied, but Mr. Winston Churchill has scored heavily against .-Viose who have represented his father as a firm Protectionist by quoting an extract from a speech 'delivered after he hid obtained high Ministerial rank. "Can the Fair Traders," he asked, "prove simply and in a manner intelligible to the people at large that France, Germany, and Austria— . coundies there there ace high protective duties— are more flourishing and more prosperous than we ..%re ?" To those who pointed to the United States and New South Wales as examples of flourishing Protectionist countries—an invitation which sounds rather odd in face of the devotion of New South Wales to the Free Trade policy—he retor- ted. that there was not the smallest analogy 'between these more or loss self-contained countries and an island like Great Britain; which has far more people than it can feed. With the figures -set forth in the now famous Blue-book befora us few Protectionists would have the hardihood to assert that France, Austria, and Germany enjoy prosperity comparable to our own.

IT is satisfactory to learn that our iron menu lecturers are taking steps to meet foreign competi- tion on much more practical lines than the Pro- tectionists recommend. They have, as the Economist points out, taken steps to cheapen the coat of production, and the American methods are being adopted at many of our works. Phis is likely to lead to lower prices during any period of de- pression ; and as this is exactly the time when foreign competition is at its worst, it may be found -unprofitable then to continue dumping on any large scale. This is the way to meet the present difficulty, and not resort to fiscal changes, which cannot but fail to be injurious to the trade of th 3 country as a whole. "Better bear the ills we have than fly to others that we know not of."

From the German wire-drawing trade comes a pitiful wail of its inability to compete with English and other foreign competitors. Dumping," it appears, is at the root of the mischief. The rolled wire, which is the raw material of the trade, is controlled by a great syndicate, which "dumps,' its material abroad au 140 s. per ton, while the German consumer has to pay 2505. Hence an agitation has been started to prevent "foreign firms of wire-drawers being fed at the expense of the German industry." Unless something is done it appears exceedingly probable that the German wire-drawing industry will be crushed out of existence by the competition of British and other wire produced at a cheaper rate owing to the oper- ation of the Protectionist tariff in Germany. Yet our new Protectionists persist in assuring us tha Protection ensures to German manufacturers the supply of their home market!

9ersonal. Alderman James Fairclough has been appointed a .governor of the Grammar School. -Mr. and Mrs. Thomas E. Sangster, of Manchester, . have been appointed manager and manageress of the Conservative Club, Sankey-street, in. succession to Mr. and Mrs.. G-. Watkins who have resi,olicieldpitely. positions which they have so creditably "There were Over 200 applicants. Mr. Sangster, was for four years steward of the .Ardwick Conservative 'Club, and on his resignation was not only accorded hearty vote of thanks- for his services, but elected an honorary member. Sankey Harriers. • The members of this club mustered in strong force .at the headquarters, Black Horse Inn on Saturday afternoon. Three packs—slow,.intermelliary and fast —were turned . out, each at five minutes intervals. Seven miles of good country were traversed in the direction of Penketh and Bold. The novices showed -up splendidly, keeping well in the running. J. Riley captained the packs, and J. H. Prince acted as whip. Championship Prize for a Warrington Baker. Mr. Toft, 98, Bridge-street, winner of the " Baker and Confectioner" Challenge Cup, London, 1900 and 1902, has been successful in winning the Champion- -ship Prize in competition for the best Hovis Bread. This competition was arranged by the Hovis Bread Flour Company, Ltd., and took place in Manchester . -on the 15th inst.' the judge being Alderman W. F. -liowkett, J.P., of Birmingham, trustee and member of the Council of the National Association of Master Bakers. A New Debating Society. The first meeting in connection with the forming of a debating society in the Fairfield Ward was held •on Tuesday evening last, There were about twelve _young Men present, and it was -unanimously decided to proceed with the promotion of the' society. The meeting. then proceeded to oppOint the necessary Officers, Committee, &c., and discussed the proposed 'programme for the opening session. Considering the 'enthusiasm shown at its first meeting, a good future is promised for the Fairfield Literary and Debating LADIES BEST GLACE BOOTS and SHOES, UNDER the CLOCK, MUD GE-STREET.—Ad7t-• q` Glimpses of Ruskin." • • This was the subject of an interesting lecture de- livered before the members of the Warrington Society -on Thursday evening by the Rev. R. Wilkins Rees. Alderman Bennett presided and in his introductory Tremarks expressed the indebtedness of the Society to the Corporation for granting a renewal of the lease of the Old Academy-,--The lecturer dealt .with his subject most ably, describing Ruskin as an ;unsurpassed prose writer and a Strenuous teacher. The most interesting portion of the lecture had refer- qende to Ruskin's visits to Hawarden, his couversa. lions with Mr. Gladstone, and subsequent correspond- ,ence mostly with the younger daughter of the house. Ruskin was .a prolific letter-writer and his letters were thoroughly characteristic of hint At the close ..of the lecture there was a short discussion,taken part iii by Mr. C. Madeley, Mr J.. Moore Murray, Mr. T. May and Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins and the lecturer was . .cordially thanked. Social Gathering at Ellesmere-street. ' A social gathering of teachers of a specially interesting character was held in the Ellesmere-street alission Hall on Thursday evening, the principal bjtct of which was the • presentation of a memento .0f esteem to each of three late teachers of the school "un the occasion of their marriage. The recipients— all of whom were present—were Mrs. Skelhorn, nee Miss Moore;- Mrs. Gfbbous, nee Miss Bates; and Mrs. Dutto nee Miss Whittaker, all of whom u, had been long connected with the school. After a,very inviting tea, daintly served by wives and 'friends of the teachers led by Mrs. Sherburn, the presentations were made by Mr. John Barlow. Mr. John P..llison and Mrs. Pattison , as fellow teachers very 'aPpropriately and feelingly expressed the good wishes of the subscribers for the future happiness and well !ring of the newly-wedded friends and their husbands. he superintendent of the school, Mr. W. H. lierburn, who presided, cheerily supported all the remarks of the previous speakers. Music and parlour ,;•,^larnes followed, while songs were given by Mr. H. H. Taylor and others. ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLASb NIENERAL WATERS.—Advt.
MEMO

The Mayor's Gift. The bust of His Majesty the King, which the Mayor has kindly presented to the town, will be unveiled by the Mayoress at the Mayoral " At Home " to be held in the Parr Hall on Thursday eyening next. The bust will be on view to the general public at the Parr Hall on Friday and Saturday next, from 10 a.m. until 4 p.m. each day.

The Mayor and the Council. Alderman Sutton will move a resolution at the next meeting of the Town Council on Tuesday evening con- veying the thanks of the Council to the Mayor for the satisfactory manner in which he has discharged the responsible duties devolving upon him as MAyor and chief Magistrate.

The Cheshire Potato Crop, Cheshire farmers- .attending Crewe market on Saturday are loud in their complaints as to the enormous damage caused to the potato crop by the abnormal rainfall. Some of the potato lands are still under water, and the tubers which cannot be g3t in are rotting from disease. At the market on Satur- day the price of Cheshire potatoes rose from 4s. 6d. to 7s. per load. Parish Church Sale of Work.

A. saln of work iii aid of the Parish Church Restora- tion Fund, for which I'lso is required, was opened in Fairfield Schools on Thursday afternoon and con- tinued yesterday. Lady G-reenall performed the opening cremony on Thursday, and Mrs. John Coxon discharged that duty yesterday, the Rector presiding on each occasion. We regret that owing to unusual pressure on our space we are unable to report the event as fully as we had desired. On Thursday the proceeds amounted to :£93 and the amount raised yesterday was £52 10s. Miss Massyjwill reopen the sale this afternoon. Success of a Warrington Student. .

Miss Ethel Mottram,;ho recently obtained a Ches- hire County Council Scholarship of £5O per annum for three years, has been successful in passing the admission examinations for the Royal College of Art, South Kensington. These examinations comprise painting from life, modelling,architecture, and design. The admissions are classed (1) those paying college fees, (2) those who obtain free studentships which are awarded on the position of the candidate s at th examination. We congratulate Miss Mottram on her admission as a free student of the Royal College of Art.

Workmen's Tram Tickets. It is announced that on and after lionday next workmen's train tickets will be issued between Latch- ford and Rylands-street. Early morning cars will leave Rylands-street at 5-10, 5-40, and 6-10 a.m., leaving Latchford at 5-25, 5-55, and 6-25 a.m. The tickets will be available only for the journey on which they are issued, on cars leaving the termini up to 8 a.m. and after a p.m. on ordinary week-days, and up to 8 a.m. and between 12 noan and 2 p.m. on Satur- days. The fare will be each way, and the tickets can only be used by artisans, mechanics, and daily labourers going to and returning from work. ,

The Proposed New Street. The following is a copy of a resolution passed by the Warrington Property Owners' Association at a meeting held on Wednesday, the 21st inst. A copy has been forwarded to the 'town Clerk asking him to plane the same before the next meeting of the Town Council :—" That this Association representing a rateable value of upwards of £lOO,OOO. records its strong objection to the proposed street leading from Rylands-street to Sankey-street being made, owing to its close proximity to Bridge-street, and to the heavy burden of rates; and further that if a second street is required, it is of opinion that .a 40ft. street is inadequate. The Association also begs to draw your attention to the mat that in your arrangements for the purchase aud completion of the said land, the question of betterment has apparently not been considered."
BASSINETTES AND MAIL CARTS in latest art
shades.-=J. S. G,IRLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51,53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Wild Flower Competition. _ _ _ _

Just before the school holidays notice was sent to the various elementary schools in the town that prizes were offered by Mr. Linnaeus Greening, for collec- tions of wild flowers gathered during the holidays. Twelve schools responded to the invitation and sent parties of children, upwards of 300 altogether, to the preparatory lectures delivered by Mr. Deane, assistant curator of the Museum. Four orders were selected, viz, the cabbage, pink, parsley and sage families. The prizes have been awarded to the following com- petitors :—Herbert Womersley (People's College), first; Ruby Wats (Wycliffe School), second.; Fred Gilbert (Heath Side Schools), third. The successful collections are being exhibited for a short time in the bird-room.
a-
"Notes on a Journey Round the World.",

At the weekly meeting of the Wycliffe Young People's Sooiety on Monday evening, Mrs. Ziba Armitage, of Newton Bank, gave an interesting account of her journey round the world. There was a large attendance, presided over by the Rev. John Yonge. In a pleasant conversational style, Mrs. Armitage described the places and scenes which in- terested her on her tour. Perhaps the mot interest- ing part of the lecture was that devoted to a descrip- tion of what she saw on her visit to the Tonga islands and Samoa in the Snith seas. The natural beauty of these islands, and the habits and customs of the inhabitants were described. The lecture was rendered additionally interesting by the exhibition of a large number of curios brought from the islands At the close, Mrs. Armitage was heartily thanked fo . her lecture, Nthe proposition of Mr. Bindloss,seconde r by Mr. J. Hawthorn, and supported by the Chairma d Ambulance Competition.

_ . . • The annual competition for the Crosfield Challesge Shield took place in the Gymnasium on Saturday last. The judges were District Superintendent Secretary A. L. G-arnett of Oldham, and Doctor *Pooley cif Dalton-in-Furness. A preliminary contest took place first between Warrington and Liverpool to decide which should be left in for the final, and this resulted in a win for the hitter. The teams left in for the final then, were Briarfield, Hulme, Preston, and Liverpool,' Crompton and Kendal failing to • arrive in time to compete. After a stiff contest the judges awarded the teams Ist, 2nd, 3rd and 4th in the order named. Captain G. R. Crosfield made a neat speech, and kindly presented the shield to the winning team, also a box of the firm's well-known Erasmic Soap to each individual, at the same time inviting all the teams and visitors to become the guests of his brother Mr. Arthur Crosfield at the Patten Arum Sixty sat down to partake of the feast, and did full justice to the g,031 things provided. After dinner Captain Crosfield gave the toast of the King, and after that had been honoured Colonel Trimble, C.M.G.Y.D.,Deputy Commissioner Of. No. 4 District, rose, and after thanking Captain and Mr. Arthur Crosfield for their kind hospitality to the Ambulance men present, and for the interest they took , in Ambulance matters generally, asked all present to drink to their health. The toast was drunk with musical honours. After several songs and recitations had been rendered, the party broke up to catch their respective trains. Poor Children's Summer Camp. Very satisfactory reports were submitted at a meet- ing of the Poor Children's Summer Camp Committee held in the old School Attendance Offices on. Tuesday , afternoon. In the absenee of Mr. F. W. Monks the chair was taken by Mr. J. Moore llurray. There were also present :—Mr. W. 11. J. Jenkins (hon. secretary), Mr, A. H. Lee (hon. treasurer), Inspector Hackett (N.S.P.C.C:), and Mr. Henry Taylor (police court missionary). The Hon. Treasurer rep orted that the total receipts (amounted to :£167 ISs. 7d., and the .expenses to ,t 1.28 25., which left a balance in hand ,of £39 16s. 7d. There are also cooking utensils, &c., to , the value of about :£6O, wliich have been stocked ready for use in the next camp. Mr. Jenkins, in his report, spoke of the splendid time the boys spent, and said that by means of the camp poor boys, who would not otherwise know what a wholesome change from home surroundings meant were . brought into an atmosphere in the highest ' degree conducive to their , physical well-being. The "intolerable snobbery of life " was leavened and alleviated by findino• that there 'were real friends anxious and willing to dO all within- their power to brighten the young lives. A feeling of " chumship " sprung up which had a most wholesome effect on the boys' demeanour and bearing after a few days. Their intelligence was brightened, and a keener interest taken in their surroundings. The report ° and treasurer's statement were unanimously' adopted. A sub-committee consisting of the Rev. W. Bracecamp, and the Secretary and Treasurer was appointed to make inquiries with a view to securing a site for a permanent camp. The Chairman remarked that if the use of a building were obtained they might look further into the suggestiou of using it as a convales- cent home. Messrs. F. J. Emson, F. H. Aukland, A. Malcolm, and Gordon Dawson., the officers of the camp, were specially ,thanked for their services, and thanks were also accorded to the Secretary, Treasurer, and the subscribers.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday October 24, 1903.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday October 24, 1903.
RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
FATALITY AT NORTON PRIORY.

On Tuesday, Richard West, in the employ of Sir Richard Brooke, Bart., of Norton Priory, near Run- corn, was killed. He vias, cleaning the windows of the tower of the Priory, when the ladder on which he was standing broke in two completely, and he fell to the ground, a distance of twenty-three feet. His head was badly fractured, and Dr. Carruthers, of Halton, was quickly summoned, but West died a few minutes after his arrival. Deceased, who was twenty-four years of uge, was over six feet in height, and had served through the South African War with the 2nd Cheshire Volun- teers.

div.head: SHOCKING NEtLECT CASE AT WIDNES.
div.p: SHOCKING NEtLECT CASE AT WIDNES.

At Widnes on Monday morning before the Mayor and Alderman Wareing, John and Mary M`Mahon, resid- ing at 55, Victoria-street, were charged with neglecting their four children in a manner likely, to cause them suffering.—Mr. Knowles prosecuted on behalf of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, and presented to the court a shocking string of facts. The case had been under observation for a long time, and, despite numerous warnings, no improve- ment was made. The house betokened destitution. The children were emaciated and ill-fed. The house was frightfully dirty and devoid of furniture, the only utensils in the house being a frying-pan, basin, and cup, The man's habits were drunken, and he was described as a drunken, lazy fellow. The wife had, never been seen the worse for drink, and, according to Inspector Hob- den's evidence, she appeared to be thoroughly cowed and kept half-starved. The husband, in asking for a, chance, said that he was to blame, and not his wife. He had never given her a penny for three weeks. The bench dismissed the charge against the woman, and sent M'Ma.hon to gaol for six months.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
EARLESTOWN MAN BURIED ALIVE.

Mr. Brighouse, coroner, held an inquest at the Waggon Hotel, Haydock, on Monday, on the body of Thomas Brown, collier, of 14, King-street, Earlestown, who on Thursday last was killed in the Wood Pit, Haydock, belonging to Messrs. It. Evans and Co. Mr. Hall, Government inspector of mines, attended. Deceased was killed by a fall of roof whilst following hisemploy- ment. Zacharia Case gave evidence that he saw the men at work late at night. Later he found that a huge fall of roof had taken place. Deceased was btiried under the fall, and when dug out he was quite dead. A verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. EARLESTOWN CHARITY CRICKET MATCH.

The disposal of the proceeds arising from the Police v. Press and Tradesmen's cricket match at Newton-le- Willows during the summer months was completed on Friday. The balance in hand was £3B 12s. 9d., of which £2O has been given to the Northern Police Orphanage, £5 to Earlestown Medical and Surgical Aid Society, £2 2s. each •to Warrington Infirmary and National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children, £3 Bs. 9d. to an Earlestown family, and £3 each to two Newton families in needy circumstances, thus disposing of the whole balance. " Votes of thanks to the hon. treasurer (Inspector Foster) and the hon secretaries (Mr. J, Sandiford and Sergeant Bancks) and to the committee were passed.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ACCIDENT TO A. ST. HELENS DOCTOR.

About noon on Saturday Dr. Masson, St. Helens, met with a rather serious accident at the toll-bar, Prescot- road. He ,was going his round, when his horse was startled by a passing motor. The animal ran away at a rapid pace into Lugsmore-lane, and collided with a gas lamp, with the result that the trap was wrecked, and the doctor and his coachman were both thrown out. Dr. _Masson received a severe fracture of the leg, and the coachman had his collar-bone broken. Dr. Graham and other medical men were quickly on the scene,and the patients were subsequently removed home. A ST. HELENS HUSBAND'S TROUBLE.

Thomas Forster, collier, of Carnaxvon-street, was charged, at St. Helens, on Monday.with wife desertion. Relieving Officer Richardson said the man's wife and three children were admitted to the workhouse on the 10th ult, and the man had absconded.--Forster said his wife had left him eighteen times this year.—When Mrs. Forster appeared in the dock the man said she had been locked up.—The police said that on August 10th the woman was sent to goal for seven days for prostitution. Forster said that was why he went away, and he thought it was about time he got a home in another part of the country.— Forster, on oath, said he had been laughed at and pointedat fdr two years because of • the woman. He went into Yorkskire, and then into Wales, and at the end of five weeks he got work and communicated with his son, whom he had asked to take care of the children The son's wife said they took the children to their house, but the mother came and took them off to the workhouse.—The chairman said they must certainly dismiss the charge of desertion.—Forster agreed to pay 3s per week to refund the cost t 3 the guardians on con- dition that he was free of" that woman " (laughter).

div.head: BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHFORD.
div.p: BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHFORD.
Annual Sale of Work.

This annual sale has been the means of assisting the treasurer to keep a clear balance sheet, and gives an opportunity to outside friends to assist in carrying on the work. div.head: Child's Sad Death.
div.p: Child's Sad Death.

Coroner Brighouse conducted an inquest at the Police Station on Wednesday afternoon touching the death of Catherine Booth Smith, the six-year-old daughter of Samuel Booth, plasterer, 2, Amelia-street. The evidence showed that on Thursday of last week deceased was left in the kitchen, her mother having occasion to visit a neighbour's sick child. The mother had only just entered the neighbour's house when she heard screams mid on rushing home found deceased in the kitchen with her clothing on fire. A. verdict of "Accidental death " was returned.
BEST BOOTS FOR. ALL.—UNDER theCLOCK..—AdVt. A Compliment to the Borough Trefiurer.

At the meeting of the Finance and Estate Corn- mittee,the Borough Treasurer laid before the Com- mittee the Order of the Local Government Board adjusting the financial relation between the County and the Borough. It was resolved that the Com- mittee deisre to record their appreciation of the able services rendered by the Borough Treasurer in con- nection with the satisfactory settlement of the claims of the County and the Borough, and that an honorarium of fifty guineas be voted to him for such services.

div.head: Draughts --Lancashire v. Yorkshire._
div.p: Draughts --Lancashire v. Yorkshire._

The eighth inter-county match between Lancashire and Yorkshire will be played to-day at Leeds, be- tween teams numbering 25 players aside. The pick of the players of both counties will be engaged in the contest, which will take place in the Trades Hall, Upper Fountain Street, Leeds, commeneing at 4 p.m., and concluding at 7 p.m. At the time of writing the full composition of the Lancashire team has not been officially declared. Two Warrington players, F. Dunne and J. Roberts, are included, and it was ex- pected that there would be eight players from Liver- pool, the remaining fifteen being made up from Man- chester and East Lancashire. At present Lancashire hold a lead of one match, and no doubt great efforts will be made to retain the laurels, though the visiting team is undoubtedly always at a disadvantage in these encounters.

FOR CLASS AND CHIN. of every description try F. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. Forthcoming Local Government Board Inquiry. The Local Government Board have appointed Major C. E. Norton, R.E., to hold an inquiry at the Town Hall on Tuesday next, into the application of the Corporation for sanction to borrow £lO,OOO for works carried out under the Private Street Works Act, 1892; £18,315 for purposes of public street improvements, and £1,750 for the purposes of Sankey Recreation Ground. The loan for private street works is necessitated by the decision of the Council to extend the time for the repayment of private street accounts to seven years. The public street improvements are in Bridge-street and other parts of the town. With reference to the Sankey Recreation Ground, Lord Lilford has given two of tile four acres acquired for this purpose. In the days of the Little Sankey Parish Council, Lord Lilford made the gift of two acres of land for a recreation ground, off Liver- pool. This Site was found too small and unsuitable and the larger site which has now been acquired will better suit the needs of the neighbourhood.

div.head: MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
div.p: THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.
THE NOMINATIONS.

As far as we have been able to ascertain the follow- ing is the full list of candidates for the elections on November 2nd : Wards. Candidates. TOWN HALL Councillor Lord, WHITECROSS Councillor Barton, BEWSEY Councillor W. Pierpoint, ORFORD f Councillor Peacock, ( Mr. F. Stott, f Mr. John Ashley, ST. JOHN'S ( Mr. John Maginn. (Councillor Hulse, FAIRFIELD t Mr. J. Povey. tam ~ { Councillor John Evans, HOWLEY • Mr. W. Benson, - Mr. C. Roddy, ( Mr. James Critchley, S. AUSTIN'S 1 Mr. T. H. Ashcroft. (Mr. S. B. Stringer, L ATCHFORD t. Mr. W. J. Wilson.

To-day (Saturday) is the last day for receiving nomi- nations, and papers must be handed in at the Town Clerk's office before 5 o'clock. According to the nomi- nation papers already received, there will be contests in six of the nine wards into which the town is divided. As yet no one has come forward in opposition to the return of Councillor Lord for Town Hall Ward, Coun- cillor Barton for Whitecross Ward, and Coun- cillor Pierpoint for Bewsey Ward. Mr. J. Rymer Young, J.P., was invited by the Liberal tom- mittee to contest Town Hall Ward, but declined. lln St. Austin's Ward Mr. James Critchley will oppose Mr. T. H. Ashcroft, the official nominee of the Non-Trading Committee. In his address Mr Critchley says he is in favoup of a full and impartial inquiry without further delay, as to the trading of the Council for the last few years. Mr. E. Plinston has definitely decided not to contest Orford Ward, where Mr. F. Stott, the candidate' of the Independent Labour Party, is opposing the re-election of Councillor Pea- cock. As far as we can gather there appears to have been some misunderstanding in the matter, Mr. Plinston being under the impression that two vacancies wOuld have to he tilled on November 2nd, owing to the retirement of Councillor Upson. This, however, is not the cake, as a bye-election will have to be ar- ranges for a later date. Counzillor Sampson will not attempt to retain his seat as the representative of i Latchford Ward, but Mr. W. J. Wilson s coming for- ward as the Conservative candidate. His opponent is Mr. S. B, Stringer, the nominee of the Non-trading Committee. Councillor T. J. Hulse has accepted the invitation to stand again for Fairfield Ward, but owing to the delicate state of his health he will not, it is anticipated, be able to take an active part in the contest. Councillor John Evans has been prevailed upon at the eleventh hour to contest Howley Ward. Here there will in all .pro- bability be a three-cornered fight. Mr. W. Benson is the official Non-Trading candidate, and Mr. Charles Roddy, licensee of the " Royal Arms," Bank-street, ha also decided to enter the field. He informed our repre- sentative last evening that he was coming out as a "Non-Trader." Mr. John Maginn has opened hii campaign in St. John's Ward and his address appears in our advertising oolumns. "I shall continue" he says "to insist upon a full and searching inquiry into the alleged illegal trading with the Corporotion by the members or their friends I mean a real inquiry held immediately for T am convinced that no real reforms can be effected until , the present campaign of abuse and scurrility has been brought to an end."

div.head: FISCAL PROBLEM.
div.p: THE FISCAL PROBLEM.

MR. EDWIN WOODS REPLIES TO CRITICS. Sir,—ln your issue of October 10th I ventured to ' state the loss to this country if 1,000 tons of rods were bought from abroad instead of being manufactured in England. This seems to have disturbed the minds of a few people who have thought proper to reply to my letter but did not sign their names. I never reply to any letters unless the writer's name is attached, but I don't think they can feel offended if I pass them over this time. I mayjust mention in passing that I am under the impression that " Basanio "was in great pain or suffering from irritation when penning his epistle' and I hope that whatever was troubling him has by this ' time passed away. I Now with respect to Mr. Parker's reply. He must I excuse me if I don't agree with him, as we seem to hold opposite vieWs on this matter. Before going further Ilet me state that lam not in favour of taxing raw material from any country, and I would advocate that all corn and food should come in duty free from the Colonies. Mr. Parker says: "From my point of view it seems that, as buyers of anything cheap that the foreigner can offer, we benefit the industry with which we are associated, and add to the prosperity of our coantry." I will ask Mr. Parker if he thinks this out- weighs the seviousness of our men in the iron trade remaining idle while foreigners are d0i1y,.6 the work. Now, for the sake of reasoning, carry this further and say, let us stop all our works and not manufacture any- thing, and •purchase all goods from the foreigner. According to Mr. Parker's argument this will be of the greatest possible benefit to our country. But in that case what will be the position of the working man whose means of livelihood will be taken away from him ? Again Mr. Parker says, "it should be certainly one of I our objects to safeguard as far as wise and practicable I the mineral wealth of our island, and anyone like Mr. Woods who buys iron upon which other countries have lavished their national resources, is a benefactor to this country and does his countrymen no injustice." Again carry this point to its logical conclusion. Don't get any ore, coal, or limestone in Great Britain, and what will be the result? Our men must starve while men in other countries are working full time. Let us see what took place in 1902. The total imports from foreign countries of manufactured iron and steel into England amounted to 1,134,000 tons. Now let us see the loss in labour this will be to the working man alone for 12 months. It requires about 3,402,000 tons of ore and about 793.800 tons of limestone, and about 1,701,000 tons of coal, which kturned into coke'to make the ore into pig iron, and about 510,300 tons of coal to turn the pig iron into billets, and about 623,000 tons of coal to make the billets into steel, so that to produce 1,134,000 tons of steel, we see that it is a loss of labour in producing 7,030,100 tons of raw material, which, added to the loss of the steel and iron bought from foreign countries, makes a total of 8,164,100 tons. Up to nowl have dealt only with Iron and Steel not worked up into machinery. Now take the imports of machinery etc. which were poured into this country by the foreigner from October 1892 to October 1893 (say for 12 months). The total amount is £5,893,050 sterling Add to this £5,893,050 the value of the 1,134,000 tons of manufactured irpn and steel previously referred to, which at an average of £6 per tort amounts to £6,804,000 and you get a total of £12697,050 worth of goods imported in one branch of trade alone. The total imports of all manufactures for 1902 was 140 millions, and as it is admitted that one half of the value repre- sents wages, we have here a clear loss of 70 millions last year which would have been earned in weekly wages by the working classes of this country. On the face of these Ifigures I ask,whyallowall these millions worth of goods 'to come into England duty free from foreigners who tax our goods, While our people could make them,'when if we produced them in England our men would have this money to spend with the shopkeepers,and the shop- keepers and men who saved money would build houses &c., and this would givean impetus to the building and other kindred trades, and the men who work in the building trade would circulate their earnings amongst the shopkeepers again, and so improve trade ganerally that men in all classes and professions would benefit by it throughout Great Britain? I have neither time nor inclination for newspaper correspondence, but I have felt it to be my duty at this time of crisis to state my views, which, though they may not accord with the theories of political economists, have been formed in the practical school of business life.
Yours etc., EDWIN WOODS.

div.head: Mr. Parker on Mr. Chamberlain's Newcastle Speech.
div.p: Mr. Parker on Mr. Chamberlain's Newcastle Speech.

Sir,—Mr. Chamberlain's task at Newcastle was no light one. He had to answer the arguments of six of the ablest statesmen in the ranks .of the Unionist, and Liberal parties. The answer will no doubt be considered as able or weak according to the point of view of those who approach it. It is only as we come to details of these answers that we can hope to form a correct con- ception of their strength or weakness. Dealing with Mr. Asquith's contentionthat the selec- tion of 1872 as a starting point was a misuse of figures, 'and,that it was unfair because this was the year in which values rose abnormally through the high priced exports which went to France and Germany to make up the waste caused by the Franco-German war, Mr. Chamberlain answers this by saying in effect, "Very well if this year does;not please you,we will take five year periods. Take the quinquemnal period 1870-1875, and compare it with 1895-1900." But in so doing Mr. Chambe- rlain commits the same error that invalidated the com- parison of 1872)with 1902. I have before me the Board of Trade Chart in the Blue Book recently issued to assist this enquiry, a chart Mr. Chamberlain would doubtless have before him in framing his argument. This diagram indicates the movements of exports by a line which rises and falls according to the variations in the values of exports from 1872 to 1902. Unfortun- ately it is impracticable to reproduce the chart in this letter. My readers would see at a glance that in the quinquennial period 1870-1875 the indicating line, starting at 1870 the beginning of tile war, suddenly rises from a normal point, touches its highest in 18711, and does not reach the normal level until the end of .1875. The shape made by this line in the five years looks exactly like one of the precipitous Alps, say the Matterhorn rising from, and descending to a plain. It will be seen that the quinquennial period 1870-1875 embraces this pyramid, and so invalidates the compari- son.• It is somewhat significant that the Comptroller General, Sir Alfred Bateman expressly warns his readers against taking this period for comparison, and it is singular that in face of this warning Mr. Chamberlain should adopt it as his starting point and when it is pointed out to him that the year 1872 is not a fair one instead of frankly acknowledging this error, repeats it in another form. The Board of Trade Blue Book avoids the error by taking normal periods, and compares the relative growth of exports per head of the population as follows.
Average Average 1875-1879. 1894-1899. 2 s. d. 2 s. d. United Kingdom France Germany United States 2 16 3 2 18 4 _ _ . . ....

It is thus clear that taking the visible exports per I head of the population in the four countries, there is very little difference in the relative growth. We appear to have fallen behind a little, although we still occupy a place a long way ahead of the other countries. If however, we take the years 1900, 1901, 1902, and the nine months of 1903, it will be found that we are again forging ahead at a greater speed than the other coun- tries. It, must however be remembered that the above figures are calculated, on the visible exports. If the invisible portion were added, as it ought to be, the English figures would he inceeased far more than the othersffinasmuch as we now do half of the carrying trade ' of the world. To make it clear to those who have not givenspecial attention to the matter, the earnings of our ships areclassed as "invisible exports "because they are not included in any declaration of value. Our exportsare the declared valueat the port of departure, but the foreigner has to pay the freight either to the shipowner, or to the sender. in the Blue Book just issued, these freight earnings are now reckoned as 90 millions per annum. Going back to say 1872 and reckoning by the tontwe, we have increased our invisible yearly exports bby 48 millions, while the increase of Germany under this head is only 5 millions. France has no increase. and United States has a con- siderable decrease. But again looking at the curve indicating the weight of exports, apart from the value, we can observe how steady, and eontinuous, the growth of our exports is, and it shows clearly that the rise of 1872 was the result of an appreciation of value, and scarcely affected bulk. Those in the leather trade can remember how leather went up after the declaration of war four pence per pound in a week. Weight is not an absolutely correct guide any more than value, but of ; the two it is the more reliable, and we have since 1872 , nearly doubled the weight of our exports. l' Turning his attention to the growth of imports Mr. Chamberlain tells us "In 1872 we imported 63 millions of manufactures and 139 millions in 1902." Now what Mr. Chamberlain calls "manufactures" the Board of Trade classes as "manufacturise and partly manufactured goods." The distinction may appear to be small but it is one which largely affects the argu- ment. in these partly manufactured goods. are such things as oil, tallow, manures, glue leather, iron in its, various crude forms and all other like things whichmay have passed through Tone stage of their manufacture,but which to our manufacturers are raw goods. In speak- ing of these Mr. Chamberlain says " they could just as well have been made in this country" What absurd folly is this? Take the case of hemlock tanned leather we buy in quantity from the United States. This has largely contributed to make the prosperity of towns like Leicester, Kettering and Northampton, it has increased the spending power of the people by lowering the price of their footwear, and has aided us in otir exports. Mr. Chamberlain's statement that we could make it just as well here, as far as it applies to ' our imported leather is lsnown to every tanner to be utterly erroneous. How could any British tanner having to depend on European tanning agents expect to be able to make leather at the same cost and quality as

the American tanner with hemlock bark at his door cost- ing only 21s. per ton? Now, what is true of the tanning trade is equally applicable to most other industries, and those engaged ; in such will agree that a very small proportion of these Warrington partly manufactured goods "could be made just as well Runcorn here. Doubtless some of these goods could be pro- St. Helens duced at home but only at a greater cost, and this the Leigh consumer would have to pay. Any limitation of im- Widnes ports will react upon and lessen our power to export. Wigan Mr. Chamberlain altogether mis-states the claim of the Free Traders in respect to the importance of imports in judging of the country's prosperity. What is claimed is, that exports are only of importance for what we get for them in a word, our imports. Suppose I export goods and the firm to whom they are sent fails, and there is only an apparent composition of two shillings in the pound which the lawyers take, what benefit would I have by this export? Nothing at all. The export is only of benefit to me for what I get in return for it. So it is in national affairs. We do not send goods out of the country for the fun of the thing, or as a gift, we export for what we get in return, and the greater the value of imports we can get in return for our exports the greater is our wealthandprosperity. Mr. Chamberlain says, no doubt jocularly. "How [ wish that I could deal with economic facts." There are a great many of his countrymen who wish so too, and what strikes us in Mr. Chamberlain's speeches is that whenever he leaves generalities and perorations about Empire, and comes down to figures, he invariably misuses them, and manifests an unfortunate facility for inaccuracy in his efforts to compel economic facts to adjust themselves to his political aspirations.
• CHARIiES E. PARKER. Penketh, October `j:lnd, 1903.
The South-west Lancashire L ugue Table up-to-d.at as follows : FR Pts. •

To-day, Warrington renew the struggle with Swinton. The Blues have a very favourable record to look back upon in .their Northern Union engagements against Warrington, but I shall be much surprised if that record is not besmirched after to-day. Time was when Swinton could"wt win at Warrington, and they should certainly find it impossible to win to-day. The " Lions " have been in a very bad way this season, and last Saturday succumbed by 11-0 to Broughton Rangers. Chorley, Wallwork, and Burris, are all re- ported crocked, but a big effort will doubtless be made. Warrington ought to win; but they will need to show much better form than they have done in past engagements with Swinton.

For once in a way Warrington should have a full team. Harris and Dickenson are both in their accus- tomed places and It. Bate receives a trial at half back with Davies. Mahoney is debarred from playing by the working-clause. The team will therefore be:. Hallam, full back; Fish, Isherwood, Dickenson and llarris, three quarters Davies and Bate half backs; Boardman, Morrison, Naylor, Morals, Swift, Harin.er Lunt and Edmonds dn forwards.

The new scrummage rule proved a bit awkward on. Saturday, • and it ,vas amusing at Widnes to see Referee Priestly craning his neck to count the num- ber of men in the front row. Penalties were frequent until the men realised the necessity of packing" three three, two." Could the correct scrummage forma- tion have anything to do with Warrington holding the Widnes eight so comfortably ? Further trial is necessary before one can pass an opinion on the working of the rule.

With regard to the 12-aside game, the critics in Yorkshire are very dubious and openly suspicious. They appear to think that the aim of the Lancashire advocates of the change is to extinguish and render useless the good old Yorkshire forward. Ido not see myself that there will be any less requirement of good scrummakters. There will certainly be no room for aldermanicishirkers. On the 12-aside topic" Old Ebor'' says: "The 12-aside system to my mind is largely exploited in the interests of present Lancashire players, and I have a suspiCion that the extraordinary tactica which have crept-into forward play—and which origin- ated in Lancashire—have been largely designed with a view of bringing all forward play into contempt,and therefore of hastening the alteration to the 12-aside game. No doubt this opinion will be scouted in certain quarters, but nevertheless it is one that I feel to have some justification in forming and holding."

Delivering himself further this well-known critic adds: " Equally illogical will be found,in my opin- the notion that a team of 12 men can be run at less cost than 15. If better results are expected from 12 men than from 15, is it not obvious that the 12 will require, and, in facr, will be entitled to a better re- ward? Moreover, I am perfectly certain, even from the little I have seen of the game, that 12 aside is only.possible to highly-trained men, and the demand for the abolition of the employment clause and the adoption of out-and-out professional- ism will finally prove irresistible. I don't suppose these remarks will be at all palatable in certain quarters, but I do know that they reflect a very large proportion of opinion in Yorkshire, outside the official committee-rooms. We know very well what made Yorkshire so long in the ascendant. Yorkshirernen sold' some of • their birth- right when they became parties to the crazy punt-out rule, and now they have been asked to eclipse them- selves altogether by sanctioning a style that wchild make football a game purely for . sprinters and handlers, and of little good to man of physique and strength."

The Lancashire-Cheshire County match, 12-aside, will be played at Broughton on Wednesday afternoon, when, perhaps `Old Ebor " will be present and favour the public with some additional comments on the game.

div.head: MACEDONIAN CRISIS.
div.p: THE MACEDONIAN CRISIS.
NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. By " Ovalist."

There were at least two contented teams on Satur- day evening, and these two hailed from. Warrington and Widues. Yet they had during the day; played one another a very keen game resulting in a pointless draw. Warrington were content because they took a depleted side away with them and had not much hope of gaining points, while Widnes also had reason to rejoice in sharing the spoil with a team admittedly much stronger and more cal43le. As the Chemidals had, Moreover, only acquired one solitary point from all their previous engagements they (lid a good day's work in doubling their assets in the League, table.

One rarely sees a good game between South-West Lancashire teams, and particularly between Widnes and Warrington. The local rivalry is too keen to allow of any indulgence in the finer arts of football. Every man is in deadly earnest, and this is manifested by the way he ,smothers an opponent when he gets the chance., Widnes v. Warrington is no parlour per- formance, but a go-ahead "get there first " struggle which suits the eager partizan though it may not exhilarate the casual observer.

The Widnesians started with high hopes of success. for the forces on the other side were not at full strength whereas they themselves had " all on." They soon found their level, however. If Warrington were in a poor way, they themselves failed to exhibit any superiority. In fact there was scarcely ever any prospect of a score. True, Warrington attacked with some persistence in the first half, when they had the assistance of a goodly breeze, hut the work behind the pack was so shockingly poor that the homesters were never in great danger. Fish did appear to have a chance once, but he threw it away, and nothing happened before the interval.

There may have been some'people who expected the Chemicals to sweep the board on resuming, and for a time they fostered That impression. . Hallam was very steady behind, however, and after the first few impetunus rushes had been staved off, Warrington found their feet again. They even penned the home lot behind the quarter line. and Fish frightened his foes by sprinting down to the corner. His effort fizzled out like a wet squib on meeting Tilley, for in attempting to punt over that worthy's head he placed the ball in his hands—to the relief of one section of the crowd and the disgust of another.

Warrington 'pegged away without much idea but plenty of determination until Wailing—the prospective Widnes right wing star artiste—did an original thing. Warrington had ventured to pass when this individual nipped in, gave the ball a violent thump which knocked it yards up the field and then regaining possession he ran like—something or other--and finally placed the ball behind the posts with the air of a conqueror. The Widnesians tossed somesanlts and yelled in a way that froze the blood, while visions of the South-West Lancashire championship floated through their dis- torted imagination. What the referee had been doing nobody knew. Perhaps he was out of breath and could not whistle in time, but he 'promptly disallowed the try on Isherwood's appeal and brought the ball back to the "scrum?' in the home quarter. Then the Wilderspool.whisper rent the air, while the Widnes folk were as downcast as if bankruptcy stared them in the face. The rest of the play was very tame and the result gives a fair indication of respective merit.

Not much praise can be fairly allotted. . The War- rington forwards however, gave a great display against an eight which has generally oerplayed them at all points. They quite held their own from start td finish, or Warrington's fall would unquestionably have been heavy. The Widnes folk were vastly sur- prised, for they quite counted on beating the visiting front rank to a pulp. Unfortunately, the Warrington halves were appalling. They never, 'hardly, did the right thing or the speedier men behind must have scored. Of course, not much could be' expected from an untried novice like Jordan, though he showed plenty of dash, and with practice may yet make a player. Davies was very poor,and the value of his work has faded away to nothing. He neither beats his man nor gives a go id pass, and the only thing in his favour is that he defended well. But a half-back should attack, not defend, and until Warrington find a man who can inaugurate an attack their future prospects are dismal. Nothing can be lost by a change, and there is an imperative call for that.

Hallam was seen at his best. In fact the two full backs are the only men worthy of individual praise. Both got through a heap of work splendidly. Else- where, Widnes are in a bad way for backs. Lally is the best and even he makes little headway, while the centres are deplorable. They must have been badly shown up if Dickenson had been on the visiting team. I think Tom L twi and 03. had better resuscitate "Butcher" Rispan.He may be slow, but he knows the game and can catch a ball. The other pair are helpless, except in the tackling line. Widnes prospects are far from bright at present.

The position of the League leaders was in Iv) way changed as the result of Saturday's games for they succeeded in drawing at Hull after a deadly struggle in which the Rovers led at half-timet but were in a minority five minutes frcm the finish. Hunslet easily defeated Batley, and now tie with the Rovers for second place, while Oldhatn, Bradford, and Warring- ton are all on the same mark. Huddersfield achieved a notable performance by recording,their first win, at the expense of Wigan. There are yet three clubs, Widnes, Keighley, and Wigan who have not yet won a match.

div.head: MR. R. H. PEARSON'S CONCERT. Madame Ella Russell's Visit to Warrington.
div.p: MR. R. H. PEARSON'S CONCERT. Madame Ella Russell's Visit to Warrington.

Warringtonians are promised a rich musical treat on Tuesday, November 3rd, when Madame Ella. Russell and a first-class concert party will appear at the Parr Hall. The concert has been arranged through the agency of Mr. R. H. Pearson whose enterprise, we hope, will meet with the reward at the hands of the music- loving public which it certainly deserves. Madame Ella Russell is so well-known that itis hardly necessary to call attention to her distinguished qualifications. Educated under Lagrange and San Giovanni, she entered upon her Italian career, exceptional successes following one another in Italy, Spain. France, Germany, Austria and Russia. Her achieve- ments led to her engagement at Covent Garden, and her debut as Gilda was one of the most successful of any connected with that historic opera house. Her appearance at the State concerts, Buckingham Palace, led to numerous commands to sing before the late Queen Victoria. We are sure that many of our townspeople will be anxious to avail themselves of the opportunity of hearing so distinguished a vocalist. The other mem- bers of the concert party—all artistes of repute are— Mdlle Rosa Olitzka (contralto), Mr. John Coates (tenor), Mr. Mans Hale (bass), Miss Muriel Elliot (pianist), M. Louis Pecskai (violinist) and Mr. Hamilton Harty (accompanist). Mdlle. Rosa Olitzka, the Polish contralto, whose international fame h brought her an engagement for the Wagnerian Festival at Berlin, is one of the most versatile artistesbefore the public. She has sung in the principal concerts in London Paris, Berlin, and Vienna. Mr. John Coates, the Yorkshire tenor, is one of the most successful of our English vocalists, both at home and in Germany, where he has sung in opera over fifty times during the past two years. He has been specially chosen to interpret many of the works Dr. Edgar. Mr. Marts Hale, the young English bass, has studied in Florence and Milan with various masters. He has a sympathetic voice with a high range, and received warm praise for his singing at the orchestral' concert he gave at St. James's Hall last November. Miss Muriel Elliott was born in London, and studied the piano with Miss Alice Clinton and Stavenhagen. She has toured in the chief provincial towns here as well as in Germany. M. Louis Pecskai, the well-known violinist, is a native of Trieste. He came to London when quite a youth, and has studied with various masters, including Wilhelmj. M. Pecskai has toured all over Europe, and has created quite a sensation in Italy, having been commanded several times by the Dowager Queen to play at the Court. Mr. Hamilton Harty was given his first oppor- tunity by Madame Ella Russell. She had been summoned to sing before the late Queen, and took the young Irish- man, fresh from his studies in Germany, to accompany her. Queen Victoria was pleased and asked Mdme. Russell to present him. He is now acknowledged to be one of the best accompanists in the kingdom.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

DARING BURGLARY.—For the 3rd time in a short period the premises of the Co-operative Society were broken into on Monday night, or the early hours of Tuesday morning. Since the last entry was effected, special precaution had been taken, and a dog kept on the premises. The animal had evidently been tampered with, for the entrance was effected from the yard. The catch on a pair of heavy double doors was forced open, and finally, a panel of another door to the shop was burst, and through this the thief had crawled. Tobacco seems to be about all that was taken, as no cash was left on the premises. The burglary caused much com- motion in the district on the news becoming known. TANNERY BAND,—The Pcnketh Tannery Prize Band, were at Runcorn on Saturday last, as contestants in the 3rd Annual Brass Band contest promoted by the Runcorn Cycle Club. The event was held in the Public Hall,and there wifs an entry of eight bands, and six of these competed. The test piece was a selection entitled "Songs of Ireland," (H Round), and is of a very musical and tuneful character. The adjudicator, Mr. Peter Fairhurst of Wigan, placed the successful bands as follows. Ist prize and silver cup; Sutton-road St. Helens ; 2nd prize, Penketh Tannery ;3rd prize, Parr St. Peters ; 4th prize, Crosfields ; sth prize, Runcorn St. Edward. Mr. Fairhurst in the course of his remarks said that the first and second bands, were remarkably close, only one point dividing them. W.Rimmer of Southport, Conducted the Penketh band.

Farm Fire at Croft Shortly before noon on Sunday information wa.s received at the Warrington Fire Station that a fire was in progress at the farm of Mrs. Weir, Cockshott Farm, Croft, Deputy-Superintendent Turner and nine men proceeded to the farm and found that a stack, situated amongst others, had been. alight. The services of the brigade, however, wet.° not required, as the farm hands had managed to ' extinguish the flames by Pulling down al() stack. That damage is covered by insurance.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
SCENE IN A PENKETII PUM,IC-HOCSE.

At the Warrington County Petty sessions on Wed- nesday, John Thompson and Frederick Thompson, Pen- keth, father and son were chargedwithbeing disorderly and refusing to quit the Red Lion Inn, Penketh, when requested by the landlord George Davies, on October 5 The elder defendant said ha was in sucha state that he could not possibly say what happened, and the younger denied the offence. Mr. Arthur Browne,who Arosecuted -said Mr. Davies was landlord and proprietor of the Red Lion. An inquest was held at that place on the night of the above date by Mr. Brighouse,and the elder defendant was a witness, road the younger was present expecting to be called, There was to be a supper held in the room after the inquest, and shortly before ,eight o'clock the elder defendant had to beiput outowing to trying to create a disturbance with some tannery men. Mr. Davies who was upstairs, came down, and saw the younger defendant pulling his coat off. A crowd of about thirty persons were watching the bother. Mr. Davies told him to go out, but he refused, and the elder defendant then came in again. Miss Davies was sent for the police, but she could not find the constable. Mr. Davies then went out, and on his return he found that the men had been put out.—Evidence for the prosecu- tion having been called, the elder defendant said thathe was helplessly drunk, and he remembered nothing about it. The younger defendant said he was trying to get his father out of thehouse.—John Thompson was fined 10s. including costs, and FrerZerick Thompson was dismissed.

div.head: Warrington Borough Police Court.
div.p: Warrington Borough Police Court.
Minor Cases.

MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Councillor Thornton, Messrs Birchall, Hayward and S. Wright. TERRORISING WORKHOUS E INM ATES.—George Mather was charged that, being a pauper inmate of the Work- house, he was disorderly and refractory on Saturday night.—Mr. Aubrey, master of the Workhouse, said he heard an unusual noise in the day room, and on going there he heard the prisoner using disgusting and threat- ening language to some old men. The priFoner was con- stantly terrorising the old men in the house, and this case was brought to make an example of him.—Prisoner was sentenced to twenty-one days' imprisonment.— Prisoner: Thank you, sh.. I shall be as bad again when I come back. OBSCENE LANGUA G E.—On the evidence of P.C. Sweeney, Catherine Howard, a stranger, was fined ss. for making use of obscene language in Buttermarket- street, at 8.55 on Saturday night. BEGGING.—George Henry Murray was fined ss. for begging in Sankey-street at 9 o'clock on Saturdaynight. —P.C. Whittaker proved the case.
WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. T. Birehall (in the chair)
and J. R. Young.

ARREARS OF M.rAINTEN.ANCE—.—homas Wrall, Har- purhey, Manchester, was charged with £l6 14s. arrears of maintenance due to his wife, under an order made for 12s. a week on December 5. 1902. He said that he was not certain of the amount. The Bench decided that unless prisoner made a distinct and proper offer of payment he must go to gaol for one month. FRlDAY.—Before Mr. H. Roberts (in the chair), Alderman Smethurst, Councillors J. Roberts and

Thornton, and Mr. HePherd. ASSAULT CASES.—Edward Jackson, Birchall-street, was bound over to keep the peace, and ordered to pay the costs for assaulting his wife, Elizabeth Jackson, on October 10th.—Joseph Leigh, 228, Knutsford-road, was convicted of an aggravated assault on his wife, Nellie Leigh, and a separation order with 15s. per week alimony was granted.—Mr. Steel represented the complainant.

Scene After the Widnes- Match. At Widnes on Monday, Michwl Hennessey, 5, Hill- street, Warrington, was charged with stealing a silver chain and pendent from John Pemberton, Sharp-street Warrington. After leaving the Widnes football ground on Saturday afternoon Hennessey and Pember- ton, who were acquained, began to wrestle. Both fell to the ground, and when on the ground Pembertci alleged than Hennessey snatched his chain. He was given into custody.—Another Warringtonian named Spencer was charged with resisting Inspector Strick- land; Sergeant Williams and Police-constable Moseley in trying to rescue Hennessey. Both pleaded guilty. —The police complained that prisoners incited the crowd to rescue them, and they were rut to a considerable inconvenience by being rushed."—Hen- nessey.was sent to gaol for one month, and Spencer was fined ss. and costs or fourteen days for attempt- ing to rescue.—Henry Bate a young lad living in Morrisey's Yard, Warrington, was fined 10s. and costs for throwing stones at Sergeant Williams while he was taking the prisoners into custody.
