div.head: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON EDUCATION COMMITTEE.
CLOSING OF ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS. The P3wer of the Medical Officer,
SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION QUESTION.

The moiittily meeting of the Warrington Education. Committee was held at the Town Hall on Mondv even- ing under the presidency of Mr. F. Monks. There were also present:—The Revs. Morley Stevenson, E. .1. Willcocks, John Yonge, and Father Wilson, Colonel .1. D. Buckton, Alderman Smethurst, CouncillorsPiervoint, Dodds, Davie% Brophy, Ellison, Craik, and Wilkinson, Messrs. A. J. Jolley, T. May, J. Fulton Smith, E. Plins- ton, G. Walker, and E. J. Guest, with Mr. J. Moore Murray (Director of Education.)

div.head: PROTEST FROM MR. MAY.
div.p: A PROTEST FROM MR. MAY.

When the minutes of the last meeting were submitted for confirmation, Mr. May said he wished to point out that the Finance and School Management Committees were meeting in secret. They had no published rota of the dates and hours of meetings and, although he was sure they had no wish to keep other members of the Education Committeo in the dark, the effect was just the same, and two-thirds of the committee were abso- lutely ignorant and in the dark as to what the other third" was doing. •

The CHAIRMAN : What has this to do with the minutes of the last meeting ? Mr. MAY said he wished to protest against voting cm bloe for the minutes of the two commitees,seeing that he hadno opportunity of knowing when the meetings were held.
Councillor PIERPOINT : Mr. May Is • referring to minutes that are not before us. He had thorn in his possession, I suppose, a month ago. _ _
, The CHAirtmiv : You are eirely out Of order, Mr May.
The minutes were then confirmed. DRAFT FINAL ORDERS.
Mr. MURRAY reported the receipt of draft final orders in respect of Fairfield and Sacred Heart Schools.
FINANCE COMMITTEE. THE CHARGE FOR USE OF SCHOOLS. THE CHAIRMAN THREATENS TO LEAVE THE MEETING.

At a meeting of the Finance Committee a letter from the Secretary of the Association of Foundation Man- agers of Church of England schools, forwarding a copy of a resolution passed at a recent meeting of that association, to the effect that, in case of schools where the fees charged amount to threepence or more per child a week, the proportion 'to be refunded to the :uanagers of that school should be one quarter,but that, where the fee charged is less than threepence, one-half of the tltal amount should be repaid to the managers was read, but the committee considered that it would be inadvisable to take any action in the direction indi- cated at the present time. Other minutes of this com- mittee were published in our last issue. In moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. A. J. Jolley said the minutes of the School Management Com- mittee contained a request to the Finance Committee with referende to the holding of a violin class at St. Mary's School, Buttermarket-street. The Finance Committee, of course,acceded to the request, and would accede to any other request of a similar character. Councillor PIERPOINT seconded and called attention to the fact that on visiting the school of which he was a manager on Friday last he was told by the school- keeper that she had no coal, coke, firewood or cleaning materials, and she was providing soap at her own ex- pense. He hoped the committee would at the earliest possible moment see that the schools were supplied with the necessaries he had named.

Alderman SMETFIURST pointed out that a penny bank was held in St. Paul's schools and he did not think it was right that they should have to pay is. per time for theuse of the schools for that purpose. He was of the same opinion in regard to the holding of Band of Hope meetings. Mr. MAY supported the protest. The Committee, he thought, ought not to condescend to take note of shil- lings, as more time and moneylwere lost jn noting them than theamount was worth. There ought so be a sort of incident fund so that the Director could exercise his judgment without putting shillings through the books or charging them. - -
CormallOr DODDS thought that primarily the matter ought to come up for discussion with the School Management Committee's minutes. The CHAIRMAN: It was referred by them to the Finance Committee.

Councillor DODDS : As far as the financial part goes, but not the principle of the thing. Mr. WALKER said it appeared to him that the violiti class was a private class, and the teacher received some pecuniary benefit. If that were so, he ought to pay rent for the room.
Mr. MAY rose to speak but The CHAIRMAN ruled him out of order. Mr. MAY: I will ask a question. The CHAIRMAN: I don't know that you are entitled to do that.

Mr. MAY asked whether the Committees would in future be good enough to publish a rota of their meet- ings so that other members who wished to attend might make themselves acquainted with the business. A serious i tern of expense would have to be considered in regard to the building of new schools, and how could they ex_pect him, or other members of the Committee- _
- the diIIIRMAINT: I must request yo-u-to-s-it---do-w-n-. It is entirely out of order and entirely irrelevant to the matter before the committee.
Mr. MAY: You said I was out of order last t;me, and now I have put myself in order. The CHAIRMAN: If you won't sit down I shall leave the room altogether.
Mr. My: I beg to sit down with a protest. Councillor DODDS contended that the matter should be discussed with tbe School Management Committee's recommendations.

Councillor SMETHURST attempted to address the meeting but was ruled ouc, of order. Mr. A. J. JOLLEY said that with regard to the point which had caused some searching of heart with some members of the committee, the cases mentioned were not analagous in any way to the one under considera- tion. The violin class was conducted by a bead teacher exclusively for the benefit of the scholars, and any similar application, for any educational purpose, from any school would be carefully considered by the com- mittee, and he had no doubt a favourable decision would be given. There was a wide difference between such a class and denominational work, whether of a temperance character or for the promotion of thrift. Penny banks and that sort of thing were all very well, but they were not exclusively educational A penny bank conducted by a teacher for the benefit of the scholars would be on a far different footing from one conducted by a church or chapel. The violin class was absolutely for the benefit of the scholars; otherwise the committee would not have entertained it.
Mr. WALKER: There are no fees charged? Mr. JOLLEY : lam told not. '

The Rev. Father WILSON explained that the class was in the nature of a continuation of the day school. It was conducted immediately after the time of dismissal about fifteen boys receiving instruction, _ _ _
The minutes were confirnied, Mr. May being the only dissentient.

I SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. ELEVEN SCHOOLS CLOSED. I THE POWER OF THE MEDICAL OFFICER SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION QUESTION. I Most of the recommendations of the Schcol Manage- ment Committee appeared in cm: last issue. The ques- tion of the need for additional Lchool accommodation in the borough, having been discussed, it was in. view of the terms of sect;on Bof the Education Act, 1902, re- solved that it be a recommendation to the Education Committee that the Board of Education be asked whether the provision of temporary school accommoda- tion is to be regarded as equivalent to the provision of new public elementary schools for the purposes of that section, and whether it would be necessary for the three months' notice required therein for the propcsal to provide such temporary school accommodation, to be given. I Instructions were also given for a retern to be pre- pared and submitted to the Committee of the number of children residing outs,de the bo.ough attending schools within the borough.and of the children residirg within the boront,h attending schools outside thereof; and 'Or enquiries to be madeas to any suitable premises . available tor the purpose of providing the required I accommodation.—A letter from the Managers of St. 1 Mary's (R.C.) school, asking for petmission for violin class to be held by Head Master immediately after school hours, was submitted and it was resolved that the Finance Cormr:ttee be requested, in 'wiring arrange- ments with the Managers as to tbe charges for the use of schools at fmes other than those during which they are used as public elementary schools, to giant the free use of the rooms to the h' .d teachers ler purposes of as educational cbatacter and connected with school work. It was resolved, that, with a N ieW to th 3 rdop- tion of a scale of salaries foc head t2achers,the Director be requested to prepare alhd submit to Pia Committee a report as to the orgarosation of the whole of the ele- mentary schools in ill.e borough. At a Later meeting requisitions for prize books for the higher grade and girls' departments of the Fairfield National school, and for medals for the boys', girls' and infants' departments of the Heatbside National school were submitted and approved. It was resolved, that con- sent be given to the appointment of the follovC_ng teachers, their engagements to be determinable by one month's notice,to expire on the last day of any calendar month, given by or to the committee. viz.;—Warrington British, Mr. Frederick K. Maddrell, assistant (certifi- cated), £95; Warrington British, Miss Edith A. Stone, assistant (certificated), £B5; St. Mary's (R.C.), Miss Mary A. Breen, rssistant (certificated), £B5. Consent was given to the appointment of the follow- ing evening school teachers, viz. :—Hamilton-street, Mr. Arthur E. Hoyle, Heatbside, Mr. G. Thomas, ss. per evening, together witha bonus of 3s, 6d. for every student in their classes, making 75 per cent. of the possible attendances ;Technical Institute, Mrs. Adelaide Jeffries and Mr. Samuel J. Price, ss. per evening. _ _ _ _
A letter from the Principal of the Training .dollege, asking for permission for certain students to attend the Secondary school for a month for practising purposes,

div.head: Examiner, Saturday, October 24R1903
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, October 24R1903

was sui.mitted, and the request was acceded to. A letter from the Rev. Neville Wilson, asking that a iloy named John Kenny may be )admitted to the pupil teachers' preparatory classes, and receive a bonus of £lO, in accordance with the resolution of the Education Committee on the 21st September last, and be indentured as a pupil teacher from the Ist August 1904, was submitted, and the application was granted. Communications from the Medical Officer of Health intimating that the following departments had been closed until November 9th owing to the prevalence of infectious disease, were read and noted, viz.:— School. Department. Heathside N. Boys' Girls' and Infants'. Hamilton-street. , St. Ann's N. In'fants'. ~ Wycliffe B. Mixed and Infants'. Silver-s tteet St. Peter's. InF 9/ ants'. Warr iu.ton P. „
Fairflerd N. !I • St. Benedict's. St. Alban's. Mixed and Infants'. St. George's Infants'.

The Committee proceeded to consider certain suggestions made by the Medical Officer of Health with reference to the method of dealing with cases of infec- tious disease in the elementary schools, and after some discussion, it was resolved that the heads of schools, or departments of schools, be directed (a) in making up their daily record of attendances, to take note of cases in which the absence is stated to be dueto scarlet fever, diphtheria, measles, smallpox, chickenpox, mumps, influenza, whooping cough, sore throat, erysipelas, ring- worm, skin disease of the head, itch or ophthalmia; (b) to be careful to observe signs suggestive of the same diseases among their scholars ; (c) to notify at once to the Medical (Meer of Health, all cases of the:3 diseases ascertained in either of these ways; and (d) to send home at once all children found to be suffering from these diseases, and, in cases of scarlet fever, diphtheria, measles, smallpox, chickenpox, mumps, ' influenza and whooping cough also the brothers and sisters.—lt was resolved that Mr. George Shawcrossj Pendlebury be appointed as Assistant Art Master at the School of Art, at a salary at the rate of £lOl per annum, the engagement to date from a date to be hereafter fixed, and to be determinable by one month's notice, to expire on the last day of any calendar month, given by or to the Committee; , That Miss Helen Fairclough and Mr. Herbert H.Dell be appointed as art pupil teachers at the School of Art under the terms of Article 52 of the Regulations for Schools of Art and Art •Classes ; that the various schools be closed for the Ckristmas holidays from the evening of Wednesday, the 23rd December 1903, until Monday the 11th ;January 1904; that application be made for the use of the Corporation Arms as a badge for the scholars attending the Secondary school ; that the revised tender of Messrs. Philip Son and Nephew amounting to sd. each, for the supply fa school registers, be accepted ' • that ap- plication be made to the Chairman b f the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, for the loan of specimens for the botany class at the Secondary school. Instructions having been asked, as to the steps to be taken for carrying out the small repairs to furniture needed In the various school* it was resolved that arrangements be made with certain tradesmen to carry out, in turn, the repairs needed; the period for each being not more than six months. The Committee recommended that, in view of the additional cleaning required consequent upon the opening of the Secondary school, it be a recommendation to the Finance Com- mittee that the wages of the two present cleaners be increased from 7s. 6d. to 10s. per week, and that two additional cleaners be engaged at a weekly wage of 7s. 6d. each.

The Rev. MORLEY STEVENSON moved the adoption of the minutes with the exception of the resolution re- farriwr' to the appointment of Miss Breen to St. Mary's school, as she had since resigned the appointment. Ai) alluded to the loss which the School Management Com- mittee had sustained by the resignation of Alderman Monks. Of course in a large body like that they could not all agree on all points,and although they might have differences of opinion at certain times, he was quite sure that anyone who had worked with Alderman Monks must have felt his genuine desire for the educational good of the town. (Hear hear). He (the speaker) felt, the School Management Committee would be very dis- tinctly poorer for the loss of Alderman Monks's ex- perience and advice. Councillor Craik seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor PIERPOIIa called attention to the closing of schools by order of the Medical Officer of Health. He did not know what was the number of scholars affected, but there was no doubt it meant that a very large number of boys and girls were turned out of the schools. It seemed to him to be a very awkward con- dition of things, and one that should be avoided in future if possible. The CHAIRMAN: It is a very serious loss to this Committee.

Councillor PIERPOINT referred to the resolution re- quiring the notification of infectious diseases, and said he thought it was a step in the right direction. The closing of al school was a serious loss to the Education Committee and, in addition, it was a serious interfer- ence with the education of the boys and girls turned out of the school. He agreed entirely with the sugges- tion that the cases should be notified and he thought he would go even a little further than that. No doubt it would be a great deal of trouble to masters to have to notify the cases, and if the Education Commiti;ee could see its way to grant a small fee to the masters for the notification of each case, he thought there would be more careful attention paid to the work. Alluding to the appointment of an art master, Councillor Pier- point said he had not had an opportunity of going into the question of the School of Art's financial position, but—
The CHAIRMAN: The mastdr is in place of an art mistress.

Councillor PIERPOINT asked for information as to whether there had been any increase in the number of pupils which would necessitate the substitution of an art master for art mistress; or was the appointment made because the rules of the Education Department required it. He had no objection to cost so long as they had pfficiency. Mr. MURRAY explained that the art master would take the place of an art mistress who had been receiv- ing £BO per year. Councillor PIERPOINT: SO it is an additional cost of E 24.

Mr. MAY again raised an objection to sub- committee meetings being held "in secret" and sug- gested there should be a published rota in order that all members of the committee could make themselves acquainted with the business. Councillor PIERPOINT : Do I -understand that Mr. May wishes to have a notice of the meeting of every sub-committee when he is not a member? Mr. MAY: No. The CIIAIRMAN: That is the effect. Mr. MAY said he only asked for a list of meetings to be published. After further discussion Mr. PLINSTON explained that there was a rota of meetings of the School Attendance Committee, and certain gentlemen who were not mem- bers of the committee were called in to assist in the work once a month. Mr. May, he thought, wanted the opportunity of attending other committee meetings so that he might know what was going to be discussed and help the members to do their work. Mr. MAY: Not all. The ClikißmAN: Mr. May, you must sit down. There is a limit—

Councillor WILKINSON: • Mr. May wants to be a member of all committees. (Laughter). Continuing he alluded to the appointment of an art master. It was thought by several gentlemen inside and outside the Council, that Warrington was going backward in art. There were no opportunities whereby any pupil could obtain higher grades of art in Warrington. They had very good teachers of designing, freehand and model- ling, but there was no one to teach landscape painting in water colours or oils. He was proud to see the:Com- mittee was moving in the right direction and tiley hoped for a return of the successes obtained in the days of Mr. Christmas Thomnson.

The CHAIR MAN : Unless there is a very considerable change there will be: an alteration later on. Councillor Wm-KEN-30N : I am glad to see you are making this alteration. Alderman SMETHURST was not in favour of the pay- ment of schoolmasters fcr notifying infectious diseases. The ORA I RMAN said the question came up at the last meeting of the Comm:ttee and there was very consider- able discussion on the propoaal submitted by the Medi- cal Officer of Health. There was such a thing as riding a hobby to death, and they were very much at the mercy and in the hands of the Health Com ttc a and Medical Officer of Health. He thought it was a very serious matter that any IPAD, such as the Medical Officer of Health, should have power to close eleven elementary schools in the town. The committee expressed them- selves pretty stron z7y on the point—and he hoped with some effect. It rested to some extent with the Health Committee. and be thought he might say that the School Management Committee had gone quite as far as they were inclined to go under the circumstances. The feeling at one point took a rather ridiculous turn—when the Medical Officer as good as said thatchicken-po was almost a fatal disease. He (Mr. Monks) bad given them an idea of how this thing might be "ridden to death "and incur a very Serious expenditure, and the Medical Officer also indicated that they would want additional inspectors to look after these children. The resolution embodied all that the Committee proposed to do at present. late Rev. Jon g YONG E said he was afraid the Chair- man did not hear the Medical Officer quit 3 correctly on the point of chicken-pox. He (the speaker) did not understand him to say that it was a fatal disease. He thought Dr. Gornall said quite the opposite. He gme them some information that was new to him (Mr. Yonge) and, he thought, to other members of • the Com- mittee, with re-d to the seriousness of measles. They were told that measles was a more serious disease in point of fatal results than scarlet fever. (Hear, hear.) That might or might not be the cart He hoped the Medical Officer of Health would feel he had gone quite far enough for the present. He had 'closed the eleven day schools, and he had sent polite reqiiesta that the Sunday schools should also be closed, and if it went on much longer he would want them to close the churches and chapels. (Laughter.) Colonel BITCKTON considered the recommendation in regard to the notification of infectious diseases was"

little bit of a revolution in Warrington." They wanted to appoint head teachers as sanitary inspectors. (Laughter.) As a matter of fact head teachers had been doing the work for a long time so that it was nothing new. The CHAIRMAN: It has been done informally. Colonel BUCKTON said the Medical Officer was not omnipotent in the matter. He had not an absolute right to close the schools. If he did so, and the managers objected, they could appeal and an order could be made for the re-opening of the schools. The Medical Officer of a large town like Warrington ought to be most care- ful before he made such an order. It was the opinion of many people that he might do far more harm by clash-A the schools than by allowing them to remain open. (Hear, hear). In town 6 the clos'lg of schools did not serve to isolate children; except, perhaps, in the case of infants who could not get about like the older scholars.

41The CHAIRMAN : That view was very strongly im- pressed upon him. Colonel BUCKTON, continuity'., painted out that it was proposed to ngage someone to wind Pp the school clocks and he: did not see why the work could 'not be done by the school cleaners. In regard to the wearing of the Borongh Arms as badges by the students at the Secondary school, he understood the use of the arms was confined to persons engaged in Corporation business. He did not sea why the . tholars should be authorised to wear the badges. They were not paid officials of the Corporation and he did not think the Secondary school should be recognized more as a school in the borough than any of the other schools. Mr. MAY: Each 'child who wore the badge would have to pay a guinea a year. (Laughter.) Mr. JOLLEY said it was hoped by strengthening the School of Art staff to increase the efficiency of the school. Anyone who had close association with the school in recent years would be compelled regretfully to admit that the efficiency of the institution did need increasing. They sincerely hoped the new appointment would be effective in that direction. In regard to the proposal to pay the head teachers for notifying infec- tious diseases, he thought that on reflection Councillor Pierpoint would see that such a system might easily ' lend itself to abuse, and at least to exaggeration of mild symptoms. As indirectly bearing on the somewhat unfair suggestion that any Committee tried to keep its doings secret, he would ask them to refer to the resolu- tion—" That, with a view to the adoption of a scale of salaries for head teachers, the Director be requested to prepare and submit to the Committee a report as to the organisation of the whole of the elementary schools in the borough." it woald be within the recollection of most of the members that a scale for assistant teachers was drawn up some tinieago. The head teachers had had to wait, and would have to wait a little longer, but no injustice would have been done to them because the Committee decided that any scale fixed should be opera- tivea.s from Ist April last. Now that the schools were under the local authority the organization could be based on better and broader lines than was possible be- fore, and the Committee felt it was desirable to very carefully consider the organization of all the schools before settling the remuneration:of the head teachers.lt was not a secret at all, but a very painful and pressing fact that they were hampered for school accommodation in Warrington, not merely for elementary purposes but for all educational purposes. That was a subject which required very full and careful consideration both from the Committee primarily, and secondarily from the TownlCouncil. He was pleased to see that the School Attendance Committee had sent in a list of recommen- dations, and he hoped in view of the extreme urgency of the matter that further recommendations would be submitted, iso that the school equipment throughout would be materially improved. The Rev. M. STEVENSON, in reply, said that with regard to the health question, he felt the force of what had fallen from the lips of one or two of the members, but they were really very much under the thumb of the Health Committee. It was a serious thing when an expert like the Medical Officer of Health made a very strong recommendation to lay it aside and disregard it. The Committee might feel sure that the recommenda- tions were not come to without serious deliberation and thought, and long conferences with the Medical Officer in which everything was done to make him see the importance of the step which he advocated. With regard to the small matter of clock-winding, his experience was that if they had a res- ponsible person to do the work he was able to do those little repairs to the clocks which made for the efficiency of the school. The money, which was a very small matter, would not be wasted or mis-spent. With regard to the badge, Mr. May was an authority on these matters—(laughter.)—but he would like to point out that in many public schools,boys wore badges and even members of cricket clubs were allowed to do the same. (Hear, hear.) He should think some such arrangement might be possible here. (Hear, hear.) The minutes were carried, the only dissentient being Mr. May, who said he should protest until he had an opportunity of coming to hear the proceedings. Councillor PIERPOINT : What are you protesting about!now ? (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN : I understand his 'protest amounts to this—that he has plenty of time on his bands and he wants to be invited to attend the meetings of every committee.
Mr. MAY : To be "allowed " not "invited." The CHAIRMAN: It is a matter for this Committee to consider whether they will put Mr. May on every committee.
Councillor PT9RPOINT : That is the proper way out of the difficulty. (Laughter.) Councillor CRAM: it will be difficult to transact business if you do. (Laughter.)
SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION. TWO NEW SCHOOLS TO BE BUILT.

Councillor ELLISON moved the confirmation of the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, which were to the effect "That a special grant of Os. per head be made to theßolton and County of Lancaster Certified Industrial SchoOl, in respect of the annual seaside camp. That the necessary arrangements be made with a view to the commitment-of girls to a Roman Catholic Industrial school. That, in view of the increased school accommodation required in the Latchford district, the managers of the Latchford National school be asked to consent to the conversion of the mixed department into a girls' school. That, provided the managers of the Latchford National school consent to such conversion of the mixed department into a girls' school, it be a recommendation to the Education Com- mittee to provide a school to accommod Lte 500 children (300 infants and 200 boys) ; and that it be' a recommen- dation to the Sites and Buildings Committee that the plans for the proposed new school should be prepared so that, ifAtecessary, an extension could be made of the boys' depfftment to increase the accommodation to 300; and that it be a recommendation to the Education Committee to provide a new school to accommodate 300 infants ill the immediate neighbourhood of the ex- isting St. George's Mission school in Brick-street. CouncUlor Ellison pointed out that the attendances were not as satisfactory as usual owing to the preval- ence of measles. With reference to the minute re the Latchford National school Councillor Ellison said that the request of the Committee had been agreed to. The accommodation was very inadequate, and there were many children going to Warrington to be educated who ought to be kept at Latchford. It was proposed to put the work in hand without delay. Councillor S. DAVIES seconaed the minutes: Councillor WILLIAM PIERPOtNT said he took it that the girls to be sent to the Roman Catholic scheol would be Roman Catholics.
Mr. MURRAY said that was the intention of the Com- mittee. There had been great difficulty in getting any industrial school for Roman Catholic girls. The minutes were passed and the committee rose.

div.head: EAILLESTOWN MEN FINED AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: EAILLESTOWN MEN FINED AT ST. HELENS.

At St. Helens on Monday, Benjamin Conway, of 27 Rathbone-street, Earlestown, was charged with obac,ruc- ting Edmund Hawes, foreman porter for the London and North-Western Railway, and with leaving a train while in motiori. William Anderton, of 98, Earle-street, Earlestown, was charged on two similar charges, and also with assaulting John Thomas. The evidence was that both men went into a first-class carriage on the 11.20 p.m. train to Earlestown on Saturday night. Foreman Hawes told them to get out and go into a third-class compartment. They caused a great disturb- ance, jumped on and off the train when it was in motion, and when arrested Anderton kicked Thomas. Police- constable Griffiths said both men were a bit drunk, and they tried to knock Hawes's pocket-book out of his Funds when he was booking the names Anderton was fined £1 4s. fid., and Conway 14s. 6d., or fourteen days each.

div.head: BOY LOVER'S DRAMATIC SUICIDE,
div.p: BOY LOVER'S DRAMATIC SUICIDE,

, A boy named William Henry Hickman was reported on Monday to have committed suicide under very sen- sational circumstances. The deceased had been recently courting a girl contrary to the wishes of his parents. When the father remonstrated with him he flew into a temper, and declared his determination to terminate his existence. He ran out of the house, and threw him- * self into the Birmingham Canal in the presence of • sister. She raised an alarm, and a woman threw apron to him to enable him to be dragged out of t e water. He refused help, and sank.

div.head: WARRINGTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON.
Fire at the Baths Hotel.

An outbreak of lire occurred at the Baths Hotel on Tuesday evening but fortunately the flames were extinguished before any serious damage was done. At about seven o'clock, Miss Gittens was in her room when the gas flames ignited the curtains. She called for assistance, and a number of men. in the. vaults helped to put out the flames. The fire brigade turned out with the reel cart, but thAir services were not required. The window frames were blistered,and the carpets and dressing table damaged by fire and wafer.

div.head: UNDER the CLOCK or GOOD BOOTS.—.Advt. Sunday School Teachers' Association.
div.p: UNDER the CLOCK or GOOD BOOTS.—.Advt. Sunday School Teachers' Association.

There was a large attendance at the quarterly meet- ing of the Sunday School Teachers' Assoc'ation held in St. Barn.abas' Schools on Monday evening. The vicar, the Rev. J. H. G. Hollingworth, presided. An interesting and helpful "model lesson" was given by the Rev. A. IL Lester, of the Training College During the evening refreshments were served. PUBLIC BENEFIT. UNDER the CLOCK for BEST BOCT 3 in LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Warrington P.S.A. _ _ _

Mr. Thomas Duckworth presided at an open meet- ing of this society held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Sunday, when there was a very large attendance. Miss Houghton (of Daresbury) sang "The Garden of Sleep," and Miss Pollie Hough- ton "I will extoll Thee" and "The Rose," each item being admirably rendered. Mr. W. A. Sandford, of Edinburgh (late of Warrington), gave an address. FOR CLASS AND CHTN.& of every description try J. S. GARLAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street, Warrington.—Advt. The Latchford Baptist Literary and Debating Society. At a meeting of this society on Monday evening Mr. Arthur Ford, who now resides in St. Helens, read a paper entitled, "Do any benefits accrue from Debat- ing Societies ? " He showed in an able manner that some of our greatest men of the day owed their suc- cess in after life to debating societies. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Ford for his paper. The following members took part in the discussion : Messrs. A. Albinson, J. Adams, D. Hamblett, S. Unsworth, H. Shakeshaft, T. Albinson, B. Ford, J. Albinson, and W. Bamber.
ASK for CUNNINGHAM'S HIGH-CLA.SS MINERA WATERS.—Advt. "Salt andlits Formation." - - - -

The first -meeting of the \season of the Polyglot Society was held on Wednesday evening in the Old Academy, Bridge-street, when Dr. Markel (one of the Vice-Ptesidents of the Society) lectured in German on "Salt and its Formation" to a large assembly of the members. The lecture was accompanied by blackboard illustrations, and many interesting experiments were given. At the end of the lecture the components of salt,namely the metal sodium and the gas, chlorine, were shown' It was also demonstrated that these substances when allowed to come into contact with each other formed "ordinary salt." A vote of thanks moved by Mr. Hulme seconded by Mr. Gerrard and supported by Mr. May was followed by a short discussion, which brought a very enjoyable evening to a close.
A GOOD RESOLUTION.—Wear ALF TAYLOR'S Wonderful Boots.—Advt. Boy Knocked Down by a. Motor Car.

On Saturday afternoon:a little boy named Shaw, who resides in Manchester-road, was knocked don by a motor car at the Cemetery tram terminus, and sustained serious bruises about the head and body, Along with other boys, Shaw was collecting tickets as the passengers alighted from the trams. He failed to notice the approach of a motor car in charge of Mr." George Rogers, of Manchester, Rd. and waskuocked crown. When picked up he was bleeding profusely .from the head. He was carried into the Cemetery Hotel, where he was attended by Dr. Bennett. ,No bones were broken, but Shaw had some of his teeth knocked out. He was carried home—a short distance away—and subsequently attended by Dr. Joseph. FIRE GRATES of every description.—J. S. GAR- LAND, Furnishing Ironmonger, 51, 53, and 55, Bridge-street,Warringion.—Advt.

div.head: Hamilton-street _School Swimming Club.
div.p: Hamilton-street _School Swimming Club.

At the Corporation Baths on Frida—y evening the schoolboys attending the Practising Schools, Hamilton- street, held their fifth annual gala. During the summer months, an average of 120 scholars a week have taken advantage of the special tickets issued by the Baths Committee, allowing them the use of the first class plunge bath on Tuesday and Friday after- noons. Many of the boys have learnt to swim,and the prizes offered for the races caused great competition. The chief event was the contest for the:championship of the club and silver medal. This was won, after an exciting race, by Eric Barnett, A. Shaw being an excellent second and P. Daniells third. The other events• resulted as follow :—One-breadth handicap: 1, G. Lewis; 2, W. Harrop ; 3, J. Taylor. Scramble across the bath—Standard V.: 1, J. Roberts; 2, J. Hill; 3, G. Isherwood. Standard IV.: 1, G. Pester; 2, J. Wilson; 3, G. Rothwell. Standard lii.: 1, R. Littlewood ; 2, W. Brown; 3, J. G-reaves. Neatest dive: 1, J. Lawless; 2, S. Brown; 3, E. Barnett; 4, A. Dickenson. Costume and candle race (which caused immense fun for the boys): 1, A. Shaw ; 2, G. Eyres ; 3, A. Appleton; 4, W. Jolley. Mr. Barlow, the manager, kindly officiated as judge.

div.p: IL M. ASATON'S LIFFI TONIC is the KING OF

TONICS.-63, SANKEY-STREET, Warrington.—Advt. Field Club. The winter session opened on Friday with an entomological evening at the Museum Lecture Room. Mr. T. May was elected president in succession to Mr. Womersley, resigned. In acknowledging the honour Mr. May referred to the good work of his predecessor, and concurred with other speakers in wishing him success in his new sphere of work in South Wales. Mr. W. Mounfield commented upon the wet and un- favourable season, which had been not only a hindrance to collecting but a check on the numbers of species of many insects. He suggested that more attention to breeding would throw light on the life histories of the lepidoptera. He exhibited a most interesting set, of insects found either in the larval or adult form in con- signments of foreign timber. Mr. Collins exhibited 18 out of the 26 British species of crambus, one of which he had taken for the first time when with the Field Club in Del amere Forest on August 3rd. Mr. Robinson and Mr. Deane briefly described their displays, the latter also calling attention to that of Mr. Howarth, who was himself unable to attend, but whose beauti- fully mounted illustration of the life history of a dragon fly was much admired. Messrs. L. Greening, C. White, and J. Moore Murray took part in the dis- cussion and congratulated the exhibitors on the beauty and neatness of their work. The club is evidently very much alive, and its work of enriching the collec- tions of the Museum is being admirably fulfilled.

div.head: IN ill I( ' GO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
div.p: IN ill I( ' GO-OPERATIVE SOCIETY.
LIVELY MEETING.
THE DISTRUST OF PUBLIC MEN.

Mr. T. RIRCTIA.LL, J.P., presided at the quarterly meeting of the Warrington Equitable Industrial Co- operative Society Limited., held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street, on Monday evening. There was a good attendance which included Mr. W. Jeffrey, Mr. W. Ford (cashier), and Mr. A. H. Rathbone cmanaging secretary).

div.head: QUARTER'S TRADE.
div.p: THE QUARTER'S TRADE.

The report showed that the sales for the quarter amounted to £31,883 10s. lid., as against £29,200 12s. sd. for the corresponding quarter of last year, showing a difference of £2,683 7s. 6d. in favour of the present quarter. The profits, after providing for all liabilities, depreciation, interest on capital, Sze., would allow a dividend of 3s. in the £ on members' purchases, with a balance of £206 3s. sd. to be carried forward.

The Committee desired to point out that the Shoe Department was not receiving that support from mem- bers which the quality of the goods deserved. Pass Books must be kbronght in for December quarter on Monday, December 21st, and Tuesday, December 2nd.

Thc CHAIR:NEIN remarked that it was forty year- since the Society was established and its position now was very different from what it was in those days. Notwitstanding the considerable depression in trade they had had a very satisfactory quarter and the sales were more than they would have been, had they not commenced to pay a dividend on sugar. There was plenty of room for extension. One of the branches was doing as much business as the central stores, and, that of course, meant a loss of trade to the centre. He thought the members should go in for propaganda work in order to increase the society's business, and mention to their fellow workmen the advantages of membership of the society and induce 'as many as possible to join. Mr. 13; rchall pointed out in S t.Helens there was a society which had more than doubled the Warrington Society in half the time, although the town was not much larger than Warrington. It was very desirable that they should obtain more business at Sankey-street. There seemed to be some doubt whether Co-operative Societies should advertise or not. He suggested that if the members desired to advertise they should follow the example of the Manchester Equitable Society, which every quarter displayed a placard outside the central stores and branch establishments announcing the amount to be distributed in dividend.

div.head: report was adopted. PROPOSED ENLARGEMENT OF THE COMMITTEE.
div.p: The report was adopted. PROPOSED ENLARGEMENT OF THE COMMITTEE.

Mr. MAYBURY gave notice that at the annual meeting he would move that the number of committee men be increased from eight to twelve, and that the four additional members be elected at the annual meeting. Mr. W. LOWE rose to speak on the subject, but another member questioned his right to do so. The CHAIRMAN thereupon ruled Mr. Lowe Out of order, and requested him to resume his seat. SUGGESTED REMUNERATION FOR COMMITTEE-MEN.

Mr. MA.YBURY informed the members that at the annual meeting he would move that each member of the committee be paid £2 lOs per annum for his services. He pointed out that at the last meeting a grant of £lO each was made to the committee and the sum of .£9O appeared on the bahince sheet for that pur- ppse. He thought it would be advisable to pay a stated sum each year.

div.head: L-ATCEIFORD v. KERSAL A.
div.p: L-ATCEIFORD v. KERSAL A.

- - -- This match was played at Kersal on Saturday, and very fast and interesting play resulted in a win for the visitors. The ground was in splendid condition, a)d the Weather very favourable. From the start play was very even, neither side being able to claim any advantage. Eventually Grounds broke through the defence, and scored a neat goal for the visitors. Nothing further Was scored before half-time. On resuming, the visitors had slightly the best of matters, and for a considerable time kept the home goal pretty warm, but were unable to obtain any tangible result, as the home defence was very sound. Play was transferred to the other end, but liallows and Conway were in fine form, breaking up the home combination on many occasions. Wilkinson was also prominent in goal, clearing several terrific shots. For a time play ranged in midfield. Banks secured the ball near the home 5 by a tricky bit of play, and scored a splendid goal. From this point play was very even, and nothing further was scored. Latchford won an ex- ceedingly pleasant game by two goals to nil.

div.p: LATCHFORD A v. KERSAL B.

div.head: REASON TO 8E THANKFUL.
div.p: REASON TO 8E THANKFUL.

In Skelsmergh, Kendal, lives a man who has had a remarkable restoration to health and strength. He is Mr. Charles Braithwaite, and for along time he suffered sO severely from backache that he was unable to move hand'or foot. Mr. Braithwaite says : "It would come upon me without a moment's warning and I had to go aboutSfor days half-doubled up. My back was so bad that I didn't dare to turn round in bed. I. bad a doctor and a deal of medicine, but I did not seem to get anything to do me good. "I then began taking Dodd's Kidney Pills and they gave me relief from the first. I kept on with them, and /low I can truthfully say they have quite cured me. I have never had an ache or pain since taking them, nor have I ever been off work, and, although I have fre- quently got wet through and had to work in my wet ' clothes for hours al yet I have had no sign of a return of 18 old trouble. lam therefore satisfied that my cure va y perfect and permanent one, and I can recommend Dodd's Kidney Pills as a sure cure for backache."

div.head: LANCASHIRE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. More Training Colleges for Teachers Needed.
div.p: LANCASHIRE EDUCATION COMMITTEE. More Training Colleges for Teachers Needed.

At the meeting of the Lancashire Education Com- Mittee, on Monday, Sir H. F. Hibbert, Chairman moved the adoption of the report of the Higher Education Subr committee, which stated that there was undoubtedly a Pressing necessity for more training colleges for teachers. Tiae sub-committee were of opinion that the burden of supplying these colleges ought to be treated as a charge on the Imperial Exchequer, which Might be carried out by increasing the Government grants given to these institutions. Whether this was done or not colleges Must be provided, and the committee proposed to have a conference with the Cheshire County Council and vatiou,s county boroughs in Lancashire and Cheshire, together with the Government Inspectors, with a view of trying to bring about some joint action on the part Of these authorities by which the cost of the provision of training colleges for Lancashire and Cheshire might be shared by all the authorities interested. The sub- committee also stated that many of the best students who had gained scholarships in cotton weaving and spinning had been precluded from taking them up owing to the expense entailed in attending classes being greater than they felt justified in incurring. To remove this in future the sub-committee had recommended scholarships, the sub-committee to consider the advisability of paying the school fees of students in addition to the amount of the scholarships.

div.head: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAM-
div.p: LIVERPOOL AND NORTH WALES STEAM-
SHIP COMPANY.
The Past Season's Operations.

The directors of the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Company, Limited, have issued the report and statement of accounts of the thirteenth year's work- ing of the company's steamers. After deducting the sum of £3,639 14s. 3d. for depreciation, and placing the sum of £l,OOO to the credit of reserve account, the amount available for dividend and other purposes, in- cluding the balance brought forward from last season, is £4,153 4s. out of which the directors recommend the payment of a dividend of 5 ner cent per annum, free of income-tax, carrying forward a balance of £968 4s. The ships have been well maintained in a state of efficiency and repair out of profits, and the sum set aside for depreciation is at the rate of 6 per cent. The conditions have been adverse, and the payment of a dividend of 5 Per cent under the circumstances is satisfactory. The ' retiring directors are Mr. W. M. Rhodes and Mr. Henry Mac Iver, who are eligible for re-election The greatest praise is due to Mr. W. H. Dodd, managing director, and Mr. T. G. Brew, secretary, for the result of their untiring efforts on behalf of the com- Pany under such unfavourable circumstances. The • • annual meeting will be held in the Law Association Rooms on the 30th inst.

div.head: WHITECHAPEL MURDERER TO DIE.
div.p: WHITECHAPEL MURDERER TO DIE.

Charles Jeremiah Slowe, a dock labourer .and militia corporal. was sentenced to death at the Old Bailey on Wednesday for the murder of Martha Hardwick, a bar- mnaid at the Lord Nelson Tavern, Whitechapel. The .ccused had often been seen in the tavern, but the girl, lt was stated. was unfriendlyand apparently wished to avoid him. The prisoner entered the house just after nudnight and fatally stabbed the girl, being captured after an exciting chase.

div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Queen of Italy, who next month is to be our guest, is tall and graceful, whilst the King ranks with the Tsar of Russia, as one of the shortest sovereigns of Europe. The Queen, when onlya Montenegrin Princess was expected to become the bride of the Tsar, and when quite young she went to live at St. Petersburg to master the Russian language. She is perfectly acquainted with French and Servian, and has published poems, not only. in'llussian, but also in these languages under the pseu- donigm " Ferfalla Azzurra." It is only since she ~married the Prince of Naples—now the King of Italy— that she has become fluent in Italian, but she is an ex- tremely accomplished woman, with a distinct gift for poetry, and is also an excellent artist. A brilliant match.—Lord Helmsley, whom it is said Lady Marjorie Greville is to marry, is the grandson and heir of the Earl of Feversham. Lady Marjorie, the daughter of the Earl and Countess of Warwick, is not yet out of her teens, whilst Lord Helmsley is only 24 so that it is a somewhat youthful match. It is one of which even Lady Warwick might well be proud, as Lord Feversham is not only very wealthy, but his seat at Duncombe Park is full of priceless paintings and art treasures. He is close upon seventy-four years of age, but still entertains many guests, among whom members of the Royal Family have often been included, but he is perhaps best known through his daughters, all of whom made a sensation in Society on account of their remark- able beauty. • Famous Sportswomen.—Lady Howe, who has been entertaining a large party at Birmingham for the Musical Festival, is a daughter of a former Duke of Marlborough and is a noted sportswoman, and a wonder- ful whip. She drives a four-in-hand, and is often to be seen on her coaoh in Hyde Park during the London season. Neither motoring or cycling have robbed some women of their love of horses, and among these may also be mentioned the Duchess of Newcastle, who is noted for her fine horsemanship. Though married to the Duke in 1889, she is still in the early thirties, and keeps up all the sporting traditions of Clumber House. The Duchess acts as "Master" of the famous Clumber harriers, and is very popular in the smart hunting world. A Postponed Retirement.—M. Paderewiski, the great pianist-composer, is reported to have lost his fortune, and instead of being able to retire as he intended, he is obliged to start his recital work again. No one has ever before approached him in the vast sums he has received fOr his pianoforte recitals, but presumably the great musician is not a good man of business, and, as with so many great artists, money easily- earned is *apt to easily go. How many popular favourites on the stage have failed until it is too late, to learn the value of money. and fortunate are those inclined in this way, who receive it warning in time before their professional career is ended. Are we becoming less Musical ?—Tt is generally supposed that, as a nation, we are becoming more musical, but that was not the view taken by some of the clergy at the Church Congress. Clergymen have very practical means of judging, and it would appear to be their opinion that there is less ability and enthusiasm in congregational singing than there used to be. Such, however, could scarcely be the case in Wales, where at least the people keep up all their traditional love of song. Some of the clergy do not attach sufficient importance to the place of music in worship, but the well-attended churches and chapels are usually those where the music and singing is of the better kind. Parisian Fashions.—London has been slow this season to adopt any settled fashions for the winter, but to judge from the lead given by the big Parisian establish- ments, sleeves will continue to be immense, and as dis- figuring as they are inconvenient. Our own modistes and tailors have shewn more moderation, but even so, the dangling sleeve requires almost more management at table, and in the drawing room, than the long walk- ing skirt does on a wet and muddy day. A better word maybe said for the short round skirt which the Parisian ' dressmakers are favouring, though it is guaged, or semi- hooped to an extent that almost extinguishes what little pretensions it can make as a graceful walking dress. The French wiater coats have all of them shoulder capes of some sort or other, but the best houses in London are already discardihg capes, and also that style of coat which is of the long military description, buckled in at the back like a guardsman's. These two particular features in winter coats are evidently to be left to the masses, and avoided by the classes. The Most Popular Fur.—Moleskin has become one of the expensive furs, but it is not so durable as some, and it necessarily suffers from the large amount of sewing it requires. No less than seven or eight htindred skins are required for a long overall coat. On the average they do not measure more than 4ins, by 21ns., and as many as two hundred are used for the broad scarf stoles, now so fashionable. These stoles cannot be purchased for less than £lO or £l2, whilst £5O is not out of the way for a moleskin coat, but it is not " everlasting wear," as is the case with some furs. Until recent years it was scarcely in demand at all except for gamekeepers caps and waistcoats, but the furriers now have a diffi- culty in obtainingan adequate supply of the fur of the " little gentleman in black velvet," as the mole used to be toasted by the White Rose party. The little animal is now in its ;winter fur, when only it is valuable, and the.professional,mole catchers must be rapidly making their fortunes.

Superflous Decoration.—Lace and fur i a combina- tion no longer tolerated by the dressmakers,and tailors. They have however by no means given up the idea of adorning and decorating fur, andare substituting silk muslin for lace. Moreover they insist that this shall, in colour exactly match the fur. It always seems a very unnecessary procedure to decorate goodfur, but if any- thing in this way is deemed desirable, we should do well to remain' faithful to lace. Silk muslin soon gets out of condition, and is by no 'means so effective as good lace. Wide velvet strings form the favourite fastening for fur stoles, velerines, and coats, the ends usually reaching well below the knees. Tiresome Modes.—Blouses are distinctly more simple than has been the case for some time past, and all the best fasten down the back. This ideaaffords consider- able scope for a decorative front, but unless one is • possessed of a maid, blouses that fasten behind are e mistake. It is not always posssble to discover at the precise moment, someone ready and able to help One into such a garment, and to endeavour to fasten it one- self means pulling it out of shape. It is better far, to attempt some form of side fastening even though /he procedure is a little complicated and troublesome. The collarless blouse is now an idea of the past. Collars are high, and just sufficiently stiff to keep their shape. MAD GE.

div.head: BOWLING.
div.p: BOWLING.
MAIN AT BANK QUAY.

A successful bowling main, which was commenced four weeks ago, for the benefit of William Smith, who has been incapacitated from! following his employment for a considerable time, owing to a severe illness, has been brought to a conclusion. The large num- ber of 350 entered for the first round, the ultimate winner being Mr. J. Hutchinson, who played from scratch, and Mr. Williamson was second, with one start. The prizes had been given by various gentlemen in the own. The first prize was a clock, and the second a set vases. There were otherprizes to the total value of about £l5. On Saturday evening the committee waited upon Ms. Smith, and the handsome sum of £.3-0 was presented to him by Mr. H. E. Pooley, who has acted as segretary for the committee. Mr. Smith was deeply affected, andde§ires to thank all for their very gener- ous support and sympathy during his affliction.

div.head: Manchester Poultry and Pigeon Show.
div.p: Manchester Poultry and Pigeon Show.

As will be seen from our advertising columns, the sth 'annual show of prize poultry, pigeons rabbits and Cavies is to be held for the first time this year at Belle Vue Gardens Manchester on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday 27th, 28th and 29th inst. There will be fireworks on Wednesday and Incubators in operation showing chickens hatching. There are 3250 exhibits, north, south, east and west practically from John D'Groats to Lands End. The astonishing 'value of prize poultry and pigeons was amply illustrated at a sale which was held on Saturday last in the Coal Exchange Manchester when a single'bird realised £6O and two others £5O the net result from a sale of 71 birds being 886 12s. 6d. Manchester Show has be- come. on 'of the leading fixtures of .the season and is well worth a visit. Sir Humphrey. De Trafford Bart is again President.

FAILURES, IN ENGLAND AND WALES.—According to " Kemp's Mercantile Gazette," the total number of failures recorded in England and Wales during the week ending Friday, October 16th, was 192, viz. :—New bank- ruptcy proceedings published in the "London Gazette," 103; deeds of arrangement registered, 89. The respec- tive numbers in the corresponding week of last year were : Bankruptcies, 96; deeds of arrangement, 84—total 180; being a net increase in bankruptcies of 13, and a net increase in deeds of arrangement in 1903. to date of 295.

div.head: Examiner, Saturday October 24, 1903. FASHIONS OF TODAY I, THE SITUATION IN
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday October 24, 1903. FASHIONS OF TODAY I, THE SITUATION IN

The modes have become somewhat more ;ettled the last few weeks, and we are able to more easily determine the style and material Df our early winter toilettes. After the first outburst of novelties the fashions become more settled, and the eccentricities and ex- crescences which mar their beauty are rapidly toned down or vanish altogether. Many are the modes that disappear almost as soon as they are created, and are in reality only efforts towards novelty on the part of one or other of the leading and most enterprising fashion makers. October, however, brings with it a sense. that the fashions are more settled and that the dull season, as regards affairs sar- torial, is at last at an end. Everything this
UL COAT.

season seems to indicate that the leading in- spirations of the best dressmakers will be drawn from the early seventies, and that our dress will correspond in a modified manner with the dress of that period. We cannot pretend to greet this state of affairs with any enthusiasm, for the full skirts, dolman-like mantlz, and tight-fitting bodice of that period do not agree with our ideas as to the artistic recpirements of dress and many people prefer to retain as much as possible of the more becoming modes which have hitherto been ou: portion. .

'lie three-quarter coat sketchid is of a style which, though not very new, is ever popular and will be ,found invaluable for winter wear. It is easily slipped on and will stand plenty of hard wear. A coat of this description can be made of rough serge or frieze or any of the innumerable artistically coloured tweeds which are so reasonable in price and so enduring. Rainproof covert coating is, however, the material par excel- lence, and will always keep its look if sent occasionally to the tailor to be pressed. The

girl who prides herself on the neat itt and smart appearance of her tailor made garments will find the few shillings spent on having these cleaned and pressed by her own, or her brother's, tailor a real economy in the long run. Do not ,on any account entrust work of this nature to a woman tailor as it never gives satisfaction. Tailor made coats and 'skirts have this season returned to their severe, but undoubtedly - smart, traditional simplicity, and we find the Newmarket basque amongst the newest models. The blouse sketched is of alimple style and would make up nicely in viyella or flannel with a few ornamental buttons and a dainty cravat and collar. It is really best to have a blouse, however plainly made, cut to measure and fitted, although at first it may cost a little more to have this done. The ready-made blouses do not fit as a rule, as they are only made in certain stock sizes and therefore do not allow for variations of figure. Of course I do not intend to convey the impression that all ready-made blouses are necessarily ill-fitting, as there are many people who find no cause for complaint, but these fortunate individuals are generally of

div.head: COSY DRESSING GOWN.
div.p: A COSY DRESSING GOWN.

• slender build, as there is usually a lack of fulness in the bust measure of a cheap ready. made blouse which bans it for ever from the wardrobe of those to whom nature has been liberal in the matter of flesh. The more ex- pensive blouses, whose prices are ,never less than one guinea, will be found to be better cut and more liberal as regards material. Still, to my mind, if one is willing and able to pay a good price it will always be found better to have the blouse made to measure, while greater scope is offered at the same time for the display of originality. The cosy dressing gown illustrated recom- mends itself, and is a really necessary garment. There is nothing of the tea gown in the fashion of the one depicted, which is designed strictly for bedroom wear and suggests in its aspect a cosy chat by the fire with the con- genial confidences in which girls delight while brushing out their hair for the night. I should recommend a nice bright crimson or cerisi flannel for its construction, although blue and green are likewise becoming and even a warm yellow has been exploited by a brunette with eminently satisfactory results Yellow is not only a colour for the dusky tressed damsel, but can be worn by a blonde provided she is possessed of a good clear natural complexion. The addition of a fine muslin or washing silk frilled fichu would add to the dressiness of this gown, but when such is added it must be made to be easily removed for washing purposes, and not stitched in at the finishing of the neck, as is so often the case in a dressing gown which has been bought ready-made'

div.head: MACEDONIA. By PROFESSOR BRYCE, M.P.
div.p: MACEDONIA. By PROFESSOR BRYCE, M.P.

It is a hopeful sign, cheering to those who feared that Britain had begun to lose that sympathy for freedom and humanity which was her glory half a century ago,that even at a time when grave domestic questions were occupying the national mind there should have arisenso strong a feeling of indignation at the detestable cruel- ties of the Turkish Government in Macedonia, so general a demand that British influence should be exerted to secure the liberation of the Eastern Christians from the oppressions that have made life intolerable to them. This demand is all the more significant because the movement is outside all party lines. It has not been got up by any party or in the interest of any party—it is the spontaneous expression of national sentiment. Though the facts known in England are amply sufficient to justify the demand I refer to, there is a general desire for more detailed information, and constant requests for such information reach theßalkan Committee. They are prepared to supply facts and to an wer questions—indeed, that is largely the purpose fors which they exist; andeveryone who wants to have a fuller mastery of the subject than he possesses will do well to communicate with them. Meanwhile, I comply with the request addressed to me to call attention to -a few of the salient features of the present situation;and I shall try to do so in the most concise way. I. It is sometimes asked: What is the special re- sponsibility of Britain? and the question deserves a reply. In 1878, when• Russia had vanquished the Turks, she dictated a treaty by which nearly the whole of Macedonia, including the districts which have been the scene of the horrible massacres reported during the last few weeks, was taken away from the Sultan and mad g a part of the autonomous Principality of Bulgaria created by that Treaty (Treaty of San Stefano). Lord Beaconsfield's Government objected to this arrange- ment on the ground that it unduly weakened the Turkish power, the maintenance of which they deemed essential to British interests. This was a deplorable error, as Lord Salisbury himself—then Foreign Secretary —lived to admit. But the selfish and short- sighted view then taken by the Government prevailed. A Congress was called at Berlin, the Treaty of San Stefano was set aside, and by the Treaty of Berlin the districts in question were handed back to the rule of the Turk. Reforms were, of course, to be introduced—this is a regular part of dealings with the Sultan. The Turks promised to introduce them, and a scheme for their application was drawn up. But nothing was ever done to carry them out. The state of Macedonia became worse rather than better, and the tyrannies and extortions and outrages from which the people suffered drove them at last to insurrection. But for the action of Britain in 1878, Macedonia might have been as free, as orderly, as peace- ful and progressive as Bulgaria has been since 1878 under her autonomous government. Unhappily, it is easier to do a wrong than to set that wrong right. Britain would willingly set it right now. But, as the old adage says: He that will not when he may, When he will he shall have nay. We find to-day that the selfishness our Government shewed in 1878 is being shewn by Austria and Russia now. Nevertheless, we are bound in honour to persevere, and do our utmost to retrieve the unhappy results of 1878. It is a solemn national duty. IT. This Macedonian insurrection is net an isolated event, nor does it come as a surprise. All the Christian populations that live under Turkish rule would rebel if they saw a chance of success. Things are no worse in Macedonia than they are, and have been for a century past, in Armenia. This rebellion is the inevitable result of Turkish methods of government. So long as these methods continue—and they are incurable—so long as men are not permitted to reap the fruits of their 0%.11 labour, and are murdered when they tly to protect themselves; so long as women are outraged and girls abducted with impunity—so long will the oppressed rise against the oppressor. Some deplorable things have doubtless been done by the insurgents. It is always so. Long-continued brutality and injustice breed a fierce spirit in the sufferers which breaks out in fierce deeds: the violence of their revenge is a messure I of what they have suffered. 111. No scheme of reforms, such as that which Russia and Austria drew up last spring,is of the slightest use so long as the application of it is left to the Turk. The experience of seventy years his shown that he never fulfills his promises, never improves his adminis- tration. The only thing to be done is to get rid of Turkish administration altogether, to turn out their officials and their soldiers, and put the country under a Christian Governor from some European country who is not amenable to the Sultan and whom the Sultan cannot dismiss. To cut the country entirely loose from the Sultan would be better still. but it is for the moment sufficient to remove his direct rule—that will put a speedy end to the existing horrors. IV. The question is not one of Chistians versus Mussulmans. The large majority—two-thirds, or more —of the population is Christian. But the Mussulmans have almost as much to gain by a strong and just ad- ministration as the Christains have, and most of them would (when the passions of war have subsided) wel- come the change. In all the regions that have been severed from the Turkish Empire during the last forty or fifty years—in Bosnia, for example, and in Bulgaria —the Mohammedans are better off than they ever were before.

V. No one doubts for a moment that the Turkish I Empire will before long come to its end, and that its days, in Europe especially, are now quickly drawing to a close. Why should the sufferings of the existing generation of its subjects be neeilessly prolonged? or why should a large part of the existing generation be permitted to be exterminated by sword and famine, as the Turks are deliberately trying to exterminate them by the massacre of women and children as well as of men, by the burning of villages, and driving the 'wretched survivors to die of hunger in the mountains? The number of houses that have been destroyed in the vilayet of Monastir alone is estimated at 12,000, the number of refugees homeless and starving at 72,000. Since it is plain that the Turk must eventually go, the sooner he goes the better. VI. The danger of a European war is con- jured up now, as it was during the Armenian massacres of 1895-6, in order to find an excuse for delay. But the truth is that delay increases the risk of war, because it protracts a situation which becomes more menacing the longer it is left unsettled. It is suggested that Russia and Austria may come to blows over the _ultimate disposal of the Euro- pean dominions of the ;:valtan. If this ever happens—a calamity which may surely be avoided—it will not be brought any nearer by the immediate emancipation of Macedonia from Turkish 4411 e. So far from leading to war, that course will tend to avert a conflict, by remov- ing some of the chief elements of peril and allowing all questions that may subsequently arise to be dealt with more calmly and deliberately than is now possible. The action which Britain, France, and Italy areasked to take will be entirely in favour of a pnrific settlement. ,VII. What is the present ult,ty of Britain, and what ought her policy to be? NV.Jether it will be necessary to use force to compel the Sultan to submit to the en- mancipation of Macedonia a matter on which it is hard to pronounce without knowing more of what is actually passing between Mm and the Powers and be- tween the Powers themselves than we are at this moment permitted to know. lithe Powels, or even a majority of the Powers, act together, be will of course submit at once, as he did at Dulcigno in 1880, under the pressure of Mr. Gladstone's Government, and as he did in Crete a few years ago. If Britain, with the concur- rence of France and Italy, who are believed to be in general sympathy with the policy of emancipation,were Ito take steps to apply force, the Turks would perceive that further resistance was useless. But in the first instance it is obviously the best course to endeavour to avoid the necessity for any recourse to forcible measures by securing the assent of Austria' and Russia. as well as of France and Italy,-to the measures which they I now to be essential, but which they have hitherto been slack in pressing for • that is to say, the withdrawal of all Turkish control from the insurgent provinces and the establishment of an administration independent of orders from Constnntinople. A European Congress has been suggested ;but it is a slow process, and the right solution is so plain to those who have followed the similar cases of other liberated countries that it may be doubted whether a congress is really needed. There are already signs that the two neighbouring Powers, whose backwardness has exposed them to the charge of callousness, are beginning to recognise the need for more drastic action. Possibly this may be in some measure due to the representations believed to have been made bythe British Government, and to the remarkable display of feeling which we have seen in this country during the last three weeks. It may well be that the chilling and timorous evasions of Mr. Balfour's most regrettable letter, with his half-apologies for the Turk, did not represent the maximum of what might be looked for from the Ministry, and especially from the Foreign Secretary. Be thatsus it may, the present agitation can do nothing but good. Let us hold meet- lags; let us send up resolutions; let the will and mind of nation find due expression, if the Ministry are disposed to act firmly, we shall strengthen their bands, and we may trust that the voice of Britain will awaken a responsive echo in France and Italy, and will help to rouse that public opinion in Russia also which I ought to be now, as it was in 1876, a powerful factor I in affecting the action of the Czar.

div.head: THELWALL NUISANCE. Parish Council and "Gross Mismanagement."
div.p: THE THELWALL NUISANCE. Parish Council and "Gross Mismanagement."

At a meeting of the Thelwall Parish Council on Mon- day evening a discussion arose with reference to the "The'wall nuisance." Mr. N. Taylor presided, and there were also present:—Admiral Jones Parry, Messrs. Roebuck, Astall, Houghton, Tuck, Hewitt and \V. B. Cook (clerk). Admiral Jones Parry said the whole affair had been bungled by the Rural District Council, and now they had to pay for it. The total cost of the work was £362 19s. 8d.9 which had been apportioned as follows Thelwall, £l4l us. Bd.; Grappenhall, £56 175.; High- way, £lO7 165.; and Messrs. Long and Son' £56 15s. That did not include the cost of Professor Delapine's report, £lO5, and there was £3B, the cost of printing it. He (the Admiral) had a motion befcre the District Council te resist payment, but as the County Council were paying half the expense he thought it best to drop it. The matter had been dealt with ma very loose way. The County Coun- cil first put it in the hands of Dr. Vacher ; he gave it to Dr. Adams, and Dr. Adams gave it to Professor Delapine, without any instructions whatever from the District Council. Dr. Adams wrote to the Council's Clerk to ask him if he was exceeding his authority in instructing Professor Delapine, and the Clerk replied that he was acting within his authority. Personally he thought that the Clerk was wrong on that point. If Dr. Penny's report had been adopted a lot of expense would have been saved. Again, ths report ought to have gone to the County Council and not to the Rural Council. No one knew how the report came to be printed, but the bill would have to be paid. Professor Delapine said he was instructed to examine and report on the nuisance at the Tannery, but if that was what he was instructed to do, why should he go to the drain in Weaste-lane? The ventilating shafts had been placed one near Mr.Naylor's house and one in front of Mr. Hewitt's house, so that when the wind was in the west the stench would be driven into their houses. The nuisance, despite what had been done, still existed. There were so many different views that they did not know where they were. Dr. Adams, at one time, said the effluvia from the Tannery was the worst in England, and now he said there was no nuisance from the Tannery. The County Council had intended to pay the whole of the cost of Professor Delapine's report,but the Local Government Board refused to allow them to pay more than half. He suggested that a resolution should be passed to the effect that the Council considered the whole thing had been mismanaged. On the motion of Mr. + Roebuck, seconded by Mr Tuck, the following resolution was passed : "That. the Thelwall Parish Council, as representing the inhabi- tants of Theiwall, though they are not in a position to resist payment of the expense allotted to them, think that the interests of the ratepayers have certainly not been considered, and they consider that the whole matter has been grossly mismanaged, especially in regard to Professor Delapine's report. The Admiral remarked that if any of the members wished to see his copy of the report they could do so, but to his mind it was simply a "mass of contradic- tions."
RAINFALLVRECORDS BROKEN.

Allprevious reliable records of rainfall in a year in London were officially broken at noon on Wednesday the total for 1903 up to date amounting to 32 inches, as opposed to the previous best of 31,99, during the whole twelve months of 1879. In every month except February the rainfall in London has exceeded the nor- mal, June heading the list with 6.17 inches—a record for that particular month, and only second to November 1880, when 7.29 inches were recorded.
