div.head: LIBERALISM IN THE KNUTS-
div.p: LIBERALISM IN THE KNUTS-
FORD DIVISION,
THE PROSPECTIVE CANDIDATE AT GRAPPENHALL
Criticism of Mr. Chamberlain's Proposals.
GOVERNMENT'S POLICY CONDEMNED.

The Knutsford Division Liberal Association opened its winter campaign on Wednesday evening with a well- attended public meeting in the Parish Room, Grappen- hall. Mr. C. Jackson Holmes presided and was sup- ported on theplatform by Mr. Alfred J. King, presid- ent of the Association and prospective Liberal candi- date for the division, Mr. A. IT. Crosfield, Captain G.R. Crosfield, Councillor F. R. Roberts, Mr. A. H. Rathbone, Mr. R. H. Owen (hon. secretary),and Mr. Joseph Smith (Liberal agent). Tf-fF. CHAIRMAN'S SPEECH.

The CHAIRMA.N said he thought they must in the first place acknowledge the courtesy of their most esteemed friend the Rector of Grappenhall, for so willingly assenting to the use of the room for that political meet- ing. (Hear, hear.) He was very glad to find that in one respect the Rector was somewhat mistaken. He• told them that they could have the room with pleasure, as far as he was concerned, but he made use of some such expression as " And I wish you joy," intimating that probably they would have no audience at all. He (the speaker) thought that for Grapponhall they were having a very good meeting indeed. (Hear,hear.) The object of the gathering was to introduce Mr. King, who, they expected, when the proper time arrived, would be the adopted Liberal candidate for the constituency, and also to hear a speech from Mr. King on the present political situation. Possibly they woule like to know WHO MR. KING WAS

so he would tell th.Miii -M-r. King was the son of Mr. Alderman King, the father of the Manchester City Council, who had for over fifty years devoted a consider- able portion of his time to public work in Manchester. Therefore, if they had the son of such an able father, it stoke well for the prospects of the division if Mr. King were returned to represent it. There was an old saying "like father, like son" and therefore they would expect Mr. King to possess the same amount of business capacity as his father in regard to public matters. At the present time they seemed to be rather in a muddle. They did not really know who was the leader of the Conservative party. At Sheffield they had Mr. Balfour wildly clinging to office and declaring that as long as he was the reteitecl leader of the Conservative party he , would lead. On the other hand, they had the Conserva- tives claiming Mr. Chamberlain as their leader. Let them look a little nearer home, and see if they could ascertain who was the leader as stated by the present member for that division. The honourable member for that division held a meeting at Stretton last, week and declared he was a follower of Mr. Chamberlain. A follower of Mr. Chamberlain in these days simply meant protection and retaliation. Protection meant Toryism and Toryism meant legislation by a few of his aristocra- tic friends who had thehonour of occupying places in the gilded chamber. Referring to the proposed tax on corn Mr. Holmes said there was no doubt an impression abroard that if they levied such a tax it would enable labourers to obtain higher wages, but he thought that if they looked into the matter closely they would find that was hardly the case. (Hear,hear) lathe immediate district there was some land which • would probably yield a luxurious crop. But who received the benefit-of it? He contended that the money simply went into the pockets of the landlord, who because he was so fortunate as to own the land was enabled to obtain a higher rent. The labourer he ventured to state, would not receive any higher wages on the rich yielding farm than on the poor farm. At - the next election they would have before them in that division a very stiff fight indeed. They had a tremendous majority to turn into a majority on the other side. That could not be done simply by attending meetings, but they could win the seat if all the electors made a:determined effort on the day of the poll. They must ffot only vote themselves, but they must each induce a friend to vote for the Liberal candidate. That constituency would then, instead of returning one of their aristocratic friends whose interest lay so much in the land, be represented by a gentleman engaged in commercial pursuits, who would be much more in tonch with the electors at large than the Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton. (Applause.) MR. KING AND CURRENT POLITICS. THE FISCAL QUESTION.

Mr. A. J. KING then addressed the meeting. He said that was the third year during which he had had the honour of holding the office of President of the knuts- ford Division Liberal Association and not until that night had he had the pleasure of making the acquaint- ance of the Liberals in that part of the division. The division covered a large area and contained a great num- ber of polling stations, many of which were very difficult of access. Grappenhall had been chosen as the place for the opening of the winter campainn, in connection with which twenty-four meetings had already been arranged. At the present time there seemed to be no end to the making of speeches, and when one read Mr. Chamberlain's speech' at Glasgow, and the replies which had been made by Lord Spencer, Lord Rosebery, Mr. Asquith, Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman, Mr. John Morley and a host of others, it struck one as being useless for any ordinary mortal to attend a meeting I and try to find anything fresh to say. At the same time, he thought they would agree that it was useful to have those meetings, as they gave oppor- tunities for Liberal to meet Liberal, to encourage each other, to strengthen theirpolitical faith, and to impress upon each other what to his mind w is almost a religions duty—that every man in the division should take an interest in the political questions at present before the country and do his best to see that the representation of the division was somewhat altered t the next ' election. Mr. Chamberlain had told them that the election was to be fought on one issue. They were all prepared to discuss his fiscal proposals to the utmost of their power,and to meet argument by argument, if not abuse by abuse. But he thought they should also make up their minds that they would not have the elec- tion fought upon that one issue alone, or upon any one I issue. They had enough of a single issue election and its results inl9oo, and they could not afford to allow the record of the Government during the past eight years to pass from the memory of the people. They were told at the last election that everyone who voted against the Government was a traitor, and that every. vote given against the Government was a vote for the Boers. They had indications that Mr. Chamberlain thought that cry was even yet not exhausted. In the course of a speech the other day to the miners at Cupar he spoke of protection as "that which some people called protection but which he pre- ferred to call patriotism." It was not a big step from that to tell them that everyone who did not vote for Chamberlainism and protectionwas a traitor. That was the kind of argument they might have to deal with in the coming election. As Lord Spencer. said, Mr. Chamber- lain was perhaps the ablest man and certainly the cleverest tactician and the best platform orator they Igid at the present day, but he was also a man who, if he made up his mind that a certain object was to be attained, was utterly reckless and unscrupulous in the methods he adopted to attain it. The Government, contended the speaker, no longer retained the confidence or represented the opinion of the country. Alluding

to • THE TERRIBLE STATE OF THINGS IS MACEDONIA., Mr. King said they sometimes complained in this country of the tax and rate collectors, but what would they think if they lived in a country like Macedonia where the taxes were farmed out? There a Pasha paid a certain sum to the government and was sent into the country to screw. all he possibly could out of the population. Instead of collecting the tax on a fixed basis the Pasha came down and valued the farm pro- duce and told the owner that he wanted half of it for taxes. If he did not get it he not only seized the man's property but had the power to inflict the grossest out- rages. The -Macedonians had at last risen into open rebellion and the result was that the Sultan pouredmore troops into the country with undisciplined bands at their !heels to perpetrate outrages on the popu- lation. We were told that owing to the masterly performances of our war organization in South Africa England held a position of greater prestige in the continent of Europe than she ever held before. Mr. Balfour, however, voiced the sentiments of the nation in regard to the Madedonian crisis by giving a philosophical discourse on what he calledthe balance of criminality and he came to the conclusion that the balance of criminality was on the side of the rebels. He (the speaker) did not think the premier voiced the feelings of the Christian population of this country. (Applause,) Mr. King proceeded to criticise the Government's EDUCATIONAL LEGISLATION.

He did not think it ;as—in-accordance with the wishes of the majority of the people that the voluntary schools should be sup Ported entirely out of the public funds without public control, that the School Boards should be abolished, and that the privilege of the women of haying direct representation on the educational government of the country should be done away with. 'When they remembered that more than half the children and three-fourths of the teachers were girls, was it not right that women should have an equal representation On the school management? The one point which above all condemned the Act in the eyes of Liberals and Non- conformists was the imposition of religious tests upon what was now a great branch of the civil service. (Applause.) It was to remedying the great defect. of the educational legislation of the past two years that a Liberal Government, when once in office would have to direct its first attention. He did not think Mr. Balfour represented the enlightened opinion of the country OD
THE DRINK QUESTION. During the past year or two the magistrates—for the greater part Conservatives—had awakened to the fact that they had the power, which they were at liberty to

exercise, of refusing to renew a licence at the end of the year if they considered it was not required in the interests of the surrounding population. In a few instances the magistrates had exercised that discretion. Consequently the drink trade went up to Mr. Balfour in a state of panic, and the Premier promised at the first opportunity to bring in a Bill to give the brewers and public-house owners a permanent property in their annual licences. He (the speaker) believed that one of the main objects which had induced Mr. Balfour to patch up this rem- nant of a Government and meet the House of Commons next year, was that he might have the opportunity of making a bid for the drink interest by br i inging n a Bill to permanently endow the trade with property in annual licences. Mr. King also maintained that the in- creased value of ahouse created by a monopoly ought to be brought into the public coffers. (Applause).

Speaking a the RECKLESS AND EXTRAVAGANT EXPENDITURE incurred by the Government, Mr. King pointed out that when the Liberals went out of oflice in 1895 the Budget was about 95 millions per annum. The Budget for this year was 143 millions. The Governme,nt had increased the expenditure of the country on a police footing by something like 45 million per annum, they had added 160 millions to the national debt, andhad brought down the price of consols—which was the standard of the credit of this country—from 11,2 to below 87 a few weeks ago and 89 at the present time. The speaker pro- ceeded to call attention to

THE FISCAL PROPOSALS. Mr. Balfour, he observed, said he was not at the present ' time prepared to tax food, but his reason was not because he did not agree with the tax in principle but because he thought the country would not stand it. If he thought the country would stand it he would go as far as Mr. Chamberlain. As further evidence of the fact that it was Mr. Chamberlain's programme they had to deal with Mr. King quoted an article from "The Times." Many members of the Government,he contiriued, would support Mr. Chamberlain, but as long as they were in the Government they were obliged to confine themselves to Mr. Balfour's official programme. The member for that division, however, did not feel himself hampered by any such restrictions, and supported the whole programme of Mr. Chamberlain. The Hon. Alan de Tatton Egerton said" the colonies were our empire, and had we not got to consider them ?" One would suppose that the 42 million people in the United King- dom might also be included within the borders of the empire. (Laughter.) The total white population of our self-governing colonies was only about 11 millions, and the inhabitants of British descent numbered only 8 millions. Why, asked the speaker, should the colonies suddenly become so disloyal as to leave us and break up the empire, unless we gave them a 2s. preference on corn? In 1893 the colonies showed their loyalty by sending us the best of their men to help us out of that horrible mess in South Africa, into which the bungling of our ministers had got us. (Applause). Why were they loVal in 1899 when there were no preferential tariffs? They were told that the Liberals worshipped the fetish of Free Trade. He was glad to say the bulk ' of the Liberal party believed in Free Trade as the VERY BEST POLICY FOR THE HOME COUNTRY. They also believed it would be the best policy for the Colonies if they could see their way to adopt it. It was because in the past the country had adopted the Liberal policy towards the Colonies of giving them complete fiscal freedom that they were loyal to us. It was by continuing that policy only, that they would remain loyal in future. Mr. Chamberlain told us that our trade was going to pieces and was being destroyed by the protective tariffs of other countries. (A Voice: " And it is, right enough.") They were not going to deny that in certain markets it was getting more and more difficult for 113 toexport our goods. Foreign countries kept up their duties and we could not get in. In spite of that, our general trade and prosperity were increasing in a most remarkable manner, and the pro- posed remedy would be ten times worse than the disease. (Applause.) Mr. King emphasized the advan- tages which England obtained by means of the" most favoured nation" clause which was inserted in our treaties with mostcountries. We were in abetter posi- tion than any other country in Europe to send goods into protected countries. Alluding to the IMPORTS OF MANUFACTURED GOODS the speaker said a very large proportion of them con- sisted of goods which we ourselves could not by any possibility produce. Something like £20,000,00 worth of timber in the various stages of manufacture was imported each year and this, the speaker contended, was all to the benefit of our building trade. The amount paid in wages in the building trade for the building and rebuilding of houses was estimated at £17,000,000 per annum. There were other imports which, though manufactured goods, were still in themselves raw materials for other industries in this country. It was complained that the manufacturers of steel and iron in its cruder forms were being beaten out of the market by the 4" damping," of raw iron from America and Germany. He did not think that was so to the extent that they were told but in any case it was to the benefit of the machinists and people who manufactured goods from iron in this country. So much so, that the Germans were complaining that they could not compete with England and other countries in the manufacture of machinery for exportation, because we were able to buy German-made iron cheaper Mandl() Germans themselves could obtain it. Mr. King also instanced how in his own business he could bufGerman bleaching powder at £3 per ton whereas the Germ ins had to pay £3. The speaker then dealt with the argument that Vies consumer would not have to pay a tax on corn. He W`l a large consumer of wheat and flour in his business and prior to June 1901, when the shilling tax was about to be levied he received letters from the gentlemen who supplied him with wheat, starch, and flour, informing him that on June let he would have to pay an extra Bs. 4d. or whatever the amount was for the goods.A 2s.duty in itself would only make a differerce of about a farthing on a 41b. loaf, but there were other causes always at work to lower or raise the price of flour. The speaker showed that if the price of flour were increased by the duty and the other causes, the Icost of 'a 41b. loaf might soon be raised id. If we began with a 2s. duty we would not stop there very lon.. In 1883 France began with the is. duty on corn and it had been raised by degrees to about 12s. In support of his contention that the consumer paid the tax Mr. King said that if they compared the price of wheat in Paris and Berlin with the price in London they would find that within a few pence the difference was the amount of duty which had to be paid for the corn to go into France and Germany. People said what a terrible thing it would be if, so long as we depended on foreign countries for food, one of the countries quarrelled with us and cut off the supply: At the pre- sent time we gathered our food from all quarters of the globe. Under Mr. Chamberlain's scheme instead of getting them from America and Russia we should obtain all our supplies from our own colonies. When we were at war with a great European nation all that colonial, , food in British or Colonial ships, by international law would be contraband of war, and LIABLE TO BE SEIZED. At the present time, when food was corning in from America or Russia so long as those countries ware neutral and were not engaged in a war in which we were engaged, they would take care that their neutral ships came to this country with food stuffs. To his mind the circumstances of the country in case of war would be infinitely more disastrous if we depended en- tirely upon our colonies for food. Mr. Balfour said that if we had the power of putting on retaliatory duties we should not need to do so. The other countries would be so frightened that they would give in without in other words, we had to play a game of bluff. Experience showed that the game of bluff did not. pay. If we once began putting on retaliatory duties, the other countries would make their duties still higher. Mr. King quoted figures to show that in a tariff war between France and Italy the trade between the two countries was reduced to less than half its previous quantity and in the end very little was gained. They admitted that the state of things in this country was not in all respects as they would like it to be. The very object of Liberal policy was to be im- proving the conditions and to be constantly bringing in progressive legislation. They believed Mr. Chamber- lain's proposals would make things a great deal worse. They did not believe that any fiscal policy would ever bring about a state of things in which variations in trade would not occur and there would never be lack of employment. Was it not a little dangerous for Mr. Chamberlain to be exciting hopes in the breasts of all those people who were feeling a little down on their luck, and holding out prospects that under his scheme there would never be anyone out of employnient again in this country and tlaat bad times in trade would never come? In con- clusion the speaker asked his hearers not to be carried away by the glamour of the name of Chamberlain and quoted n speech by Mr. Arthur Chamberlain who had declared for Free Trade. He moved "That this meet- ing condemns the past and present policy of his Majesty's Government and declares that the revelations of the War Commission, the Education Act, and above all the fiscal policy foreshadowed by the Premier and ex-Colonial Secretary have destroyed any claim they may have had to the confidence of the country." MR. CROSFIELD AND THE FISCAL QUESTION. Mr. A. H. CROSFIBLD said he had very great pleasure indeed in seconding the resolution which had been moved, and he had particular pleasure in doing so be- cause it gave him an opportunity of supporting his friend Mr. King in the plucky and cheery fight he was making in what was certainly an uphill battle' (Hear, hear). 'He did not iptend to detain them very long in seconding the resolution because Mr. King had really covered the ground so very well that he had not left much for those who followed—(laughter)—and besides it was nothis (Mr. Crosfield's) night out, for he would be on the stump next week and he would have to keep a little bit in reserve for that. (Hear, hear.) Thi fiscal question was undoubtedly a very complex one aril: they had had some useful and interesting illustrations from . Mr. King, but like some other big questions, it had its simple side which might be easily understood cif the people. We heard a great deal now-a-days abofit our export trade and our import trade but we mu4t not lose sight of the home market. (Hear, hear.) THE HOME MARKET was five times greater than our export trade and appos- ing we got Protection—for that was the object view ' of those who were advocating it—then the prices of ' food would rise throughout the country. (Heard hear.) ' The price of clothing would also rise, and ndft only

Field Club. The winter session opened on Friday with an entomological evening at the :Museum Lecture Room. Mr. 'P. May was elected president in succession to Mr. Wotnersley, resigned. In acknowledging the honour Mr. May referred to the good work of his predecessor, and concurred with other speakers in wishing him success in his new sphere of work in South Wales. Mr. W. Mounfield commented . upon the wet and un- favourable season, Which had been not only a hindrance to collecting but a check on the numbers of species of many insects. He suggested that more attention to ' •breeding would throw light on the life histories of the lepidoptera. He exhibited a most interesting set of insects found either in the larval or adult form in con- signments of foreign timber. Mr. Collins exhibited 18 out of the 26 British species of crambus, one of which he had taken for the first time when with the giqld Club in Delamere Forest on August 3rd. Mr. Robin-son • and Mr. Deane briefly described their displays, the latter also calling attention to that of Mr. Howarth, who was himself unable to attend, but whose beauti- fully mounted illustration of the life history of a dragon fly was much admired. Messrs. L. Greening, C. White, and J. Moore Murray took part in the dis- cussion and congratulated the exhibitors on the beauty and neatness of their work. The club is evidently very much alive, and its work of enriching the collec- tions of the Museum is being admirably fulfilled.

div.head: DECISION OF THE RIVERS COMMITTEE.
div.p: THE DECISION OF THE RIVERS COMMITTEE.

The report of Sir John Wolfe Barry on the proposals of the Manchester Ship Canal Company was read and considered at a meeting of the Rivers Committee. it was resolved (1) That the Committee offer no objec- tam to the proposals of the Company to construct a river diversion at Lower Walton, with a lock and sluices therein according to the plan submitted, provided they are satisfied that such work will have no injurious effect upon the river. (2) That the proposal that the Corporation should provide the Company with the necessary funds for the construction of the above works be not entertained. (3) That in the opinion of this Committee if the above works are carried out it will be necessary to divert the sewers now discharging into the liver, and that the cost of such diversion should be borne by the Company. (4) That if the appeal in the action of Crogleld and others v. the Ship Canal Company be not proceeded with the Company should pay the Corporation's costs as between solicitor and client. (5) That subject to terms and conditions being settled to the satisfaction of the Com- mittee, they see no reason why the Corporation should not exercise all the influence in theirpower to support the Company's Bill in Parliament. It was further resolved that the Town Clerk be in- structed to arrange for a joint meeting between the members of the Rivers Committee and the traders and manufacturers of Warrington ; and that the Town Clerk be authorised to consult his Parliamentaryagent on the steps to be taken to secure the interest of the Borough in the event of the Company's proposals being agreed to.

div.head: JOINT MEETING YESTERDAY.
div.p: JOINT MEETING YESTERDAY.

• A. joint meeting of the Rivers Committee, manufac- turers and traders .was held at the Town Hall yesterday. The Mayor (hir. J. Charlton Parr) pre- sided. The recommendations of the Rivers Com- mittee were unanimously agreed to, subject to the company's obligations with reference to the river, under the earlier acts and agreements being extended to the proposed works. A. conference between the members of the Council, the manufacturers and traders, and the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal Company will be held early next week when the counter-proposals already alluded to will be submitted te the Ship Canal Company.

div.head: "THE YEOMEN OF THE GUARD."
div.p: "THE YEOMEN OF THE GUARD."
AMATEUR OPERA AT WARRINGTON.
A New Ventura by Members of the Musical Society.

During the 1:1.-L two or three years the Warrington Musical Society has been repeatedly urged, and with increasing vehemence, to break thrOugh the bonds of custom and tradition which have regulated the pro- duction of oratorio and miscellaneous classical music to the exclusion of all else. Not that the work of the Society in this direction has been inferior or dis- pleasing. It has, on the contrary, been uniformly good and has, moreover, accomplished a valuable work in the education and uplifting of the taste for music in Warrington. But Warrington is not Man- chester. This m.ty be a trite saying, yet it explains everything, almost. In a small town there is not the musical public necessary for the full appreciation and adequate support of a 'society. devoted exclusively t 9 the classical in music. It does not appeal to everyone —even to the majority—and, with a longstanding in- debtedness, it devolves upon thA Warrington Musical Society to cater more for the crowd than heretofore.

In the" Examiner " we have on several occasions in recent years urged the necessity for an excursion in- to the realm of light opera, and we are delighted at the brilliantly successful -experiment a number of the members of the Society have einbarkd upon this week. The Gilbert and Sullivan operas may be re- garded as classics in the distinctive region they occupy, and the selection of" The Yeomen of the Guard " for stage production did not therefore mark, in our opinion, any sacrifice of ideals on the part of the members of the Society concerned. On the contrary-, the performances of Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, this week, have been of the highest order both musically and dramatically. The project has, moreover, been the means of two very important discoyeries—first, that light opera is. immensely popular, and secondly, that there is in the. ranks of the Society itself; a store of vocal and histrionic talent hitherto undreamed of. When the opera project was first mooted there was much openly- expressed doubt as to the capacity of the members of the' Society to . carry the thin, through without pro- fessional aid, but as rehearsal Followed rehearsal all such doubts were gradually dispelled, and the per- formances themselves have done all concerned the greatest possible credit.. In fact, opera whether light - or serious is now destined to figure largely in the future work of the Society's members. The "Yeomen of the Gaard" is one of the most popular and pleasing of the celebrated works of Messrs. Gilbert and Sullivan, and is is too well-known to call for much description here. The story itself is concerned with the intertwined fortunes of the strollin; players Jack Point and Elsie Maynard, and those of Col. Fairfax. It is tyoioal of W. S. Gilbert's magical art that Jack Point, the merriest of jesters, should .in the sequel be found to be the saddest of men, for in him is centred the tragedy of the story of the opera. It is a clever conception, and wedded to Sullivan's tuneful, catchy music, we have in "The Yeomen of the Guard," a most fascinating combination. The cast is as follows :
Sir Richard Chnlmandeley (Lieutenant t my. J. W. Bibby of the Tower) ...
Colonel Fairfax (under sentence of death)
Afr..l, Rabbit,
Sergeant. Meryll, (of the Yeamen of the }. Mr. F. Fieldhouse. Guard) Leonard Meryll, (his Son)... Mr. „F Callon, ..Inn,
Jack Point, (-a sti-ollintr_ eiter)
Mr. C. P. Gattgh.

Wilfred Shadbolt, (Head jailor and I 11Ir.W.H. Wallington.* Assistant Tormentor ... t Messrs. A. M. Ker 11 5 Gi bson.T. G.Critchley Mr. .T. Parkinson. Mr. T. J. Knowles. Mr. Dully. Mr. W. Moores. Mrs. Arthur Booth. Miss Mabel Hemm.lntll
The Headsman and Assistants
I • First Yeoman
Second Yeoi unit
First Citizen
Second Citizen ... . Elsie Maynard, (a strolling Singer)
l'hoebe Meryll,(Sergt Meryil's Daittritter
Dame Carruthers, (Rousekeeper to the 1. Miq4 Finny D Jelas Tower)) ... • Kate, (her Niece) ... , Miss Alice Daunt. Chorus of Yeomen of the Guard, Gentlemen, Citizens, &elk

A glance at the dranuctis persorve impresses one with the sense of an "unknown quantity," for not one of the artistes has, to our knowledge, undertaken previously any part in amateur opera. Suffice it to sa3 however, at the outset,that the cast is exceptionally strong in every respect and it is no exaggeration to add that very few professional companies could, in our opinion, produce The Yeomen of the Guard" more efficiently, than has been witnessed this week. Principals and chorus alike are almost uniforp-ly excellent, and it is an unceasing wonder that so much unexpected talent should have been discovered entirely among members of the Society. Could anyone wish, in reason, for a more charming Phcebe Merryll than Miss Mabel Henshall or a sweeter Elsie Maynard than Mrs. Arthur Booth? Could we desire a better Fairfax or a merrier Jack Point that Mr. J. Rabbit and Mr. C. P. Gough? These are the four chief actors and actresses but what noticeable inferiority is there in Mr. Walling- tonas Shadbolt, Miss Emily Jeans as Dame Carruthers, Mr. F. Fieldhouse as Sergeant Meryll, Mr. Bibby as Lieutenant of the Tower, or Miss Daunt as Kate? All are alike excellent. In no captious way may we say that on the other hand the weakest-link in the chain of principals was undoubtedly Mr. J. Callon jun., in the part of Leeward Meryll. He. certainly, both vocally and dramatically doos not rise to the possibilities of this small part. The curtain rises to disclose a pretty scene on Tower Green with Pho3be seated in the fore- ground spinning. She .sings demurely the snbdued and plaintive ditty "When maiden loves she sits and sighs, &c.," and from this point on- ward the whole performance goes with an admirable and inspiring swing. Miss Henshall makes a hit straight away, and the charm of her singing and acting is felt throughout the piece. Her piquaacy, ease, and naturalness, together with her clear and tune- ful vocalization, are remarkable in one so inexperienced, and there is no doubt the Society possesses in her a potential operatic star of no insignificant magnitude. Her great opportunity comes in the ballad" Were I thy bride," which she sings to her lovesick and uncouth suitor, Wilfred Shadbolt, the while dexterously relieving him of his jailor's keys in order to procure the escape of Fairfax. The rich humour of the situation,. and Miss Henshall's pretty acting, were fully appreciated and a recall enthusiastically demanded by the audience. Later, when the obtuse Wilfred consigns Phcebe to the care of her supposed brother,Fairfax disguised as Leonard some delightful solo and concerted music is heard. This leads on to the impressive scene heralded by the tolling of the bell of St. Peter's, and culminating in the awe-inspiring spectacle of the headsman and his assistants grimly awaiting the prey which ne'er becomes their's. Fairfax's high capabilities as a vocalist are demonstrated, in the ballads "Is life a boon ?" and "Free from his fetters grim," both being sung with exquisite feeling. He well merits the encore accorded to both, and again he distinguishes himself by the fine declamation shewn in his wooing of Elsie. Mr. Rabbit is one of the surprises of the opera, and the Society need look no further for a principal operatic tenor. Elsie and Point make a dual entry and achieve a dual success. The singing-farce of "The Merryman and his Maid" not only ingratiates them with the crowd of .citizens and others on Tower Green, but with the audience also, who manifest marked approval of the refrain "Heighdy ! heighdy ! misery me." Mrs. Booth sang and acted brilliantly throughout. For "0 weary wives, who widowhood would win "there was each evening a vociferous and well-deserved encore, and in such items as" 0 mercy! thou whose smile has , shone," and" A suppliant at thy feet I fall." Mrs. Booth sang and acted with deep expression. Point is one of the most difficult of parts for the amateur to attempt 1 and it is much to the credit of Mr. Gough that he sue- ceeded wholly and admirably. His einging,dancing and acting were at once entertaining and cleverand brought. out most touchingly, the pathos of the part. " Oh !. ' a private buffoon is a light-hearted loon" was a num- ber especially well sung, but he probably pleased the audience most when in conjunction with Wilfred he sings in the duet and dance "Oh! what a tale of Cock and Bull." For this they were twice recalled, and the crisp rendering of the orchestral parts in this entranc- ing item must not be overlooked. The jester also has a ' great opportunity in the trio between Placebo, Elsie,and Fairfax, where he manceuvres lo dexterously and sue- cessfally for a kiss from his companion. Finally, poor Point ceases to jest, suggesting dramatically the tragedy to which the incidents of the opera tend, and in the last scene after relating his tale of woe to the melody "Heighdy,'Heighdy, misery me, lackaday dee !" he falls heart-broken to the ground in the midst of the chorus of saddened onlookers. Tn Mr. W. H. Wallington the opera has a splendid Wilfrid,who is engaged inthe"assist- ant tormenting "—of Phcebe—from beginning to end. He was assourfaced and unemotional as a jailor should be, and it is due to say that his clever imperson- ation received cordial recognition. Mr. F. Fieldhouse made a gallant Sergeant Meryll who could sing and act well when occasion demanded. Along with Dame Carruthers, Fairfax and Kate, he shared in the hearty applause which greeted the well known madrigal "Strange adventure! maiden wedded, to a groom she's never seen." Dame Carrutherswas excellently personated by Miss Jeans who is primness and sedateness itself un- til she woos and captivates thellittle-enamoured Meryll. This gives opportunity for an oddly-contrasted duet which was smartly. sung. Miss Jeans was encored, too, for her solo, "When our gallant Norman foes," ending with the refrain, "The screw may twist and the , rack may turn." Mention must be made of Mr. J. W. Bibby who was a most appropriately lordly and com- manding Lieutenant of the Tower, with a vocal capacity suited admirably to the occasion. The chorus of yeomen, gentlemen, and citizens of both, sexes was always intelligently engaged in buttressing, as it were, the work of the choruses actors and actresses. Many of the ciruses were highly effective and meritorious, a fine sensation of

climax being often reached as in the closing of the first I act. The orchestra, though incomplete, from the fact ' that the brass wind instruments were eliminated, repre- sented in some respects a happy combination. For though theloverture and some of the easentbies lackedthe strength and tone volume necessary for their adequate musical presentment, yet on the other hand there was an undoubted gain of 'daintiness and delicacy in deal- ing with the solo and concerted parts for the principal vocalists. In supplementing the strings and the wood wind, the pianoforte and American organ presided over by Messrs. W. H. Payton and Peter Bate respectively did good service. Mr. F. H. Crossley conducted, and to his skill and tact as musical director is to be largely credited the most un- mistakeable success of this opera venture. At the con- clusion of the opera all the principals were recalled before the curtain and there was also a loud demand for the appearance of Mr. E. Thornley-Dodge the clever stage-manager and dramatic instructor, who shares at least a moiety of the honours of bringing the whole enterprise to so successful a conclusion. The Opera Committee (a sub-committee of the Musical Society), whose labours should also be recog- nized, consisted of Messrs. Bond, Crossley, W. H. Wallington, and J. Newcombe, the latter filling the offices of hon. secretary and hon treasurer.
The performance will be repeated to-night, and we quite expect that the Hall will again he filled to its utmost capacity.

am pleased to hear of the marked manner in which the Labour Representation Committee showed their disapproval of the action of Mr. Plinston in allowing himself to be nominated by the Non-Trading Association, as candidate, in opposition to Mr. Stott, the endorsed candidate of their committee,by requiring him to resign the position of chairman, and T. hope the members of affiliated societies will follow the business of the committee closelyin future. I think the action of the Non-Traders in running a candidate in opposition to Mr. Stott coupled with their statement that they will spare no expense to ensure his(Mr. Stott's)defeat, is open to severe criticism by the workers:of Warrington It clearly indicates to my mind that the Non-Traders are determined that labour shall not be directly repre- sented on the Council,ancl it behoves the working-classes to seriously consider the situation before they decide to give them their support. I myself have been in sympathy with the Non-Trading movement, up to this juncture, but I consider it is now high time to draw the line.—Yours truly, ONE OF THE WORKING CLASS. Letter

div.head: Non-Traders and Dictation.
div.p: The Non-Traders and Dictation.

notice that your comment upon a remark of Mr. Norbury Williams to the effect that the Non- traders hoped shortly to be able to dictate the policy of the Council. This was not the right word to employ and I know that it does not convey the meaning Mr. Norbury Williams had in his mind. The idea wasiandis, that by the elimination of the traders from the Council, and the exclusion of all those who have turned the Cor- poration into a milch-cow at which they have been per- sistently pulling, we shall be enabled to import a new spirit into thePouncil, and thus to mould,guide,or lead its policy. We have had enough, and .too much, of dictation from cliques and coteries in the past; the people will have no more of it from anybody. For the future the policy must be government" of the people by the people, for the penale." Mr. Norbury Williams, lam able to state, entirely concurs in this view and ' repudiates the idea which his words might perhaps Convey that we are seeking to raise up a band of ruth- less "dictators,"—our aim is precisely the opposite.— Yours &c.,
'141714 October 22nd.
JAMES DODDS.

div.head: National Service League,
div.p: National Service League,

Sir,—ln your last issue you state that our shores have never been invaded during the last 1000 years. You have clearly forgotten such items as the invasion by William the Conqueror in 1066, or the invasion of Ireland by General Humbert in 1798. And who will deny that had Villeneuve obeyed his orders instead of going to Cadiz,these shores would have in all probability been invaded by Napoleon? Yet at that period we had a fleet superior to the fleets of all the nations of Europe put together ! To-day our Navy is barely equal to that of any twe powers. That is why we are less powerful than we were 100 years ago. In addition to this you must remember that the duties entailed on our Navy are now far greater than they were 100 years ago. To-day, we import three-quarters of our wheat con- sumption, then we grew all that we required; think of the number of men of war that will be required to en- sure this food stuff being safely brought to these shores in time of war! Then again our Empire is now about eight times the size that it was 100 years ago, necessitat- ing'that our Navy must be split npjfar more than it was in the time of Nelson.

I admit in those times one might have argued with some reason that the defence of this country should be left entirely in the hands of the Navy, but when we remember that even then, with our enormous superiority over other navies, invasion was at one time very near at hand, are there not stronger grounds for saying that to-day when we have not got that :suneriority, invasion is still more possible if we are to rely as von say we must, on our Navy and on our Navy only? Yet in case you call for other testimony let us refer to what" the three Admirals Report " said. They stated that," there 'should always be an effective reserve squadron, absolutely confined to home waters, sufficient to hold the Channel and protect the coasts and com- merce of the United Kingdom." To this the lords of the Admiralty replied "This would be impossible." Can anything be simpler or plainer than this? Can anything show better that if we are relying on our Navy and on that only to avoid all possi- bility of a raid or invasion, we are Indeed insecure? If ' you reply that all European nations love us so much that we canrely on their never going to war with us, it is futile for us to con- tinue this discussion further; but if you admit (and this is all I want you to do at present) that we are not as secure as we ought to be, then I should like to have the opportunity of proving to you that, of the several remedies that suggest themselves, the one put forward by the Iv ationnl Service League is the most just, simple and effective one.

One, word more. The fact that the Swiss have great natural barriers makes it less necessary for them to undergo prolonged military training; that it does not abolish the necessity for some training is evident, or why should they train? Similarly, because we are surrounded by the sea it is not necessary for us to go through the same training as Germany and France; but, as I have shown above, we are relying too much on this barrier, and must add to its effectiveness in the same manner as the Swiss have done to their mountains. —I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
. G. R. CROSFIELD (Captain). Hon. Sec. Warrington Branch, N.S.L.

div.head: Non-Trading Inquiry Meeting.
div.p: Non-Trading Inquiry Meeting.

Sir,—l have no desire to rush into print as to my views on the non-trading inquiry. I would get to work so as to ascertain whether there is any reality in the charges made or hinted at in such strong language by members of the Non-Trading Association.o have gener- ally found that public agitators seem unable to avoid going to extremes and are apt to think that strong anguage is equivalent to powerful argument. Mr. INorbury Williams' personal attack on the commissioners appointed by the Consign was, to say the least of it, in. very bad taste. We hafe always treated him as a gentleA man and an able man of business and at our meetings he has reciprocated our courtesy. But I find there is another Norbury Williams, who likes to say spicy things in public to tickle the ears of people who like to be thus amused, or in theatrical phraseology he likes playing to the gallery. His allu- sions to myself were comparatively mild and inoffen- sive, but even here, his tendency to be smart, led him Ao exaggerate. I never used the word neutral or neutrality in the conversation referred to. I did say in reply to some remarks of his. "It is important that this inquiry should be proceeded with at once. I thinlc the town has suffered enough already by this long delay. With regard to ourerepiesentin. the Council on what you call the opposite side, ebeg to say that I have never taken sides. My desire was, when this appointment was put to me—as I felt it was also my duty—to.come to it with an open mind. I have not come here merely as a delegate of the Council but as a man prepared to make an impartial examination into this business; and if there is anybody to blame, to fix the blame." I think Mr. Williams has unwittingly borne testimony to the a,ppro- piateness of my appointment. I presume his ideal of a model commissioner is, that of a furious partisan who only looks at one side of a question and is resolute not to see the other. The sneer- ing attack on Mr. Jolley may be smart electioneering, but if Mr. Williams can reconcile it to his conscience as a Christian gentleman, he is not the manl have taken him for. I have known Mr. Jolley for many years. I have reason to believe his political faith is the opposite of mine. But I cannot help admir- ing a man who has always devoted so much of his leisure to working for the public good. I have never before heard Mr. Greening spoken of but as a clear business man, who when he was in the Council attended to his duties with an unobtrusive manliness which might with advantage be imitated by those who try to depre- ciate him.

And now a word or two as to the stoppage of the inquiry. Why will the Non-Traders persist in making false statements? Their organ the "Times" asserted two weeks ago that we. the Council Commissioners, insisted on every word of the inquiry being reported

and printed, yet we‘have again ancragain,declared that we want nothing printed or reported, but what is dis- tinctly pertinent to the inquiry. We have repeatedly said that there may be days, and even possibly weeks, when there may not be a word to report. But we mutually agreed at the outset that should anything transpire that even a minority of the Commissioners considered important, a shorthand note should be taken of it. And why, I would ask, did Mr. Williams and his colleagues, at our first meeting, agree to advertise; at once for a competent shorthand writer, the tenders to be in at our next meeting a few days later? Nay, more,why did they agree with us that it was necessaryithe ; Town Clerk should be asked toengage a special reporter for the said next meeting,when we were to decide whose tenders should be accepted? And we are now in this. ; position. We have tenders from nearly a "dozen respect- ; able business firms who have been waiting six weeks for our decision. If, as Mr. Williams now says, we ar- not likely to require their services for the next six months, ; why have we thus fooled them? At our last meeting, we urged our Non-trading colleagues to stop this jingling of words and let us j have the books in and get to work, instead of thsting time talking about it. We are as anxious as they are to save expendi- ture for we each of us will have to pay a fair share of it, but we will not risk sacrificing eificiency. Justa word as to the -supposed legal threat in our letter to the Mayor, which seems to have got on :qr. Williams' nerves. Strangely enough I meant it as likely to operate in a contrary direction, knowing the bitter- ness aroused on account of costs incurred in a certain action at law; there might be a keen desire to retaliate Bat .to Mr. Williams' reading of the paragraph as meant to intimidate anybody, we give a most emphatic denial. In conclusion our friends had better re-consider their decision and let us get to work. We will take care that no needless expense is incurred. Time is short with me but I am jealous for the honour .of my native place, and having put my hand to this work, I want to see it through. Faithfully yours,
T. MitCHALL.

div.head: Mr. John Maginn and the Non-Traders,
div.p: Mr. John Maginn and the Non-Traders,
A Challenge.

Mr. John Maginn addressed a largely-attended meeting of electors of St. John's Ward in Brick-street Mission Hall, on Thursday evening. Mr. W. H. Chandler presided and read a letter from Mr. Wm. Furness, who formerly represented the Ward, regretting his inability to attend as he had an engage- ment in London. "I believe" he wrote "that the majority of the intelligent and thoughtful electors of the Ward will record their votes for you. One cannot help but admire the independent stand you have taken. It is demoralizing to the municipal life of a town and also to its representatives when they are told that they cannot be trusted unless they receive the stamp and are approved of by a certain section, whose sole aim now seems to be to keep the town in a ferment Although they had received the consent of the Council to an inquiry, they now decline to go on with it, giving reasons that are illogical and untrue. We can only con- clude, as hinted by one of their members, that the ulterior object and purpose nowlis to turn the agitations to political account." In the course of his'address the CHAIRMAN criticised the policy of the Non-Traders. He contended that Mr. Maginn fought:the last election in a straight-forward manner and took his defeat like a gentleman. (Ap-- ' plause.) • Mr. MA GINN at the outset said he fought the last election without personalities but he found that courtesy to the Non-Traders was like giving pearls to swine. They had attacked him by all the unseemly and ungentlemanly means possible. It was now time for him to take off his coat, and he was going to do so. (Applause.) Mr. Magian then referred to the needs of the ward which he described as the worst treated Ward in Warrington. , Streets which had been made from 15 to 19 years ago remained unpaved. He advocated a circular tramway route to pass through the Ward instead of the present direct service from the Cemetery to the Central Station. Speaking of Corporation contracts, he expressed himself strongly in favour of giving work to local firms. He went on to deal with the inquiry ques- tion. He himself was a Non-Trader as far as justice and fair play in the Council were concerned, before the party was thought of, -and he was a Non-Trader still. He believed that every man who entered the Town Council was entitled to fair-play only, and a Councillor wno took advantage of the position he held as a Councillor to secure an unfair advantage over his opponents was not entitled to be in the Council. He was not, however, prepared to blackguard everyone whether they were good, bad, or indifferent, and call all people heathens who did not belong to his class of party. The party calling themselves Puritans and Non-Traders did not want an inquiry. They arranged eleven con- ditions and said they would have an inquiry on those lines and no others. He contended that they drew uP way yto of a these rules wtth no other purpose than to put* a stumbling note of the proceedings, Mr. Maginn considered referred to the inquiry from beginning to end. The shorthand ui inquiry was commenced inside closed doors—a sort of modern-inquisition. When they found it v:as doubtful in- quiry. nThible ingeblalouscke jinn the regard whether they would have sufficient victims for the Sta,,,,ta,e to burn, the Non-Traders said they would not hold b"- inquiry and they would tell "these gulls, the rate- payers "that it was in the interests of economy that they refused to proceed with it. Mr. Maginn contendea that an inquiry should be held in open court and that the press and public should be present. There shoald be one judge—a gentleman who, like Ctesar's wife, w 35 above suspicion who was learned in municipal laws and customs and had no interests either as a trader or non-trader or in the old or new Council. Such an inquiry would cost the town nothing at all- " I insist "said Mr. Maginn "on the inquiry being held on sensible lines or on their lines. If they are so anxious to save the ratepayers' pockets I make them this offer :—We hold an inquiry immediately on the lines that the Non-trading Committee laid down, and to save the town the expense that they suppose it will cost them, I John gaginn, will be .£5OO towards the inquiry, if any non-trader in the town will be ,t543° against me." (Loud applause). Mr. Maginn entered upon a criticism of the speeches made at last week's Non-Trading meeting and in conclusion sail they would never find him belonging to a clique or party. He would asan independent man support any party,any Councillor or any section of the Council that he believed was honestly, faithfully and judiciously working for the benefit of the town and of the whole community. (Applause.) He held no brief for Mr. Henry Roberts or anyone else and he wanted no one to assist him ex- cept the voters of the ward. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. HANDS, seconded by Mr• RARBITT, a resolution pledging support to Mr. Maginns candidature was unanimously passed. I Fire at the Baths Hotel.

An outbreak of fire occurred at the Baths Hotel on Tuesday evening but fortunately the flames were extinguished before any serious damage was done. At about seven o'clock, Miss G-ittens was in her room when the gas flames ignited the curtains. • She called for assistance, and a number of men in the vault; helped to put out the flames. The fire brigade turned out with the reel cart, but their services were not required. The window frames were blistered,and the carpets and dressing table damaged by fire and water.

rr 0 THE CIPAL ELECTION. 1903. ELECTORS OF FAIRFIELD WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, I have been requested to become a candidate to re- present your Ward in the Town Council at the next Municipal Election—and after serious and thoughtful consideration I have consented and now beg respect- fully to offer my services and solicit you, support and vote. I have had experience in Municipal work. having been a member of the tcwn council of St. Helens and served on the most important committees and only resigned that position a year after I came to reside in Warrington. lam not a member of any Political organization. nor am I a member of your local Non-TradingAssocia- tion, but I am in full sympathy with them in their effort to purge the Town Council of all that is legally or morally wrong. and would support them in their policy of Economy and Reform. In moving about your Ward I notim several matters waiting attention Most of your streets are insufficiently lighted, and many of your roads are in such a condition as to cause much annoyance to those people !who have to use them, and if selected would lose no time In bringing tha matter to the notice of the responainle committee. I have no axe to grind, and no personal ends to serve. but would deem it an honour to serve you and do all that lies in my power to promote the welfare of my native town. If you honour me with your confidence I will en- deavour to do all I can to serve your interests to the best of my ability. I remain .Your Obedient Servant, JAMES POVEY. 11, Springfield-street, Warrington.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE HOWLEY WAR D LADIES AND GENTLEMEN,— it is now over 9 years since you first elected me as one of your representatives in the Town Council,and as my term of office will soon expire, I have been requested to again allow myself to be nominated as a candidate at the forthcorninjelection on the 2nd November. After careful consideration I have decided to accede to that request, and now be.t to offer myself for election again on IND tiPENDICNI: LINES. During my connefttioa with the Council. I have served on the follow!ng committees :—Sanitary Works, Gas. Water, Electricity. Tramways. Rivers, Cemetery, Gymnasium and General Purposes, and have acted as Deputy-Chairman for 6 years and Chalrmtin for two years of the Sanitary Works Com- mittee. Deputy Chairman for 3 years of the Water Committee, and Deputy-Chairman for 5 years and Chairman for 3 years of the Cemetery Committee During this period these Committees have met on 1,227 occasions, on which I have been present 1,124. The Council has also, in the same period, held 135 meetings. I have attended 129. In addition I have attended numerons sub-committee meetings,of which no record has been kept. Thase figures should afford a sufficient guarantee that I have, not neglected my duties as one of your representatives, and may fairly claim to have some knowledge of requirements of the town and of the Howley Ward in particular. If it should be your pleasure to again elect me, I shall continue to discharge my duties as assiduously as in the past. I beg to remain, Yours faithfully, JOHN EVANS. Church-street.

TMUNICIPAL BLBCTION. 1933. O THE ELECI'ORS OF ST. AUSTIN'S WARD LADIES ASD GENTLEMEN. At the request of a large body of ratepayers of this ward. I have consented to allom myself to be nominate as a candidate to represent you in the Borough Council. I am an old Warringtonian, a ratepayer and em- ployer of Labour in your ward and I trust suffi- ciently well-known to gain your support. I consider your representat.ve in the Council should be just, without fear, or favour, and have no axe to grind. lam in favour of a full and impartial inquiry without further delay as to the trading of the Council for the last few years The sanitary conditions, improved lighting and better paving of the town generally and your Ward in particular would have my careful attention. I would support the fair wages Clause in all con. tracts. The widening of Warrington Bridge to facilitate the heavy and growing traffic requires prompt attention. The streets already under improvement require finishing as soon as possible to enable a through tramway system. The rates undoubtedly are too high for a town tbf. size of Warrington and while I believe in efficiency it would be my constant endeavour to obtain the best results at the most economical cost to the ratepayers.
